en: One should construct an alchemical laboratory (rasaśālā) in a place free from all disturbances, situated in a delightful region abounding in all medicinal herbs and provided with a well. (Rcūm 3.1)
In the beautiful quarter of the Yakṣa king Sahasrākṣa,
it was provided with various implements and adorned with a magnificent wall.

"What should be done and where in the alchemical hall? One should install Rasabhairava in the eastern part of the hall; fire-related activities in the southeast, and stonework in the south. (Rcūm 3.3)
In the southwest, one performs rites involving weapons; in the west, rites such as washing;
in the northwest, drying; and likewise, in the north, the rite of piercing.
One should establish the perfected substances in the northeast corner;
the collection of materials should be made for the purpose of accomplishing the elixir.
In the alchemical laboratory, there are furnaces for precipitating the essence, beautiful crucibles for heating, earth-furnaces, movable furnaces, and numerous water-vats. (Rasārṇava 3.6)
Likewise, a pair of bellows should be placed at the neck [of the furnace] made of bamboo or iron;
and there should be vessels for gold, tin, bronze, copper, stone, and clay, as well as those made of leather for the workers in hide.
One should collect all the various implements:
the churning stick, the grinding stone, the mortar, and the circular troughs. (Rcūm 3.8)
There are iron mortars heated red-hot and pestles of the same kind,
provided with thousands of fine holes for the purpose of agitating the substances.
A winnowing basket, mats for protection, stones, a small pestle, and a mortar;
crucibles, clay, husks, cotton, forest wood, gravel, and flour.
The threefold medicine consists of that which is derived from minerals, living organisms, and roots; likewise, there are fire, cow-dung, sugar, and white sugar-candy.
Small jars and cups made of glass, iron, clay, or cowrie shells;
winnowing baskets and vessels of bamboo; and small, quick-acting conch-shell trumpets.
Razors, as well as combs, and whatever else is appropriate there;
a comb-case, an ear-cleaner, and a small knife for cutting vegetables. (Rcūm 3.13)
Indeed, all that is useful there— whether it be the work ending with the cooking of juices for the purpose of sweeping the halls,
or anything else— is accomplished by means of the supreme knowledge.
Having consulted with Śrīrasāṅkuśā, one should collect everything;
otherwise, Bhairava seizes the splendor residing therein.
The *cālinī* is said to be of three kinds, and its essential nature is now described:
it is fashioned from bamboo slips and strung together with threads. (Rcūm 3.16)
That [pestle] is always praised as beneficial for grinding coarse substances;
furthermore, another pestle made of bamboo is also used for the purpose of stirring powders.
It was fashioned from the fibers of the karṇikāra, śālmali, and pārijāta trees,
joined together with a width of four finger-breadths, and was auspicious.
Another type of churn is wide with a jeweled ring, wrapped in goat-skin, its base covered with horse-hair cloth. (Rcūm 3.19)
With that [brush], one should perform the cleansing in order to remove even the most subtle dust.
Charcoal refers to the remains of fire; it is considered that *kokila* is another name for charcoal.
And those embers are called *kokilās*; they are extinguished without water.
*Upala*, *piṣṭaka*, *chagaṇa*, *chāṇa*, *upala*, and likewise *utpala*—these are synonyms for cow-dung cakes. (Rcūm 3.21)
*Karaṇḍa*, *upalasārī*, and those called *saṃśuṣkachagaṇa*;
*kūpikā*, *champikā*, *siddhā*, *golā*, and *karaṇḍikā* [are synonyms for a small bottle]. (Rcūm 3.22)
*Caṣaka*, *caṣakā*, *kaṭorī*, *vāṭikā*, *ghoṭikā*,
as well as *kacolī* and *grāhikā*— these are indeed synonyms with a single meaning. (Rcūm 3.23)
Regarding the type of physician to be employed in the work of alchemy:

"Physicians well-versed in the *Rasasaṃhitās*, those who know the *Nighaṇṭus* (lexicons), commentators (*vārttikas*), and those who understand the languages of all regions—these too should be recruited by the practitioners. (Rcūm 3.24)
One who is most righteous, truthful in speech, learned, a worshiper of Śiva and Keśava,
compassionate, and lotus-handed— such a person should be employed in the science of alchemy (rasavaidyaka).
One who holds in his hands the banner (*patākā*), the jar (*kumbha*), the lotus (*pāthoja*), the fish (*matsya*), the bow (*cāpa*), and the mark (*aṅka*),
with the ring finger resting below his own body-mark, shall possess the hand of immortality (*amṛtahasta*).

A physician who lacks instruction, is devoid of compassion, greedy, bereft of skillful methods, one who leaves black streaks [on the skin], and whose hands are scorched— such a person is to be avoided.
Indeed, at the conclusion of the digestion of the elixir, one should always cause the Aghora mantra to be recited;
the attendants should be diligent, pure, brave, and strong.
Those who know the mantras for the forms of spirits should be employed in the accomplishment of treasure;
they are powerful, full of courage, red-eyed, and dark-complexioned.
And those spells for terrifying beings should be employed in the accomplishment of the bali offering;
[the practitioners] should be free from greed, speakers of truth, and worshippers of the gods and brahmins. (Rcūm 3.30)
Those who are self-controlled, eaters of wholesome food, and wealthy, generous givers provided with all necessary implements, should be employed in the practice of *rasāyana*. (Rcūm 3.31)
Those auspicious ones are constantly devoted to the words of their guru in the alchemical practices; they know the names of various medicinal herbs, are pure, and are free from deceit. (Rcūm 3.32)

Those who know the various languages of different regions are considered fit for the collection of medicines—provided they are pure, truthful in speech, endowed with faith, and high-minded. (Rcūm 3.33)
For those whose minds are free from doubt, the *rasa* is perfected; otherwise it is not.
When the *rasa* has been perfected through the eighteen rites, he is the supreme practitioner (*sādhakottama*).

Having said, "This is the great elixir," one should consume that essence elsewhere; thus the mortal becomes perfected in the elixir—a giver and an enjoyer, not a beggar—freed from old age, honored by the world, possessing divine luster, and always happy. (Rcūm 3.35)
Rcūm 4.1: Somadeva speaks this technical terminology of mercury for the awakening of ignorant physicians, as it has been proclaimed by perfected scriptures.

Half of the perfected mercury (siddharasa) is the portion for oil and ghee; the eighth part is for the linctus (leha); likewise, the seventh part is for all well-prepared iron powders, pills (vaṭaka), and so forth.

That which is given to the best of physicians by those afflicted with disease, after invoking Dhanvantari for the attainment of total health and happiness—that is declared to be the Dhanvantara portion. (Rcūm 4.2)
The eleventh share, which is taken from merchants by physicians as a portion for medicines purchased, is indeed called the *rudrabhāga*. (Rcūm 4.3)
That physician who, having greedily seized a portion of the patient’s wealth, administers improper medicine with a covetous mind, shall be a betrayer of trust. (Rcūm 4.4)
In the scriptures, purification is prescribed even for those who have committed the murder of a Brahmin;
however, for men who betray trust, there is no purification except through death.
The mercury, ground with mineral substances such as sulphur and others that are free from moisture, until it becomes very fine and resembles collyrium, is called *kajjalī*. (Rcūm 4.6)
The seven excellent substances ground together with mercury-paste are known as "mercury-paste" (rasapaṅka).
Then, one part of butter-paste, equal in measure to the juice of *arka* flowers, and half a *niṣka* of *gandha*, should be ground bit by bit in a mortar with a pestle;
under the intense heat of the sun and with warmth, that paste will take on the form of butter.
Having ground mercury together with sulphur and milk in a mortar, it attains the state of a paste (*piṣṭatā*) through this grinding; that is considered *piṣṭī* by others. (Rcūm 4.9)
A *pātanapiṣṭī* is a paste prepared with mercury and one-fourth part gold; that *pātanapiṣṭī* bestows the supreme accomplishment of mercury. (Rcūm 4.10)
The term *kṛṣṭī* refers to silver or gold that has been processed with mercury, sulfur, and other such substances;
for it is indeed produced many times over from gold and silver. (Rcūm 4.11)
Gold-dust is cast into gold; its color is not diminished by that gold-dust.
The seed made from gold-dust serves as the coloring agent for the mercury.
Having repeatedly cast molten copper combined with *tīkṣṇa* iron into a solution of *lakuca* fruit mixed with *gandhaka*, the excellent metal (*varalohaka*) emerges. (Rcūm 4.13)
*Svarṇaraktī*:
gold that has been colored red by it is called *svarṇaraktī*. When cast into molten gold, it produces an excellence of color.
And the *rañjanī* of Tāra also effects the coloring of the seed-syllable.
In this very way, the beautiful *tāraraktī* should be prepared;
it indeed dyes silver and also dyes seeds. (Rcūm 4.15)
The *dala* of the Moon and Fire is that other metal which has been processed with mercury bound by *mṛta* [mercury] or with another metal;
having attained whiteness or yellowness, that *dala* is indeed well-known as belonging to the Moon and Fire. (Rcūm 4.16)
White and yellow petals,
combined with mercury bound by *ābhāsakṛta*,
and processed with another metal— that indeed becomes white and yellow petals. (Rcūm 4.17)
Pure iron, struck with copper seven times and then refined, becomes lovely; likewise, iron struck with stone, when repeatedly refined, becomes [excellent] nāga.
Then, having placed two palas of that pair and two palas of the ash of *tāpya* into a crucible, one should heat it firmly seven times.
That is called "non-maternal" (ayonija), which effects the transformation of the body and metals;
by means of mercury, its pill is prepared in the sāraṇā apparatus. (Rcūm 4.20)
Held in the mouth, it destroys urinary disorders entirely;
it produces firmness of the teeth and a vision like that of a vulture, as well as other eye diseases and ailments arising above the collarbone. (Rcūm 4.21)
Copper killed with *mākṣika* [sulphur] ten times and re-extracted,
and likewise purified lead— these two together, four *palas* each. (Rcūm 4.22)
When blue antimony has been struck [with mercury] seven times and rises up again, this is indeed proclaimed as the perfected *śulbanāga*. (Rcūm 4.23)
When administered by that lord of elixirs and held in the mouth of men, it destroys the entire array of urinary disorders within a mere month. (Rcūm 4.24)
By eating wholesome food for a year, one becomes free of graying hair along with wrinkles, gains the keen vision of a vulture, possesses radiant nourishment, and is endowed with complete health.
When iron is cast into another metal, heated, and quenched in a liquid, it becomes pale yellow in luster; this is designated as *piñjarī*. (Rcūm 4.26)
The portions of the moon are sixteen, and likewise the sun has twelve;
because they are rotated together as one, it is called "Candrārka" (Moon-Sun).
If another metal is cast into the metal to be processed through the blowpipe,
that which is described by physicians as *nirvāpaṇa* is indeed called *nirvāhaṇa*. (Rcūm 4.28)

The substance to be added (kṣepya) is the "carrying-away" (nirvāhaṇa) substance; it is equal in measure to that which is to be carried away (nirvāhya). The substance to be sown (āvāpya) is likewise [equal] to that which is to be sown (vāpanīya), and in the case of a specified portion, it is like the specified [portion].
That which floats upon dead water crosses over; for that indeed is iron that floats upon water.
When dead iron is rubbed between the thumb and forefinger, it enters into the various lines [of the hand]; that is designated by the name *rekhāpūrṇa*. (Rcūm 4.31)
Combined with molasses, guñjā seeds, pleasant touch, honey, and clarified butter, it does not return to its original state through heating; thus it is called *apunarbhava*. (Rcūm 4.32)
When base metal (niruttha) is smelted together with silver, it does not adhere to the silver;
then that iron is called "base metal" (niruttha), as it is incapable of being transformed back again.
In this way, if silver together with lead is smelted and does not adhere to the copper,
then it should be considered by the best of physicians to be "niruttha" (useless) and ineffective as a coloring agent.
When, through a specific process of cultivation, that [seed] becomes a particular letter—
soft and possessing diverse refinements— it is called a "seed" (*bīja*). (Rcūm 4.35)
This indeed has been declared by the physicians to be the means of crossing over:
the destruction of one metal through the striking together of two mixed metals.
From blowing [the breath] through a curved tube, that is declared to be "striking" (tattāḍana).
Powdered *dhānyābhraka* mixed with rice and bound in a cloth within sour gruel (*kāñjika*), when it has been extracted from the cloth through rubbing, is called *dhānyābhraka*. (Rcūm 4.37)
When a mineral is treated with alkaline, acidic, and liquefying agents and blown in a furnace, the essence that emerges from it is designated as *sattva*. (Rcūm 4.38)

When the crucible is filled with *koliśa* [mercury] and, through the process of heating, the *koliśa* reaches the neck of the crucible, it is considered "one-peak *koliśa*" (*ekakoliśikha*). (Rcūm 4.39)
Charcoal (a synonym) is called *śikhitrāḥ*, *pāvakocchiṣṭāḥ*, *mṛtāṅgārāḥ*, *kokilāḥ*, *kṛṣṇāṅgāḥ*, and *koliśāḥ*; these are its mutual synonyms. (Rcūm 4.40)
For liquefaction and the falling of the essence, madhuka and khadira wood are auspicious;
for upward extraction, those made of bamboo are used, while for sweating, bādara wood is auspicious.
That mercury which is extracted from [mercury] situated within a machine called the *vidyādhara*, having been rubbed with the juice of fresh ginger,
is said to be "extracted by means of cinnabar" (*hiṅgulākṛṣṭa*). (Rcūm 4.42)

Bell-metal (kāṃsya) that contains a small amount of tin, when struck with a blowpipe, releases the tin; indeed, that copper from which the tin has been released is called "attracted by sound" (ghoṣākṛṣṭa). 4.43.
Twenty palas of pure *guhyakanāga* (antimony) are made into a paste; it is ground with the milk of a female goat and smeared with realgar (*manaḥśilā*). (Rcūm 4.44)
Having enclosed it within a pair of earthen bowls, one should cook it using the "boar's pit" (kroḍapuṭa) method;
one should carefully cook it that many times until ash is produced.

Having thoroughly rubbed that [substance] with jaggery, guggulu, guñjā, clarified butter, and sāragha honey, one should then seal it inside a crucible; then, having raised it again by means of heating— Rcūm 4.46.
Then, having again applied mercury measured by a *pala* using the edge of a discus, one should smear it with the juice of white *arka* and with realgar as well. (Rcūm 4.47)
One should indeed administer twenty measures of mercury using the gajapuṭa method;
for with each application of the naga-puṭa, one should certainly effect its elevation.
One should thoroughly drench it ten times with the liquid of blue light; thus is the lead perfected, remaining in a quantity of one karṣa. (Rcūm 4.49)
This excellent mercury-elixir has been proclaimed by the one known as Guhyanāga;
when a single *niṣka* of this nāga is added to a *khārī* of molten iron, [the result is gold]. (Rcūm 4.50)
He certainly swallows a golden probe a hundred thousand times his own size;
he certainly vomits up that gold heated in safflower oil. (Rcūm 4.51)
This secret path has been indicated; Svacchandabhairava declares:
"O Varanaga, [the substance] combined with sharp blue collyrium, when firmly blown [upon] many times, [is effective]. (Rcūm 4.52)
That which is soft, black, and melts quickly is called the excellent nāga;
the re-emergence of one who has died is termed "raising" (*utthāpana*). (Rcūm 4.53)
*Ḍhālana* is considered the pouring of a liquid substance into another liquid;
it is [the process involving] *capala* produced from lead (*nāga*).
A *nāga* weighing thirty *palas*, rubbed with the milk of a *bhānu* plant, [is effective].
One should grind it and then subject it to *puṭa* firing until only one *karṣa* remains;
even with a thousand *puṭas*, it will never undergo depletion.

This [mercury] produced from nāga is designated as *capala* by the commentators; likewise, that which is produced from vaṅga is *capala*. Thus, *capala* should be prepared from vaṅga as well, without a doubt. (Rcūm 4.56)
The mercury that is merely touched by a hand that has been touched by it becomes bound;
such mercury is recommended for alchemical transmutations of metals (*dhātuvāda*), but not for rejuvenation (*rasāyana*).
For this [preparation] has been proclaimed by the Lord of the World named Kharpaṇa:
take fine *bhrāmaka* and *aśmarī* powder, combined with one-fifth part of mercury. (Rcūm 4.58)
One should grind it for one day with the root-water of the *kumārī* plant,
and also for one day continuously with the juice of *cāṅgerī*.
In this manner, one should rub it with lead purified by earth for three days;
then, with one *pala* of lead and an equal amount of tin.
One should prepare a smooth paste with ten *niṣkas* of *rasendra* (mercurial essence), and having combined it with the medicinal powder (*kalka*), one should then triturate it as before. (Rcūm 4.61)
Then, having made a paste with the essence of the best mercury and the essence of the metal, one should combine it with the previous paste as before. (Rcūm 4.62)
Having kindled a fire, one should dry it with warm *kāñjika* vinegar,
and [dry] half a *pala* of purified mercury with roasted *guñjā* juice.
Having triturated it with fermented rice-water (kāñjika), one should prepare pills the size of black pepper;
then, having placed them in a *vajramūṣā* crucible and secured the seal at the joint, one should close it up. (Rcūm 4.64)
One should indeed blow [the furnace] properly with nine bellows and two bellows-bags;
then, having gathered the essence situated within the crucible from all sides.
One should heat that essence ten times in an open crucible using a blowpipe for purification, together with ashes and salt. (Rcūm 4.66)
Having wrapped it in sour gruel (kāñjika) using the method of a sealed packet (puṭayoga), one should dry it;
then, with two niṣkas of the previously mentioned ash, [one should proceed]. (Rcūm 4.67)

Having blown upon the naga [mercury] multiplied eighty times, one should indeed cause it to be extinguished; by this much, that previously prepared elixir is certainly not digested in any way whatsoever.
This [mercury] has been designated as "capala" (fickle) by Śambhu, the Lord of the World;
yet even with this, the mercury is quickly bound, as before, with ease.
Indeed, when that [mercury] has been processed ten times with the powder of the roots of *kāravallī*,
it becomes liberated from the serpent and consumes its prey entirely.
The mouth [of the crucible] should be open in the *mūṣā* (crucible) to be exceedingly superior in quality;
for this mercury, having its digestion completed, becomes the maker of the body and of iron.
This has been stated with extreme certainty by the illustrious Somadeva. (Rcūm 4.71)
Washed with water and the excrement of earth-crawling serpents, its impurities are removed; indeed, that which has become black in color is called *dhauta* by the alchemists. (Rcūm 4.72)
The mixing of two substances by means of heating is proclaimed as *dvaṃdvana*;
the addition of silver and other metals to base metals such as copper or gold is called *anuvarṇa*.
*Bhañjinī* is considered by the proponents [of this system] to be either a reduction of syllables by means of petals or a *bhañjinī* [itself].
*Pataṅgī*.
From the paste of *pataṅga*, the state of silver and gold is produced in iron.
Having remained for some days, that dye fades away; it is known as *palikā*.
The *pataṅgīrāga* [is described as follows].
When it is colored by mercury from metal through heating over a long period of time,
that which emerges is designated as *pataṅgīrāga*.
When other substances such as iron are cast into a molten material, that which is thus added is called *āvāpa*; it is also considered *pratīvāpa* and *ācchādana*. (Rcūm 4.76)
When the metal has melted and fire resides within it, one should pause for eight *nimeṣas* and then sprinkle water; this is declared to be *abhiṣeka*.
*Nirvāpa* is the casting of what has been heated into water; it is both *nirvāpa* and *snapana*.
[The time for *pratīvāpa* and so forth.]
The addition of medicinal additives should be performed when the molten metal is perfectly pure.
When the sacrificial fire blazes with radiant flames accompanied by white smoke,
that time should be known as *śuddhāvarta*, occurring at the departure of the living being.
When a flame resembling molten metal is seen during the blowing [of the bellows],
this state of being ready to melt is called *bījāvarta*. (Rcūm 4.80)
"Cool to one's own body" (*svāṅgaśītala*) refers to that which is cool while still situated within the fire; this is what is called "cool to one's own body.
"Cool on the outside" (*bahiḥśītala*) [refers to that which is cool once it has emerged].
And the cold drawn from fire is called external cold. (Rcūm 4.81)
Indeed, the cooking of [the mercury] placed in a *dolāyantra* with alkaline substances, acids, or medicinal herbs is called "sweating" (*svedana*); it causes the loosening of impurities. (Rcūm 4.82)
Grinding with the prescribed medicinal herbs along with all acidic substances and sour gruels (kāñjika) constitutes the process called *mardana* (rubbing), which destroys external impurities.
*Ūrchana* is that which, by means of prescribed medicinal substances for rubbing and kneading, causes the disappearance of the *piṣṭatva* (pulverized state);
indeed, that *ūrchana* destroys the *kañcuka* (impurity) of tin (*vaṅga*) and the other metals. (Rcūm 4.84)
Regarding *naṣṭapiṣṭa*:

that which results from the destruction of the essential nature of mercury (*sūta*) and its subsequent reduction to a paste is called *naṣṭapiṣṭa* by the wise, for it has been utterly defeated. (Rcūm 4.85)

That which brings about the restoration of one's own nature through the application of heat, sunlight, and so forth is called "reviving" (utthāpana); it destroys fainting and physical affliction. (Rcūm 4.86)
The extraction [of mercury] situated within a vessel—mercury that has been rubbed with the aforementioned medicinal herbs—upwards, downwards, and sideways, is called *pātana* (falling down);
it destroys the impurities (*kañcuka*) produced by contact with tin and lead. (Rcūm 4.87)
The retention for three days of a liquid extract mixed with water and rock salt inside a jar is called *rodhana*, which is a type of non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpanī*). (Rcūm 4.88)
Restraining is said to be that sweating which is applied to the pot for the sake of stopping the restlessness of the [mind] that has attained vigor through confinement. (Rcūm 4.89)

Combined with minerals, stones, roots, and so forth, and placed inside a jar for three days for the purpose of the "meal" (grāsa), this process of heating is considered by the wise to be *dīpana* (stimulation). (Rcūm 4.90)
The measure of the mercury being swallowed, consisting of the substance to be swallowed, is stated as "this much";
that which is thus described is called *grāsamāna*. (Rcūm 4.91)
*Jāraṇā* is the movement of the *grāsa* (the morsel) into the womb and likewise its liquefaction;
thus has *jāraṇā* been described as having three forms by the excellent commentators. (Rcūm 4.92)
The mouthful (grāsa), the lump (piṇḍa), and the transformation (parīṇāma)—these three are known as the supreme [stages].
Furthermore, digestion (jāraṇā) is twofold: with face (samukhā) and without face (nirmukhā). (Rcūm 4.93)
The mouthless digestion (*nirmukhajāraṇā*) is said to be [performed] by the addition of seed (*bīja*) in the proper proportion; this is the digestion of the seed (*bījajāraṇā*).
Pure gold and silver are designated as "seed."
{Mukha/Samukhajāraṇā}:
The addition of seed [mercury] in sixty-four parts is called the "mouth" {mukha}; this is the "mouthed essence" {samukharasa}.
When this is done, the mercury becomes possessed of a mouth, greedy for the morsel.
"He becomes capable of even devouring hard metals;
this indeed is called 'direct digestion' (samukhā-jāraṇā) by Mṛgacārin. (Rcūm 4.96)
He who possesses the face of a *rākṣasa* and,
through the application of divine medicinal herbs, remains with his internal organs manifest,
consumes all metals and other substances; he is the one with the face of a *rākṣasa*.
*Cāraṇā* is considered to be the casting of the morsel of mercury into the mouth;
it is *garbhadruti*.
The liquefaction of that which has been swallowed within the womb is declared to be *garbhadruti*.
Having indeed liquefied external substances such as *ghanasattva* and the like externally,
for the purpose of digesting (*jāraṇā*) them by the Lord of Mercury (*rasendra*), that is called "external liquefaction" (*bāhyadruti*). (Rcūm 4.99)
Non-stickiness, fluidity, luminosity, lightness, and union with mercury— these five are the characteristics of *druti* (liquefaction). (Rcūm 4.100)

When metals, minerals, and the like are constantly maintained in a liquid state through the application of husks, grains, and so forth, that process is proclaimed as *druti* (liquefaction). (Rcūm 4.101)
*Jāraṇā* is the transformation of the swallowed [substance] into a liquid state through the application of *viḍa*, mechanical devices, and so forth;
it is called *jāraṇā*, and its varieties exist by the millions. (Rcūm 4.102)
With alkaline salts (*kṣāra*), acids, fragrant substances and the like, and likewise with potent urines—
for the sake of digesting the swallowed essence— that is proclaimed as *viḍa*. (Rcūm 4.103)
Indeed, *rañjana* (coloring) is proclaimed to be the production of a yellow or other hue in mercury by means of the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of well-perfected seeds, minerals, and so forth. (Rcūm 4.104)

*Sāraṇā* is that which, when gold and other substances are cast into a vessel containing oil and a mechanical apparatus, increases the process of *vedha* (penetration) in the metal; it is thus proclaimed as *sāraṇā*. (Rcūm 4.105)
Indeed, when a liquid mixed with penetrating medicinal substances is cast into a substance, it is called *vedha* by those who know it; and that is remembered to be of many kinds. (Rcūm 4.106)
The varieties of piercing (vedhabhedāḥ) are:
the ointment (lepa), the casting (kṣepa), the spear (kunta), the one called smoke (dhūmākhya), and the one designated as sound (śabdasaṃjñaka).
[The first is] the ointment-piercing (lepavedha).
By means of this ointment, one makes iron, gold, or likewise silver [into gold].
That should be known as *lepavedha* (smearing-penetration); and here, *puṭa* refers to the *saukara* (pig-shaped) crucible.
*Kṣepavedha* (throwing-penetration) is the act of casting [the agent] into molten metal; that penetration is designated as *kṣepa*. (Rcūm 4.108)
*Kuṇṭhavedha* is that which effects the state of gold and so forth by means of the extraction of liquefied substances using mercury held with tongs; it is called *kuṇṭhavedha*. (Rcūm 4.109)
*Smoke-penetration* (*dhūmavedha*) is said to be the production of gold and other substances within a metal by means of the smoke of a liquid cast inside when the fire is smoking. (Rcūm 4.110)
*Śabdavedha* (piercing by sound) is proclaimed as the production of gold and silver from a small amount of base metal through smelting with mercury held in the mouth. (Rcūm 4.111)
*Udghāṭana* is the removal of impurities and the like from pierced substances by means of mercury (*sūta*), as well as the manifestation of its color; that is declared to be *udghāṭana*. (Rcūm 4.112)
When [a substance] is sealed within a vessel together with alkaline and acidic medicinal herbs, and buried in the ground with great care, that is proclaimed as *svedana* (sudation). (Rcūm 4.113)
When the vessel containing mercury mixed with medicinal substances is sealed with great care and placed within a furnace constantly supplied with fire, that process is called *saṃnyāsa*. (Rcūm 4.114)

{The virtues of sweating and resting} These two— sweating and resting— are certainly the producers of the qualities and powers of the king of mercury (rasarāja), as well as the bringers of rapid pervasion. (Rcūm 4.115)
Somedeva, having extracted jewels in the form of most lucid technical definitions from the great ocean of the *Rasāyanasaṃhitā*, has with great effort composed this necklace;
let the foremost of physicians wear it around his neck for the sake of adornment in the assembly. (Rcūm 4.116)
One who has studied this chapter on the alchemist should recite it;
performing the works of alchemy, he shall not be deluded anywhere. (Rcūm 4.117)
Now, having thoroughly examined numerous systems of alchemy, Somadeva shall hereafter describe various mechanical devices in brief. (Rcūm 5.1)
Because mercury is diligently processed by the masters of alchemy to perform actions such as sweating and so forth, it is therefore called a *yantra* (apparatus). (Rcūm 5.2)
Having bound the mercury, together with the medicinal herbs, within a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) using birch bark and a triple-layered cloth,
one should indeed fasten the mercury-pouch firmly to a wooden beam with a cord.
One should ignite the fire beneath it according to the sequence previously described, while [the substance] remains suspended inside a sealed jar within a swing;
this is declared to be the *dolāyantra* (swing apparatus), which is indeed called "sweating" (*svedana*). 5.4.
The *khalvayantra* (mortar-machine) is said to be of three kinds for tasks such as grinding and so forth:
one is made of stone and is free from belching, and the other is made of metal.
The mortar, shaped like a half-moon, is indeed ten finger-breadths in height; its length is equal to one-sixteenth of a finger-breadth (one *kalā*);
it is nine finger-breadths in width, and likewise, it is six finger-breadths deep.
The neck is two finger-breadths wide, extremely smooth, shaped like a half-moon in a field;
the grinding [surface] is ten finger-breadths long—this is what is known as the *khalva* machine. (Rcūm 5.7)
In this [process], five palas of mercury (sūta) are to be ground for purification;
one should purify it in various other mortars according to the requirements of each specific case.
The circular mortar is twelve finger-breadths in width; it is circular,
four finger-breadths deep in the center, and made extremely smooth.
The grinding slab (mardaka) is flat at the bottom and has a handle for easy grasping above;
it is made of iron, nine fingers long, and the mortar (khalva) is six fingers deep. (Rcūm 5.10)
The pestle is eight finger-breadths long; this is indeed called the heated mortar.
Having fashioned the hearth into the shape of a mortar, it should be filled with charcoal. (Rcūm 5.11)
Having placed that [substance] indeed upon its side, one should blow it with a bellows;
therein the paste, combined with alkalis and acids, is to be rubbed. (Rcūm 5.12)
It flows away with extreme velocity due to perspiration; of this there is no doubt.
When made from kāntaloha iron, it becomes ten million times more effective.
The *valabhīyantra* (roof-peg device) consists of a metal vessel with two rings on its sides;
a much smaller vessel of the same kind has its interior fitted through these rings.
Having placed it upon the previous vessel, one should pour it into a small vessel;
then, having filled the large vessel with the thickened liquid and *kāñjika* vinegar, [one should proceed].
One should thus cause it to sweat for two watches (yāmas) for the purpose of awakening the mercury;
this is the *balabhī* apparatus, which is the cause of the excellence of the mercury.
In a vessel made of fine, beautiful material, the essence becomes more excellent.
[The *ūrdhvapātanayantra*]:
it should be eight finger-breadths in measure, perfectly circular, and flat at its base. (Rcūm 5.17)
From four finger-breadths below the neck, it is provided with a hollow channel,
four finger-breadths in width and depth, and firmly bound.
At the base of that vessel's lid, it is sixteen finger-breadths in width and provided with a neck sixteen finger-breadths wide.
Having poured mercury into the first vessel, one should place another vessel inverted over it;
both should be provided with a firm rim on all sides, being elevated above and depressed below. (Rcūm 5.20)
One should pour water into a trough-like basin and ignite a fire beneath it;
this, indeed, is what is proclaimed by Nandin as the *ūrdhvapātana* (upward-falling) apparatus. (Rcūm 5.21)
In the lower vessel of the downward-dropping apparatus (*adhaḥpātanayantra*),
one should place another shallow pan with its opening facing downwards,
its interior surface smeared with mercury. (Rcūm 5.22)
Having cast her into that muddy pit, one should set fire to her head;
this is indeed proclaimed as the "downward-falling" machine (adhaḥpātanayantra). Rcūm 5.23.
One should pour the liquid into a jar provided with a long, downward-sloping tube;
that tube should indeed be inserted into the interior of the belly of another jar. (Rcūm 5.24)
Then, having properly sealed the openings of the two jars with clay,
one should ignite a fierce fire beneath the mercury-pot.
One should pour sweet, cool water into the other jar; this is indeed what is called the *tiryakpātana* apparatus by those skilled in the arts. (Rcūm 5.26)
The three types of *pātana* (precipitation) have indeed been declared as the triad of instruments; for without these precipitations, the mercury (*sūta*) does not abandon its defects. (Rcūm 5.27)
Why is one not liberated from defects by three upward leaps alone?
It is because, upon digestion, [the result] occurs through the division [of the body] due to the conjunction with another substance.
Indeed, various qualities arise from the thorough rinsing of the vessel;
by means of water in the mortar and pestle, the rice grains become free from impurities. (Rcūm 5.29)
Great purification by means of falling alone has been proclaimed by Nandin.
One should place [the substance] in a wide-mouthed vessel filled with water using a tortoise-press (*kacchapayantra*). (Rcūm 5.30)
Having properly prepared a shallow pan and a wide-mouthed vessel, one should construct a basin with feces in the center of that [pan] and pour mercury into its middle. (Rcūm 5.31)
Having applied the feces both above and below, and having diligently sealed it with a *malla*, that which is placed within according to the appropriate application is called a *puṭa*. (Rcūm 5.32)
Indeed, that device known as the "tortoise" (kacchapa) is prescribed for the digestion of mercury;
having fashioned an iron crucible shaped like a brinjal (vṛntāka), which is the intermediate vessel (antarālikayantra).
It should be measured by a span (vitasti), fashioned from beautiful iron or even made of muṇḍaloha,
and placed two finger-breadths below the throat.
One should provide a ring two finger-breadths wide at the middle of the neck;
it is a lid-supporting bracelet as broad as a tamarind leaf.
Having turned the vessel upside down, one should make its opening at the base, with the lid placed inside, the crest [of the handle] intact, and the joints joined together. (Rcūm 5.36)
There, one should suspend this [substance] over the head [of the vessel], having blocked and dried it;
then one should provide the rim of the pot with a *puṭa* that produces fire. (Rcūm 5.37)
Such a yantra, known as the antarālika, should be prepared;
by means of this, one should perform the liquefaction of fragrance (gandhadruti) as well as the internal liquefaction (garbhadruti).
Having made the *tāpikāyantra*— a crucible (*mūṣā*) one cubit in length, firm with clay,
very solid in its middle portion, and provided with a two-finger-wide opening— Rcūm 5.39.
One should place a khārī measure of fragrant substance upon an alloy of iron;
one should fill the crucible on all sides with pure sand.
Then, having placed that [substance] on the hearth and repeatedly adding liquid excrement, one should kindle the fire until its flame is the size of a big toe. (Rcūm 5.41)
One should cause all substances such as iron and mica to be fully digested by the mercury;
this is called the *tāpikāyantra*, which is easy to use for the digestion of mercury. (Rcūm 5.42)

Having placed the substance such as mercury into a *pratigarbhayantra* crucible, and having covered it with gold or other materials in a large vessel (*khārī*), one should then cook it in a furnace over an acidic liquid and substances such as salt; that is the *pratigarbhayantra*. (Rcūm 5.43)
One should very carefully block the *garbhayantra*— a vessel containing a jar (*khārī*) situated within a larger pot—
by either placing earth in the pot or in the jar, and then sealing the object. (Rcūm 5.44)
Having placed sour substances and the like inside and sealed it, cooking occurs in the *garbhayantra* (inner vessel);
[this refers to] the *pālikāyantra*, which is a circular iron cup with a curved tip and an upward-pointing handle. 5.45.
This indeed is the *pālikā* apparatus for the purpose of digesting the *bali*;
it is a water-vessel (*ghaṭayantra*) with a capacity of four *prasthas*, possessing a four-fingered opening.
This is declared to be the "pot-machine" (ghaṭayantra), which is considered suitable for replenishment.
Having constructed a circular pit with bricks and having placed a vessel within it, {iṣṭikāyantra}— Rcūm 5.47.
Having placed there in the center a beautiful brick with a hollow,
one should construct around that hollow a rim (*pālikā*) one finger-breadth high.
Having cast the mercury into the pit, one should place a cloth over the mouth of the pit;
having placed sulfur there, one should seal its opening with a crucible.
Having properly sealed the space between the two crucibles with clay, one should apply a *kapota*-type (*puṭa*) firing using forest stones, but not more than that. (Rcūm 5.50)
This is indeed the brick-mechanism (*iṣṭikāyantra*); by means of it, one should digest the sulphur.
Having placed the *vidyādhara*-mechanism upon a pot and having properly sealed the pot, [one proceeds]. (Rcūm 5.51)
Having poured water into an upper vessel, one should ignite a fire beneath it;
this is the Vidyādhara machine for the purpose of extracting mercury from cinnabar.
The *ḍamaruyantra*:
having placed an inverted vessel upon another vessel and sealed them together, that machine known as the *ḍamaruka* is beneficial for the purpose of producing ash from mercury. (Rcūm 5.53)
One should fashion a pit in the center of the "navel-machine" (*nābhiyantra*) and place mercury together with sulfur therein;
one should construct a wall around the pit, two finger-breadths in height. (Rcūm 5.54)
Then one should properly cover it with a crucible shaped like a cow’s udder,
having sealed it well with clay mixed with water, using a quantity of clay equal to the height of the cavity.
Then, having poured water [into the vessel], one should ignite the fire below; this is called the *nābhī-yantra* by Nandin, the all-knowing. (Rcūm 5.56)
By this, the mercury is digested; it becomes smokeless and pure sulphur when rubbed with a decoction of *barbūraka* like a medicinal paste, using water and clay. (Rcūm 5.57)
Fine dust of decayed iron filings mixed with powdered jaggery is indeed called *jalamṛd*; it is truly impossible to break through with water. (Rcūm 5.58)
By means of "fire-clay"— that is, lime, slate, and brick-dust— rubbed together with buffalo milk,
one indeed obtains "fire-clay" (vahnimṛtsnā), which is truly capable of enduring the heat of a fierce fire.
Blocked by this clay, the mercury is unable to move, just as a man is bound by the mature love of a clever woman. (Rcūm 5.60)
Nandī, Nāgārjuna, and the lord of sages Brahmajyotis—
only Śrī Somadeva knows this, and no one else on the surface of the earth.
The *grastayantra* crucible is described by the wise as one that is enclosed within the belly of another crucible, circular and uniform from top to bottom, and flattened at its base. (Rcūm 5.62)
Indeed, for the purpose of binding the lord of elixirs (mercury), two crucibles shaped like eggplants (*vṛntāka*) have been described by those who know the art of mercury;
specifically, below their necks, there are two [parts]. (Rcūm 5.63)
A tube one span in length, with its joints well-sealed and smeared with clay;
into one end one should place the mercury, and into the other the powdered *gandhaka*. (Rcūm 5.64)
Having closed the openings of the two crucibles, one should place them in a sand-oven (*vālukāyantra*);
one should then kindle a fire below—this is described as the *tulāyantra*.
The *sthālīyantra* (pot apparatus) is prescribed for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of minerals such as mica, talc, and sulphur;
having placed copper or other metals in a pot and sealed its opening with a lid (*malla*). 5.66.
That which is cooked while situated in a pot is called the *sthālīyantra* (pot apparatus).
In the interior of the belly of a large vessel, one should place auspicious sand; this is the *koṣṭhikāyantra* (furnace apparatus). 5.67.
Then, one should place there an unbaked earthen crucible made of clay, measuring one *vitasti* in height and twelve finger-breadths in elevation.
It is six finger-breadths wide, highly polished in the middle,
with a five-fingered lid, a sharp point, and the shape of a crown.
The crucible should be neither too small nor too large, smooth on the outside at the neck;
one should place six palas of finely powdered fragrance inside the crucible.
Then, having placed a three-legged iron tripod that has been made stable,
one should set upon it an iron jar or one made of magnetite (kāntaloha).
Into that one should cast purified mercury measuring twenty palas,
and having processed the mercury with digested sulfur, one should saturate it with the juices of garlic.
Having covered it with the previously mentioned lid using the *adhaḥśikha* [seal], one should effect a joint-seal with lime, clay, molasses, and so forth. (Rcūm 5.73)
When the joints have dried, one should pour sand over them;
then, having sealed the mouth of the vessel, one should ignite a fire beneath it.
For three watches [of the night] it remains harsh; thereafter, the scent arises. That smoke, adhering to the lid, having dissolved, falls into the fluid.
For by consuming the fragrance endowed with these six qualities, the elixir becomes possessed of virtues;
it produces all the distinguished qualities specified in the scriptures.
This is indeed the *koṣṭhikāyantra* as proclaimed by Nandin;
[it is called] the *vālukāyantra*.
Having carefully placed [the substance] into a vessel filled with five *āḍhaka* measures of sand, {Rcūm_5.77}...
The *vālukāyantra* (sand-oven) is described as that in which substances such as mercury-balls (*rasagola*) are cooked;
likewise, by the insertion of salt, it is called the *lavaṇayantra* (salt-oven). (Rcūm 5.78)
Having prepared the incense apparatus, one should take an iron vessel eight finger-breadths wide and eight finger-breadths high;
indeed, there should be a water reservoir at a point two finger-breadths below the neck.
One should insert thin iron needles horizontally, and upon them, one should place thin gold leaves. (Rcūm 5.80)
One should place the smoke, which will be described right here, beneath the vessel;
indeed, one should cover that vessel with another vessel turned upside down. (Rcūm 5.81)
Having smeared the joints with clay, one should ignite a fire below;
by that means, the leaves become blackened according to the prescribed method. (Rcūm 5.82)
The mercury moves with speed, attaining both *druti* and *garbhadruti*,
by means of sulphur, realgar, mica, or indeed by *kajjalī* and dead serpents.
The fumigation of gold leaves is proclaimed as supreme;
for the sake of silver, one should fumigate silver leaves with dead mercury.
And one should fumigate with appropriate primary and secondary juices;
this is called the fumigation apparatus (*dhūpayantra*), used for the transport of substances for the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*). (Rcūm 5.85)
In a large pot, having poured in the liquid and tied a cloth tightly over its mouth, one should place the substance to be sweated therein and cover it with a lid. (Rcūm 5.86)
One should ignite a fire below it; that is the *kuṇḍaka* instrument.
Other wise men call this the *svedana* (sudation) instrument. (Rcūm 5.87)
Alternatively, [one may use] the *kuṇḍayantra*: having placed water in a pot and added grass over its mouth, one should cast the substance to be steamed inside and seal it with a lid. (Rcūm 5.88)
One should ignite a fire below; this is the *kuṇḍayantra* (or *ḍekīyantra*). One should insert a bamboo tube into the hole beneath the neck of the vessel.
Having placed two bell-metal vessels together to form a hollow cavity filled with water, one should join a tube to its opening and ensure that it is firmly fixed. (Rcūm 5.90)
The liquid previously poured into that jar with the aforementioned substances, when heated by fire, falls down from the tube into that water. (Rcūm 5.91)
As long as the entire vessel remains warm, the blending of the juices occurs; this is what constitutes the *ḍhekī* apparatus.
In the *somānalayantra*,
fire is above and water is below, while the collection of mercury is in the middle;
this is called the *somānala* [yantra], which can digest [and assimilate] the elements such as space (*ākāśa*).
The wise one should cook mercury contained within an iron tube, which has been sealed inside a vessel filled with salt; this is called the *nālikāyantra*. (Rcūm 5.94)
Now, the nature of the crucible (*mūṣā*), the clay called *mṛtsnā*, its various forms,
and its application according to the prescribed method are proclaimed by Somadeva. (Rcūm 5.95)
The crucible is indeed called *mūṣā*, *koṣṭhikā*, *kumudī*, *karahārikā*, *pātanī*, and *vahnimitrā* by the alchemists. (Rcūm 5.96)
It is called a *mūṣā* because it steals away (*muṣṇāti*) the defects that are to be stolen;
its material should be either clay or iron. (Rcūm 5.97)

A single *kākiṇī* coin that has emerged from the mouth of a crucible is better than even a hundred thousand [coins] for the proud, when obtained by bowing down before a wicked person. *Raghuvamśa* 5.98.
The application of a sealant (*saṃdhilepa*) refers to the binding and fastening of the crucible and its lid;
likewise, the filling of gaps and the sealing of fissures constitute the joining of the seams. (Rcūm 5.99)
Clay that is sandy, pale, coarse, reddish-pale,
and capable of withstanding prolonged heating is highly recommended for the purpose of crucibles.
And in the absence of that, the Valmiki and the Kaulali [melodies] are proclaimed.
The clay that has been pounded with burnt husks, hemp, lime, horse-dung, and an iron rod is indeed suitable for the purpose of crucibles. (Rcūm 5.101)
White stones, husks, burnt [substances], and firebrands should be combined with hemp-rags, lac, and dross as appropriate, along with clay from a mouse-hole. (Rcūm 5.102)
One should prepare a *vajramūṣā* crucible by taking three parts of clay, two parts of hemp and lac, one part of burnt husks and stones, and half a part of iron dross;
having thoroughly kneaded these together, one should indeed fashion the *vajramūṣā* for the extraction of metallic essences (*sattvapāta*). (Rcūm 5.103)
The *yogamūṣā* consists of soft clay originating from an anthill, mixed with burnt charcoal and husks,
combined with various types of *viḍa*, and smeared with those same types of *viḍa*. (Rcūm 5.104)
The crucible fashioned by her is called the *yogamūṣā*;
the mercury processed with this becomes far more excellent in its qualities. (Rcūm 5.105)
The *vajradrāvaṇa* crucible is made from equal parts of *gāra*, *bhūnāga*, *dhauta*, hemp, and burnt husks;
it is a crucible of the same size, kneaded with clay and buffalo milk.
Indeed, having been boiled for a fortnight and processed in many ways,
the crucible fashioned by her is called the "Vajra-melting" crucible.
A crucible made from black earth, enriched with six times its weight of burnt clay, and mixed with dross, charcoal, and hemp, is called a *gāramūṣā*. (Rcūm 5.108)
A pair of crucibles (*yāmaya*) does not melt due to excessive heating by fire;
it is like a *varamūṣā* crucible.
Charcoal from cloth and husks are equal [in weight], and clay four times that amount [is required]. (Rcūm 5.109)
A crucible made from all these materials ground together with an equal amount of clay is designated as a *varamūṣā*; it can withstand the fire for one *yāma*.

The *varṇamūṣā* is a crucible smeared with earth mixed with the powder of the red group (*raktavarga*) and saturated with the water of the red group; it is further smeared with the *kṣitikhecarī* [earth-moving] compound. (Rcūm 5.111)
That is called the *varṇamūṣā* (color-crucible), and it is employed for the enhancement of color.
Thus, by means of the white group [of substances], the *rūpyamūṣā* (silver-crucible) is proclaimed.

A crucible produced from various types of *viḍa*-clay and smeared with those same *viḍas* is called a *viḍamūṣā*, for the purpose of processing mercury and iron, or for the sake of medicinal formulations. (Rcūm 5.113)
The crucible for the extraction of vajra is made from equal parts of *gāra*, earth, snake-skin, husks, soot, and hemp; it is rubbed with buffalo milk and clay. (II) Rcūm 5.114.
Indeed, having been boiled for only a fortnight, she was described in many ways;
a crucible fashioned from her and smeared with the blood of bedbugs [was used]. (Rcūm 5.115)
When *vajradrāvaṇa* and *krauñcikā* are combined with the roots of *balā* and *abdadhāvanī*, they endure a four-watch fire once they have been processed for liquefaction. (Rcūm 5.116)
When the crucible reaches a state of liquefaction due to the application of heating,
its momentary removal is called *mūṣāpyāyana* (the replenishing of the crucible). (Rcūm 5.117)
In a crucible shaped like an eggplant (*vṛntāka*), having inserted a tube ten finger-breadths long,
it should be firmly joined at the top like a *dhattūra* flower, resembling a flower that is well-adhered. (Rcūm 5.118)
Eight finger-breadths long and provided with a hole, that is the vṛntāka-mūṣikā;
by means of this, one should extract the essence (sattva) from soft substances such as shards and the like. (Rcūm 5.119)
The *gostanī* crucible: that crucible which is shaped like a cow’s teat and has a lid provided with a spout;
for the liquefaction and purification of sentient beings, that crucible is the *gostanī*. (Rcūm 5.120)
The *mallamūṣā* has been described: the *mallamūṣā* is that which consists of a pair of joined crucibles;
it is proclaimed for the purpose of steaming substances such as the juices of *parpaṭī* and the like. (Rcūm 5.121)
A *pakvamūṣā* is a type of earthenware vessel that is sturdy and well-fired;
it is called a *pakvamūṣā* when used for the heating of medicinal compounds (*poṭalī*) and the like. (Rcūm 5.122)
The *golamūṣā* is shaped like a ball without an opening and contains the substances to be fused;
it is called a *golamūṣā* because it quickly confines the substances. (Rcūm 5.123)
That which is at the base of the *mahāmūṣā* (large crucible), shaped like an elbow and gradually widening toward the top,
and thick like a large eggplant (*vṛntāka*), is considered to be the *mahāmūṣā*.
And that [mercury] is for the purpose of roasting and melting iron, abhraka, sattva, and so forth.
The *mañjūṣamūṣā* is a crucible shaped like a chest; it is deeper than it is wide,
and a crucible measuring six finger-breadths is designated as a *mañjūṣā*.
Having buried that crucible in the ground, one should then apply the *puṭa* (heat) on top.
A crucible that is flattened at the base and circular, eight finger-breadths in height,
is called a *muśalamūṣā*; it is beneficial for mercury bound within a wheel.

{The furnace (intr.):} For the purpose of casting down sentient beings and for the purification of those already cast down, there are various types of furnaces; their characteristics are now described. (Rcūm 5.127)
A charcoal pit, one *hasta* in height, half that in length and width,
square, and enclosed by a wall made of clay. (Rcūm 5.128)
On a single wall, one should make a pit equal in width to a span (vitasti),
and a very firm and auspicious door measuring one and a half spans.
Below the threshold, a wall measuring one span (prādeśa) should be constructed as appropriate for blowing [the bellows], and above the upper beam (uttaraṅga).
Furthermore, a door should indeed be made above, measuring one span (prādeśa) in size;
then, having closed the joint of the door with bricks and having smeared it with plaster.
Having filled it with fire, one should blow upon it with two bellows;
one should cast the fire and the blowing materials through the upper opening. (Rcūm 5.132)
One should repeatedly prepare five *golaka* balls for each of the five [metals] to precipitate their essences (*sattva*);
this is the charcoal furnace for hard substances that causes the essence to fall out.
On firm ground, one should fashion an auspicious, circular pit measuring one span; then, in the middle of that, one should prepare another pit. (Rcūm 5.134)
It should be provided with a depth and width of four finger-breadths,
extending from the pit to the edge of the ground, and equipped with a horizontal tube.
One should place upon the central pit a clay wheel, slightly raised on the outside and depressed toward the cavity, provided with five holes. (Rcūm 5.136)
Having filled the crucible with cuckoos, one should blow it with a single bellows;
for this is the "subterranean crucible" (pātālakoṣṭhikā), which causes the extraction of the essence (sattva) from minerals.
The *gārakoṣṭhī* (iron-smelting furnace) for substances to be accomplished by smelting has been described by Nandin as being twelve finger-breadths deep and one span in width.
Four finger-breadths above that, provided with a ring,
one should place a discus (cakrī) possessing many holes upon the ring.
Having placed the ores there, one should heat them in a closed crucible;
this is described as the *gārakoṣṭhī* furnace, which destroys impurities in the metal.
One should construct a firm vessel with a curved neck from clay, measuring one *aratni* in size;
its mouth should be turned downward, and a tube five finger-breadths long should likewise be attached to its opening. (Rcūm 5.141)
That which is called the "crooked tube" (vaṅkanāla) is renowned for firm blowing;
likewise, the "transverse bellows furnace" (tiryakpradhamakoṣṭhī) is prescribed for the processing of mercury and other substances. (Rcūm 5.142)
Twelve finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths at its base, it is called the "horizontal blowing" [tube] and is used for purifying soft substances. (Rcūm 5.143)
{Puṭa (definition)}: *Puṭa* is the designation for the process of cooking medicinal substances such as juices and so forth, intended to bring about their transformation (*māraṇa*).
A cooking process that is either deficient or excessive is not desired; a well-cooked medicine is beneficial. (Rcūm 5.144)

The non-recurrence of impurities in iron and other metals, the increase of its qualities, and its superiority [over others] arise from it; likewise, not sinking in water, being filled with lines, and [the quality of] the *puṭa* come about through it. (Rcūm 5.145)

From the mercury (sūtendra) that has been processed in a crucible, there arises redness, lightness, rapid pervasion, and incandescence; its quality is even superior to that of the metals once they have been liquefied. (Rcūm 5.146)
Just as fire, though situated outside, enters into stone through the application of a crucible (*puṭa-yoga*), so too is it certain that iron attains qualities such as pulverization. (Rcūm 5.147)
In a large vessel, a deep and square pit two cubits wide,
filled with a thousand pieces of wood and stones, one places the medicinal herbs for the *puṭapāka* process.
One should carefully place the obstructed [substance] upon the *piṣṭaka* on the *krauñcī*;
one should then set half a thousand *vanopala*s upon the *krauñcikā*. (Rcūm 5.149)
One should ignite the fire there; this is known as the *mahāpuṭa* (or *gajapuṭa*),
which is square and deep, measuring one *rājahasta* in size.
Then, one should fill it up to the neck with thousands of stones and place therein the *kumudī* vessel filled with the substances for compounding. (Rcūm 5.151)
One should place half as many pieces of *giriṇḍa* as there were of *chagaṇa* previously;
this is declared to be the "elephant-sealed" (*gajapuṭa*) method, which bestows great qualities.
In this manner, when the sacrificial pit is one aratni in measure, the *puṭa* is called "vārāha."
A *puṭa* on the surface of the earth that is two *vitastis* in height and as wide at its base is known as a *kukkuṭaka-puṭa*.
That which is placed on the ground in the shape of a pigeon’s beak using eight forest pebbles is called a *kapotapuṭa* for the purpose of calcining the powder of raw mercury. (Rcūm 5.155)
Govara (the definition: a type of cow-dung) is dried, powdered cow-dung trampled by the hooves of cows within a pen;
that is designated as *govara*, and it is declared to be the most excellent for the preparation of mercury.
A *govarapuṭa* is that in which a sealed vessel (*puṭa*) is provided with either cow-dung or husks; this is prescribed for the successful preparation of mercury ash (*rasabhasma*). (Rcūm 5.157)
When a thick vessel filled with husks and provided with a crucible in its center is subjected to heating by fire, that is called *bhāṇḍapuṭa*.
The sand-pit is indeed covered above and below by *krauñcikā* plants,
where that sand-pit consists of heated sands.
One should properly bury [the vessel] two finger-breadths below the ground in a "mountain-enclosure" (bhūdharapuṭa) fire-mixture;
that enclosure where the lid is placed on top is called bhūdharapuṭa. (Rcūm 5.160)
A *lāvakapuṭa* is a sealed vessel made with husks or cow-dung about sixteen fingers high; where such a vessel exists, it is called a *lāvaka*, used for preparing very soft substances. (Rcūm 5.161)

Regarding the measurement of the *puṭa* when it has not been explicitly stated, those skilled in reasoning and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*) should determine the appropriate *puṭa* by considering the relative strength or weakness of the substance to be processed (*sādhya-dravya*). 5.162.
*Piṣṭaka*, *chagaṇa*, *chāṇa*, *upala*, and likewise *utpala*, as well as *giriṇḍa*, *upalasāṭhī*, and *navārī*— these are the names for dried cow dung. (Rcūm 5.163)
{Conclusion}:

He who recites this chapter, which was composed by the Soma-deities and is now scattered here, shall not seek the instruction of a guru even in the science of mercury (*rasendra*) or in the alchemy of metals (*dhātuvāda*). (Rcūm 5.164)
Now, Somadeva describes the seven Rasas that are characterized by insight and are specifically indicated for the accomplishment of Rasa in the *Śrīkaṇṭhāgama*. (Rcūm 7.1)
Sixty-eight types of medicinal juices:
*jalotpala*, *samaṅgā*, *rasā*, *jalapippalī*, *sthalaprasāriṇī*, *ciñcī*, *jālinī*, and *jalamūlakā*. (Rcūm 7.2)
Candrodaka, ardhacandra, jalāpāmārga, tiktaka, tuṣāmbu, kākamācī, jalakumbhī, and likewise śaṭī.
Uttamā, hemapuṣpī, durgandhā, sitagandhinī, māṇḍūkī, mohinī, māṃsī, pāṣāṇī, and śīśikā.
Sārivā, alambuṣā, meghanādī, śukanāsikā, potakī, hīriṇī, vajrakandikā, and aparājitā. (Rcūm 7.5)
Vanamālā, vidārī, kukkuṭā, halinīśvarī, vārāhī, bṛhatī, mūrvā, sarpākṣī, and sadacitrikā. (Rcūm 7.6)
Mālārjuna, gojihvā, garuḍī, haṃsapādikā, nandinī, śikhipādī, kāśmarī, and likewise tulasī. (Rcūm 7.7)
The wild pumpkin creeper (*vanakūṣmāṇḍavallī*), the scorpion-plant (*vṛścikālī*), the bamboo-like plant (*veṇukā*),
the pestle-rooted plant (*muśalī*), the variegated-footed plant (*citrapādī*), the *karmasphoṭī*, and likewise the poison (*viṣā*).
Ajamārī, pāṭalā, paṭolī, dhanvayāsaka, bhārṅgī, viṣaghnī, guḍūcī, vāsā, bhṛṅgī, and pāgava; // Rcūm_7.9 //

Thus, sixty-eight medicinal herbs of great power have been described; they are used for the binding, killing, as well as the digestion and fixation of mercury, for the extraction of mercury from its bond, and for the removal of all its defects. (Rcūm 7.10)

On the Vindhya mountain, on the snowy peaks, on Malaya, Gomanta, Śrīgiri, the Sahya range, and the Pāriyātraka mountain; at Kiṣkindha, the abode of the monkeys, and also on Mount Māhendra and the Mālyavat hill—let physicians report from the mouths of cowherds, herdsmen, perfected ones, and doctors that his form and name are even more abundant there. (Rāmāyaṇacūḍāmaṇi 7.11)
Rcūm, 8 {The group beginning with Sarpākṣī}:
Sarpākṣī, Vandhyakarkoṭī, Jalabimbī, and Jambukī.
Punarnavā, matsyākṣī, bhṛṅgarāja, and śatāvarī.
Śarapuṅkhā, maṇḍūkaparṇikā, brahmadaṇḍikā,
anantā, kukkuṭī, jaṅghā, kākamācī, and śikhaṇḍinī.
Sahadevī, Kapotī, Viṣṇukrāntā, Kuraṇṭaka, Mahābalā, Nāgabalā, Mūrvā, Rāsnā, and Kuriṅginī. (Rcūm 8.3)
Phaṇinī, nīlī, prapunnāṭa, samaṅgā, āmalakī, jvālinī, meghanāda, gojihvā, and padmacāriṇī. (Rcūm 8.4)
Pāṭhā, kokilākṣa, tripattrā, ākhukarṇikā,
ekaparṇī, dviparṇī, triparṇī, and likewise kṣīriṇī.
Tittiḍī, meṣaśṛṅgī, tulasī, śyāmaparṇikā,
and śvetādriparṇikā are considered the group beginning with sarpākṣī (Rcūm 8.6).
The one called the forty-six-fold is the regulator of mercury;
here, the five parts of the medicinal plants must be taken according to the prescribed rule.
In the processes of sweating mercury and other substances, in the handling of crucibles, and likewise in purification,
one should employ [the crucibles] mentioned in these prescribed operations, starting from eight and according to availability.
The group beginning with *vyāghrikā* certainly increases the qualities by eight times more than usual.
[The *vyāghrikādigaṇa* consists of:
*vyāghrikā*, *rākṣasī*, *vahni*, *cāṇḍālī*, and *gajakarṇikā*. (Rcūm 8.9)
Ṣaṭkārī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, bṛhatī, hilamocaka, śṛgālajihvikā, vahnī, madanī, and likewise lāṅgalī. (Rcūm 8.10)
Cakrikā, Vajriṇī, Vyāghrī, Kaṅkatī, Putrajīvikā, Kañcukī, Karkoṭī, Kumārī, and Padmacāriṇī. (Rcūm 8.11)
Ekavīrā, Rudantī, Lakṣmī, Narakasā, Uccaṭā, Raktacitrā, Nāginī, and Nāgavallikā. (Rcūm 8.12)
Saktukā, saktuśṛṅgī, raktasnug, yajñavallikā, śākhoṭa, meṣaśṛṅgī, hemalī, and vyāghrapādikā. (Rcūm 8.13)
Śamī, vyāghranakhī, somavallarī, arkapuṣpikā, keśinī, kāsamārī, vṛkṣarāja, and ajamārikā. (Rcūm 8.14)
Koṭarākṣī, Hanūmantī, Narajīvā, Aṅganāyakī,
Mālikā, Kākatuṇḍī, Meghapuṣpī, and Kaṅguṇī.
Furthermore, there are the anyā, tuvaravallī, jagatī, haṃsapādikā, kumbhinī, vahnimārī, sūryabhaktā, and vākucī. (Rcūm 8.16)
Rasanirjīvakārī, bhūśuṇḍī, kaṭutumbikā, devadālī, viśālā, kārpāsī, and brahmarañjaka; (these are the eight). Rcūm 8.17.
Kṛṣṇākṣīva, as well as kṛṣṇadhattūra, vanapīluka, śvetārka, yavaciñcā, kāravellī, and dantikā. (Rcūm 8.18)
Gojihvā, kākajaṅghā, śvetaguñjā, śambarā, mahākālī, sitāṅkola, māyūra, and paṭolikā. (Rcūm 8.19)
This is the group beginning with *vyāghrikā*, which is supreme for converting mercury into ash;
herein, within the seeds of the aforementioned medicinal herbs, the mercury is digested separately. (Rcūm 8.20)
{The group beginning with red snuhī}:
red snuhī, rudantī, raktāgni, somavallikā, vṛddhadāru, śākhoṭī, mohinī, and aṅgāravallikā. (Rcūm 8.21)
Barhikā, kṣīramārjārī, triśūlā, kṣīrakukkuṭī, jīmūta, kākamācī, nīlikā, and śaṅkhapuṣpikā. (Rcūm 8.22)
Having leaves shaped like betel-leaf, with small tubers, originating from Śrīśaila, and destroying [the effects of] poison—she is known as Vajraghnī and Nāgakarṇī. (Rcūm 8.23)
Jyotiṣmatī, Drumajyotis, Tṛṇajyotis, then Uccaṭā, Udumbarī, Tridaṇḍī, and likewise another, Nīlajyotis. (Rcūm 8.24)
Hemavallarikā, tāmravallarī, and cukra;
tridaṇḍī, brahmadaṇḍī, krauñcikā, and sthalapadminī.
Varā, vartulaparṇā, nāgakaṇṭhī,
lāṅgalī, nāgajihvā, arkapattrī, and likewise kāṣṭhodumbarikā.
The group of herbs beginning with *kāladaṇḍī*, *triparṇī*,
and *raktasnuhī* was prescribed by Śambhu himself for the binding, killing, and purification of mercury.
When the mercury (sūta) has been purified and rubbed with stable substances endowed with touch, smell,
and taste, it dies and is easily bound.
The *kadalyādi* group consists of:
plantain (*kadalī*), *sūryabhakta*, bitter *uṣātakī*, *drāviṇī*, *kākamācī*, *śigruka*, and *kṣīrakañcukī*. (Rcūm 8.29)
And *nīrapippalikā*—this is the group beginning with *kadalī*;
it certainly causes the liquefaction of all metals, mercury, and so forth. (Rcūm 8.30)
The group beginning with *kākamācī*:
*kākamācī*, *arkapatrī*, *kāsamarda*, *kṛtāñjali*, *lakṣmaṇā*, *haṃsapādī*, *nāginī*, and *kṣīranālikā*. (Rcūm 8.31)
Tāmbūlī, vyālikā, brāhmī, kāravallī, arjunī, carā, vārāhakarṇikā, meghadhvani, and sahadevikā. (Rcūm 8.32)
Likewise, the group beginning with *kākamācī* and including *kuruvaka* is prescribed for the transmutation (*krāmaṇa*) of mercury within both the body and metals. (Rcūm 8.33)
Ekavīrā, Mahāvīrā, Prayoga, and Hemadaṇḍikā—these four varieties are declared to be certain for the binding of mercury. (Rcūm 8.34)
It bestows physical vigor and strength, removes all great diseases, and is auspicious, granting sons and acting as an aphrodisiac through its very sight and touch. (Rcūm 8.35)
The creeper known as *ekavīrā* has leaves shaped like a corpse; when it falls, it bears a single fruit.
It is called *ekavīrā*, and it is supreme for binding mercury.
That plant from which each fruit is produced upon a separate leaf, and whose luster resembles a young sprout, is considered to be the *mahāvīrā*. (Rcūm 8.37)
The *prayogakanda* has three sections and three tips, with two fruits attached to the stalk;
its leaves resemble those of bamboo, and it grows on elephants and the Vindhya mountains.
For his middle bulb is the Rākṣasa named Prayoga;
crushed by him, the vital essence (sūta) dies and is easily bound. (Rcūm 8.39)

The *hemavallī* has leaves like those of the betel vine (*tāmbūlī*), its sap is golden-colored, and it is devoid of fruits, flowers, and the like; such is considered to be the *hemavallī*. (Rcūm 8.40)

He by whom mercury has been bound with the urine of one who has practiced the *sambandha* [union] and has been held in the mouth for a year attains the power of moving through the sky (*khecarī-gati*). (Rcūm 8.41)
{The Section on Vajradaṇḍa and Others} The staff of the vajra-garlic and the iron staff—
these three are the very selves of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, the protectors of the three worlds. (Rcūm 8.42)
Pathyā, śuṇṭhī, śilā, muṇḍī, nirguṇḍī, and viḍaṅga;
likewise citraka, trikaṭu, hema, mākṣika, and vimala. (Rcūm 8.43)
This section on Vajradaṇḍa and others is most excellent for rejuvenation;
it is the best remover of all diseases and the destroyer of old age and death. (Rcūm 8.44)
{The Group of Bhūpāṭalī and Others} Bhūpāṭalī, paṭolī, yogārī, siṃhavallikā, śūkarī, hemavallī, nāgadhārī, and mārkava. (Rcūm 8.45)
This group, beginning with *bhūpāṭalī*, serves to bind the mercury;
[it is] the group of the five jewels (*pañcaratnaka*):
*pāṭalā*, *indīvarī*, and likewise *mantrasiṃhāsanī*. (Rcūm 8.46)
And Niśācarī, Kaṅkālakhecarī, and Pañcaratnaka—
these bring about the transformation of the body into steel, effect the killing and binding of mercury,
destroy wrinkles and grey hair, and are supreme in removing all diseases. (Rcūm 8.47)
Rcūm, 9: Ghee, sugar, and honey should be known as the "triple sweet" (madhuratraya).
{The group of urines}:
the urines of the elephant, the young camel, the female buffalo, the donkey, and the horse.
One should apply the flowers and seeds of cows, goats, sheep, females, and males;
[and] the five types of earth:
brick, red ochre, salt, ash, and anthill earth. (Rcūm 9.2)
Those skilled in the application of mercury have proclaimed five types of earth;
[then there are] the three alkalis: borax, nitre, and the third is sarjikṣāra.
{The Section on Alkaline Substances} Palāśa, kadalī, śigru, sesame, apāmārga, mokṣaka, radish, tamarind, bodhi, raktarāja, and likewise girī. (Rcūm 9.4)
Kambala, other types of walls, and various kinds of alkali—this is declared to be the group of alkalies (kṣāravarga); it is digestive and possesses great potency.
It also effects the digestion of gems and the like, as well as the digestion of all metals and the like.
{The group of acids (amlavarga):} *amlavetasa*, *jambīra*, *nimbuka*, and *rājanimbuka*. (Rcūm 9.6)
The jujube, the citron, the tamarind, and likewise the *cukrikā*, sour chickpea gruel, fermented rice water (*kāñjika*), as well as the *amlikā* and the sour pomegranate. (Rcūm 9.7)
Karamarda and sour jujube (kolāmla) are called this "sour group" (amlavarga);
it is beneficial for the purification of mercury and the like, and for liquefaction and digestion. (Rcūm 9.8)
The section on salts:
sea salt, that produced from the Indus, rock salt, and that known as *viḍa*;
likewise *sauvarcala*, *rauma*, *cullika*, *gaḍa*, and so forth.
This group of salts is appetizing, digestive, and carminative;
it is liquefying and purifying for all metals as well as for ashes.
{The Group of Poisons} Śṛṅgika, kālakūṭa, vatsanābha, saktuka, and pīta— this is the group of poisons, which is proclaimed as the most excellent. (Rcūm 9.11)
This [mercury] is praised for the processing of mercury (rasakarma), as well as for its binding and killing;
yet, if consumed improperly, it certainly kills. (Rcūm 9.12)

The group of secondary poisons (*upaviṣavarga*): *lāṅgalī*, *viṣamuṣṭi*, *karavīra*, as well as *jayā*, *nīlaka*, *kanaka*, and *arka*—this indeed constitutes the group consisting of secondary poisons. (Rcūm 9.13)
Aconite (upaviṣa) is digestive, carminative, and a purgative; it is employed in certain tastes and in poisons,
such as those of crawling creatures, where no other poison is equal to that of the serpent.
{The Chapter on Oils} Sesame,
linseed, safflower, neem, karaja, rājī, white mustard, as well as the seeds of guñjā and kaṅguṇī. Rcūm 9.15.
The group of oils consists of the oils of *madhūka* and others, which is beneficial for the [therapeutic] decoction;
[the group of milks consists of] the milk of elephants, horses, women, cows, she-asses, goats, and ewes.
Uṣṭrikā, udumbara, aśvattha, bhānu, nyagrodha, tilvaka, dugdhikā, the snuhi group, and likewise uttamakarṇikā; Rcūm 9.17.
The group of milks among the juices and other substances is specified as consisting of these;
[now for] the group of bile [producing substances]: buffalo, boar, fish, goat, and peacock. (Rcūm 9.18)
The group of bile (pittagaṇa) is said to consist of the fat of the black cobra, the cat, and the mongoose, used for the purpose of killing, binding, and subduing.
The group of fats (*vasāvarga*)—
consisting of the fat derived from frog, tortoise, boar, snake, and human flesh—
is recommended for use in the preparation of medicinal juices (*rasakarma*). (Rcūm 9.20)
The group of salts (*viḍgaṇa*) is indeed specified as consisting of those of the pigeon, the blue jay, the dove, the peacock,
the vulture, and also the cock. (Rcūm 9.21)
Indeed, through smearing and heating in a *puṭa*, it is the purifier of all metals.
{The Red Group:} Safflower, *khadira*, lac, *mañjiṣṭhā*, and red sandalwood. (Rcūm 9.22)
Adrī, bandhujīva, likewise karpūragandhinī,
and mākṣika— these are to be known as the red group (raktavarga), which is highly coloring.
The yellow group consists of *kiṃśuka*, *karṇikāra*, and the two types of turmeric;
this is declared as the yellow group for the application of the king of mercury.
{The White Group}: Tagara, kuṭaja, kunda, guñjā, jīvantikā, and the white lotus root—this is declared to be the white group. (Rcūm 9.25)
The black group (*kṛṣṇavarga*) is declared to consist of plantain, the cruel creeper (*krūravallī*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nīlikā*, *nala*, mud, *kāsīsa*, *bālā*, and mango. (Rcūm 9.26)

Furthermore, the substance which is of the nature of a *jāraṇa* (digestive process) should be diligently infused with groups of red minerals and so forth, in order to truly attain such a coloration. (Rcūm 9.27)
The group of purifying agents:
The group considered to be purifying consists of glass (kāca), borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), and śiprā;
it destroys the impurities of living beings, bound mercury, and metals.
The destroyer of the hosts of Kāpālikas is called Rasavādin.
{The Section on Softening Agents}: Here, a formulation consisting of buffalo horn, ram's horn, seeds produced in Kaliṅga, and the bones of a hare destroys the hardness of iron. (Rcūm 9.29)

{The Group of Fluxionators}: This group of substances—molasses, guggulu, guñjā, clarified butter, sāragha honey, and ṭaṅkaṇa—is considered effective for the fluxioning of all metals and other materials that are otherwise difficult to melt. (Rcūm 9.30)
All alkaline substances destroy impurities; the sour taste cleanses and digests; [sweet substances] counteract dullness and poisons; and unctuous substances produce lubrication. (Rcūm 9.31)
Rcūm, 10: The great essences (mahārasa) are ghana, rājāvarta, vaikrānta, sasyaka, and vimala, born from the mountain.
Tuttha, tāpya, and rasāyana—these are metallic minerals (sattva), and they are like nectar.
The essence of Gaurī is the supreme nectar; it destroys wind, bile, and consumption; it awakens wisdom, pacifies ailments, and is the foremost among aphrodisiacs and life-prolongers.

It is strengthening, unctuous, appetizing, non-phlegmatic, digestive, and cold in potency; through various formulations, this "sky" (mica) cures all diseases and binds the lord of mercury. (Rcūm 10.2)
That which is brought from a pit dug beneath the royal hand (the central square) may yield the stated fruit;
however, that which is devoid of living beings is utterly fruitless.
The varieties of mica are considered to be *pināka*, *nāga*, *maṇḍūka*, and *vajra*;
each of these is fourfold according to the distinction of colors such as white and so forth. (Rcūm 10.4)
The Pināka bow, heated by fire, releases a mass of arrows;
having bound the impurity of one who has used it, it surely kills that man. (Rcūm 10.5)
The "Cloud of the Naga" (nāgābhra) should be prepared like a naga, emitting a sound while situated in fire;
when consumed, it undoubtedly produces the skin disease known as maṇḍala-kuṣṭha. (Rcūm 10.6)
When mica, like a frog, leaps again and again and falls upon heated mica,
it produces the disease of urinary calculi (aśmarī), which is incurable except by surgical means. (Rcūm 10.7)
Vajra-ore (vajrābhra) heated in fire and freed from all its impurities produces both body-tissue and metal; it is the supreme remover of all diseases. (Rcūm 10.8)
Clouds are of four kinds by color: white, red, yellow, and black.
White is prescribed for white rites; red and the others [yellow and black] are for yellow rites.
Although it is said in the science of alchemy that there are four kinds of excellent space (vyoma),
nevertheless, that which has the luster of black color possesses millions upon millions of times more qualities.
That mica which is glossy, has broad layers, withstands fire, is heavy,
and has leaves that are easily separable is declared to be the most excellent. (Rcūm 10.11)
A sky-like [impurity] accompanied by moon-like spots and resembling glass-dross does not digest the mercury;
if it has been swallowed, it must not be used for either metallurgy or alchemy. (Rcūm 10.12)
A sky devoid of moonlight is beneficial in all diseases, whereas a sky accompanied by moonlight, if consumed, causes urinary disorders and weak digestion. (Rcūm 10.13)
Those who, devoid of reason, have spoken of leaf-minerals and mercurial elixirs, have prescribed the poison known as kālakūṭa for the sake of sustaining life. (Rcūm 10.14)
For the sake of sentient beings and for the sake of service, one should employ purified abhraka;
otherwise, having rendered it devoid of its qualities, it will certainly cause harm. (Rcūm 10.15)
Abhra (mica) that has been heated and immersed seven times in kāñjika, or likewise immersed in cow's urine, certainly becomes free from defects. (Rcūm 10.16)
Or likewise in cow's milk boiled with triphalā— especially for the killing of abhra—
one should then prepare *dhānyābhraka* and grind it with the juices of *matsyākṣikā*.
Having made it into a *cakrī* and dried it, one should then roast it in an *ardhabhaka* crucible; indeed, one should roast it in this manner six times with the juice of *punarnavā*. (Rcūm 10.18)
Having ground it with a portion of borax (ṭaṅkaṇa) and formed it into pills, one should indeed roast them seven times using the "half-elephant" (ardhebhaka) type of puṭas. 10.19.
In the same manner, one should fume it seven times with the juice of vāsā and the juice of taṇḍulīya, according to the procedure previously described. (Rcūm 10.20)

In this manner, one should employ the perfected *ghana* in all yogas; it should be combined with a quarter-part of *ṭaṅkaṇa* and thoroughly ground with the juice of *matsyākṣī*. (Rcūm 10.21) [The killing of mica]
One should firmly compress it within the crucible until it is intensely heated; it will then become a solid mass in the form of *sattva*.
Then, having reduced it to a powder, one should soak it thoroughly in cow's ghee. (Rcūm 10.22)
One should roast it seven times in a pan placed on the hearth, repeatedly pulverizing it until it becomes the color of fire. (Rcūm 10.23)
One should roast it until it burns even a blade of grass thrown into it, or until it undergoes complete parching;
then, having ground it together with sulphur, one should treat it with a decoction of the roots of the *vaṭa* tree. (Rcūm 10.24)
One should indeed seal it twenty times with a boar-shaped vessel (vārāha-puṭa),
and again twenty times with a decoction derived from the three myrobalans (triphalā).
Having processed it with triphalā, muṇḍikā, bhṛṅga, pathyā, nīlī, and excellent roots, it should be administered in the proper dose for all diseases. (Rcūm 10.26)
Slightly inferior to the *sattva* cloud, yet changeless and superior in qualities—thus it was perfected by the process of *puṭapāka* one hundred times over. (Rcūm 10.27)
When consumed in the measure of half a *guñjā*, it becomes exceedingly endowed with qualities, acting as a supreme digestive and appetizer;
it produces great hunger and, through formulations that alleviate specific diseases, brings about the destruction of all ailments. (Rcūm 10.28)
Grain-sulphur (dhānyābhra) rubbed with the juice of *kāsamarda* should be subjected to *puṭapāka* a hundred times; it dies [becomes fixed], of this there is no doubt. (Rcūm 10.29)
Likewise, with the juice of musta and the juice of taṇḍulīya,
abhraka that has been ground with śivā, āmalaka, and saubhāgya is formed into pills. (Rcūm 10.30)
One should seal it sixty times; it becomes the color of vermilion.
Through the administration of appropriate adjuncts, it destroys diseases such as consumption and others. (Rcūm 10.31)
For the killing of clouds, [one should use] the decoction of the bark of the root of the *vaṭa* tree together with the essence of betel leaves;
or else, with *vāsā* and *matsyākṣikī*, or with *matsyākṣī* and *kaṭhillā*.
The thick [substance] of the vaṭa tree, ground with milk and subjected to twenty cycles of heating in a closed crucible (puṭapāka), becomes a solid mass resembling vermilion.
