Abhra powder (6), together with ṭaṅkaṇa, ground with cow's milk and subjected to intense heating (*prapuṭita*), becomes free of its luster after thirty cycles; it is then most excellent in quality. (Rcūm 10.34)
Likewise, when these perfected clouds are encapsulated by *tāla*,
they become exceedingly intense and even more powerful than the *rasa* [mantras].
Roughness, subtlety, floating in water, and the emergence of a reddish color [are the physical properties of ash].
And a radiance of manifold qualities arises through many layers.

[One should process] *abhra* (mica), *sattva*, and *pātana* with the juices of *kāsamarda*, *ghana*, *dhvani*, *vāsā*, *punarnavā*, *matsyākṣī*, *kāravelī*, and *haṃsapādī*, each separately. (Rcūm 10.37)
Having ground and ground it with effort, one should dry it by means of heat;
[along with] wheat flour, small fish, and borax. (Rcū 10.38)
Having added an equal portion of mica for each [ingredient], one should thoroughly rub them together;
after each rubbing, one should properly dry it with the rays of the sun. (Rcūm 10.39)

Having cast in the five products of the cow (*pañcājya*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and likewise the five products of the buffalo (*pañcamāhiṣa*), one should fashion cow-dung balls the size of *tinduka* fruits.
Milk, curd, ghee, urine, and feces are called the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*).
Having blown [the mixture] in a crucible for downward precipitation, one should cause the essence (*sattva*) to fall out. (Rcūm 10.41)
{Abhra:: sattva:: pātana::
the separation of the dross and the essence}
Having collected the dross from the crucible and reduced it to powder, one should remove the scoriae;
then, one should knead that dross with a small amount of carbonate of soda (ṭaṅka) and cow dung. (Rcūm 10.42)
Having formed balls and dried them, one should heat them again as before;
having further collected the dross and kneaded it, one should extract the essence.

In this very same way, having again smelted the dross, one should extract the essence (*sattva*). [This is the purification of the essence of *abhraka*. Then, those grains of essence should be boiled with sour *kāñjika* vinegar. (Rcūm 10.44)
Having placed [the substance] within the crucible together with the group of purifying agents and sealed it,
one should collect it once it has been properly melted and blow upon it twice again.

Thus, the essence (sattva) is proven; it should be employed in alchemy (*rasarasāyana*) after being melted and repeatedly poured into honey, oil, fat, and clarified butter, thereby softening the essence of mica (*abhrakasattva*). (Rcūm 10.46)
A base metal such as iron, which is hard, becomes soft after ten cycles [of processing]. (The formulation for the essence of mica.)
The heated globule of the *sattva* [is placed] in *kāñjika* mixed with grain.
Having extinguished it at that very moment, one should scratch [the surface] with an iron rod;
then, having heated thick, dense droplets and cast them into sour gruel (kāñjika).
Having collected that [substance] at once and pulverized it, one should let the powder circulate;
then one should fry that powder with cow's ghee three times as before.
Likewise, with the juice of *dhātrī* fruits or with the juice of *dhātrī* leaves, one should grind [the substance] on a stone slab after each roasting. (Rcūm 10.50)
Then, one should subject it to ten cycles of heating with the juice of punarnavā mixed with sour gruel (kāñjika),
and [then] to ten cycles with sulphur.
Thus accomplished, the celestial being (vyomasattva), supreme in all qualities,
may be employed at will for the process of digestion (jāraṇa) and for alchemy (rasāyana).

Divyābhra (celestial mica), when consumed in a dose of one ball (valla) combined with vellaka, trikaṭu, and ghee, conquers consumption, anemia, dysentery, colic, diseases of the stomach and bowels, burning sensations, asthma, urinary disorders, loss of appetite, difficult-to-cure cough, weak digestion, abdominal pain, and indeed all diseases through its medicinal formulations. (Rcūm 10.53)
Regarding the liquefaction of mica:
even if the methods of liquefaction are indeed taught in the scriptures and observed therein, they will by no means succeed without the grace of Śambhu. (Rcūm 10.54)

{Lapis Lazuli: Examination} Lapis lazuli that is slightly red, with a luster mixed with a reddish-blue tint, heavy, and smooth, is considered excellent; any other is regarded as mediocre. (Rcūm 10.55)
Rājāvarta removes urinary disorders, consumption, hemorrhoids, anemia, phlegm, and wind; it is a digestive stimulant, a carminative, an aphrodisiac, and a rejuvenative elixir. (Rcūm 10.56)
Minerals such as rājāvarta and others are indeed purified by being sweated two or three times with lime-water mixed with the juice of nimba and cow urine. (Rcūm 10.57)
Rājāvarta: for killing.
Rājāvarta, finely powdered and combined with sulphur and the juice of *bhṛṅga*, becomes killed by means of *puṭapāka* after seven nights. (Rcūm 10.58)
{Purification of the element [of a specific name]}:
*sūryāvartaka*, *vajrakanda*, *kadalī*, *koṣātaki*,
*śigruka*, *vandhyā*, *nīrakaṇā*, *ghana*, *nṛpaśamī*, *dhvāṅkṣī*, *kumārī*, and *varā*.
By means of the single essence of these [liquids], minerals and the like are purified through acidic cupping (*puṭana*);
they undergo softening and moistening, and when blown upon again, those *sattvas* emerge. (Rcūm 10.59)
For this yoga completely purifies the impurities of all the elements; it is the precipitation of the essence (*sattvapātana*) by means of alkalies,
salts, house-soot, *guñjā* seeds, and the fruits of *niśā*.
When combined with these, stones and rocks release their essence entirely.
Eight-sided, with eight facets, hexagonal, smooth, and heavy; endowed with pure or mixed colors—such is called vaikrānta. (Rcūm 10.61)
White, red, yellow, blue, the color of a pigeon, dark, black, and variegated— indeed, it is of eight kinds. (Rcūm 10.62)

Vaikrānta bestows longevity, promotes strength and complexion, is highly aphrodisiac, grants wisdom, and removes all humors and diseases. It kindles the digestive fire, possesses qualities equal to those of iron, is energetic, and indeed produces physical strength and iron. (Rcūm 10.63)
In all elixirs (*rasāyana*), the powerful *vaikrānta*, which is to be reckoned as foremost, should be employed in place of diamond (*vajra*); it destroys all diseases. (Rcūm 10.64)
Vaikrānta purified by being steamed in a decoction of *kulattha* beans becomes completely pure.
[Vaikrānta: killing]
It is killed by eight layers [of processing], combined with the juice of *gandha-nimbūka*.

Vaikrānta, ground by means of the process for extracting the essence (*sattvapātana*) and formed into a pill, should be placed in a crucible and heated for one *ghaṭikā*; thus the vaikrānta will release its essence. (Rcūm 10.66)

Vaikrānta that has attained the state of ash, combined with one-fourth part of dead gold (mercury), and taken in a dose of one *valla* along with *kaṇā*, clarified butter, and *vela*, conquers consumption, wasting, jaundice, hemorrhoids, asthma, cough, and malignant *grahaṇī*; it cures diseases beginning with chest wounds and acts as a builder of the body. (Rcūm 10.67)
The ash of blue vaikrānta combined with half the amount of mercury-ash,
along with an equal quantity of the essence of dead iron and mica, should be thoroughly rubbed together.

If one consumes a dose the size of a *guñjā* seed mixed with honey and clarified butter every morning according to the procedure for elixirs (*rasāyana*), one may live as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars. (Rcūm 10.69)
Consumed in the measure of a barley grain with appropriate after-drinks for each respective disease, it destroys all diseases that are difficult to overcome by other medicines. (Rcūm 10.70)
Just as the water of the Gaṅgā purifies the sins of men in twenty-one days,
so did Sasyaka drink the Hālāhala poison vomited up by Garuḍa after he had swallowed the nectar of immortality.
On the mountain called Marutāhvaya, poison mixed with nectar was indeed vomited up;
having become solidified, it became what is known as sasyaka.
Grain that has the luster of a peacock's neck and is heavy with weight is highly praised.

Just as poison mixed with a substance comes to possess qualities exceeding those of the substance itself, so too does the Hālāhala poison, when mixed with nectar, come to possess qualities exceeding those of the nectar.

Mayūratuttha is said here to remove all defects and poisons, cure anal pain, colic, and the obstruction caused by corrupted *amlapitta*; it is beneficial, acts as an elixir (*rāsāyana*), induces vomiting and purgation, destroys toxins, and removes vitiligo. (Rcūm 10.74)
Sasyaka (copper sulfate) should be well-steamed for three *praharas* in a *dolāyantra* with the urine of man, buffalo, goat, and cow; in this way, the *sasyaka* is purified. (Rcūm 10.75)
Combined with the juice of *lakuca*, sulphur, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt,
and sealed inside a crucible, it dies by means of *kaukkuṭa* puffs. (Rcūm 10.76)
Having sealed it within a crucible with lime (paṭaṅka) and the juice of *nimbū*, and having strongly blown upon copper and silver, the *sasyaka* ore releases its essence (*sattva*). (Rcūm 10.77)

Pure *sasyaka* [calamine] struck by fire and combined with the aforementioned medicinal substances will certainly release its essence (*sattva*) through the process of heating in a tube (*nalikā*). (Rcūm 10.78)
Taking this essence, which is endowed with the supreme *bhūnāga* essence,
the ring made from it, upon being touched, shall instantly become a destroyer of the *śūla*.
One shall conquer moving and unmoving poison, spirits, and the ḍākinī that has come into view;
this is the "Rāma-like" seal of Somasenānī, consisting of the syllables *tathākṣara*. (Rcūm 10.80)
This mudrā should be performed; it produces immediate visible results.
On the northern side of the Himalayas stands the great tree Aśvakarṇa.
There, the colic arose, and right there it came to its end;
the water from the mudrā, consecrated seven times with this mantra, was drunk. (Rcūm 10.82)
"It is declared by Bhāluki that oil heated over a fire with this mudrā certainly removes sudden colic. (Rcūm 10.83)
When applied as a plaster, it forcefully destroys colic occurring anywhere;
it immediately induces labor in a woman and instantly removes eye disease.

The stainless [substance] is said to be of three kinds: that beginning with gold, that beginning with silver, and the third is the stainless brass, which is characterized by their respective lusters. (Rcūm 10.85)
It is circular, provided with corners, smooth, and possessed of a surface. [Its medicinal properties:]
It pacifies wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, purifying, and a supreme elixir.
Regarding the applications of *vimala*,
the first is said to be for the preparation of gold, the second is considered for the making of silver,
and the third is for medicinal purposes; among these, each preceding one possesses superior qualities.
{Vimala:: purification} Vimala, when steamed with water from the *āṭarūṣa* plant, becomes pure.
{Vimala:: killing}
He dies by ten applications of the paste made from *gandhāśman* and *lakucā*.
Having ground [the mercury] with the juices of *saṭaṅka* and *lakucā*, along with the ash of *meṣaśṛṅga*,
one should smear it inside a crucible, dry it thoroughly, and seal it shut. (Rcūm 10.89)

When blown by six *prastha* measures of *kokila* [herbs], it becomes pure like lead; when combined with that, the mercury releases its essence (*sattva*), and the resulting mercury becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*). (Rcūm 10.90)
This *sattva*, combined with mercury (*sūta*), should be ground into a paste and thoroughly rubbed;
once the sulphur has dissolved, one should add it and digest it with three times the amount of *ālaka*. (Rcūm 10.91)
One should indeed place a stone possessing five qualities into a tube-like mechanical device;
likewise, one should add lead ash in a tenth part, as well as dead vaikrānta.
Having crushed everything together in one place and filtered it through a cloth,
one should carefully pour it into the middle of a small jar and fill it completely.
Licked with *vyoṣa* and *varā*, combined with *vimalaka* and taken with ghee, it destroys fevers caused by misfortune, swelling, anemia, urinary disorders, and loss of appetite;

it also cures pain in the roots [of the teeth], malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), incomparable colic, consumption, jaundice, all diseases of bile and wind, and, what need is there to say more, all diseases without exception through this formulation. (Rcūm 10.94)

Bitumen (*śilājatu*) is said to be of two kinds: that beginning with "cow's urine" (*gomūtra*), which is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), and another beginning with "camphor" (*karpūra*). Of these, the first kind is further divided into two types. (Rcūm 10.95)
Of these two types, the one with living organisms (*sasattva*) and the one without (*niḥsattva*), the former is superior in quality.
[It is produced] in summer from the feet of the snowy mountain, which are scorched by the fierce rays of the sun, as *śilājatu* (bitumen).
Mineral pitch (śilājatu) may exude from mountains containing gold, silver,
or copper; that which is born from a mountain containing gold is heavy and resembles the Japā flower.
That [śilājatu] produced from a mountain containing silver is slightly bitter, very sweet, and an excellent elixir; it is pale yellow, heavy, and sweet. (Rcūm 10.98)
Śilāja (bitumen) born from a mountain containing copper destroys diseases of the bile and especially removes anemia;
it is blue in color, dense, and heavy. (Rcūm 10.99)

Śilāja (bitumen) destroys kapha and vāta; it is bitter and hot, and cures the disease of consumption (kṣaya). That which, when thrown into fire, takes the shape of a phallus and is smokeless, is pure.
Then, when dissolved in water, that śilājatu indeed becomes pure.
Śilājatu certainly pacifies fever, anemia, and swelling; it removes urinary disorders and weak digestion, cuts away excess fat, and alleviates consumption (yakṣma).

It uproots diseases of the urine, destroys abdominal tumors and splenic disorders, and cures colic in the stomach, heart, and chest. It removes undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and destroys all skin diseases; furthermore, it is beneficial for both the body and for metal [alloys]. (Rcūm 10.101)

Whatever qualities reside in the mercury-derivatives, the secondary minerals, quicksilver, gems, and metals, those dwell in the mineral substance known as śilājatu for the sake of conquering old age and death. (Rcūm 10.102)
{Purification of Śilājatu}:

When subjected to steam within a *svedanī* apparatus together with alkaline substances, acids, and *guggulu*, the mineral substance (*śilādhātu*) is purified after being steamed for the duration of one *ghaṭikā*. (Rcūm 10.103)
{The killing of śilājatu}:
Encased with stone, sulphur, and realgar, along with the juice of mātuluṅga, the mineral śilādhātu indeed dies after eight *giriṇḍaka* applications. (Rcūm 10.104)

One should consume an equal measure of *kānta* iron and *vaikrāntaka* stone derived from ashed rock (*śilājatu*), combined with *triphalā*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), and ghee, in a dose of one *valla*.

This is effective for anemia, consumption, hemorrhoids, loss of digestive fire, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, spleen disease, large abdominal swellings, various types of colic, and diseases of the female reproductive organs. (Rasacūḍāmaṇi 10.105)
If one practices this for six months according to the procedure for elixirs (*rasāyana*), one shall be freed from wrinkles and graying hair and live happily for a hundred years. (Rcūm 10.106)
Having ground the mountain-born *śilājatu* with the fluxing agents and sour liquids, one should smear it inside a crucible, seal it, and heat it intensely with *kokila* [coals]. (Rcūm 10.107)
The mineral element śilājatu, resembling iron from its own mine, should release its essence like camphor.
Pale white, resembling sand, it is a mineral pitch (śilājatu) composed of camphor and other ingredients.
Karpūraśilājatu destroys dysuria, urinary calculi, urinary disorders, jaundice, and anemia.
Camphor and bitumen, having been steamed with the water of cardamom and then dried, attain purity. (Rcūm 10.109)
The wise have not prescribed its killing or the casting down of living beings.
*Rasaka* is said to be of two kinds: *dardura* and *kāravellaka*. (Rcūm 10.110)
The *dardura* is said to have seeds, while the *kāravellaka* is seedless;
the former is auspicious for the extraction of essence (*sattvapāta*), and the latter is used for medicinal herbs and the like. (Rcūm 10.111)
Rasaka destroys all types of urinary disorders (prameha), eliminates phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta),
cures eye diseases and consumption (kṣaya), and serves as a coloring agent for iron and mercury. (Rcūm 10.112)

Both mercury and the high-quality *rasaka* (calamine) have been described by Nāgārjuna; these two excellent perfected elixirs (*siddharasa*) are supreme for the transformation of the body and for the production of iron [into gold].
He by whom both mercury and its derivative (rasaka) have been made fire-resistant possesses,
without a doubt, the accomplishment of alchemical success regarding the body and metals as his servant.
Copper sulfate (kharpara), when thoroughly heated and immersed seven times within the juice of the citron (bījapūra), attains complete purity. (Rcūm 10.115)
Having been heated and thoroughly immersed in human urine, sheep’s urine, buttermilk, or sour gruel,
the *rasaka* mineral is completely purified in an iron pan.
When kept in human urine for one month, *rasaka* certainly dyes [the metals]:
pure copper becomes mercury-like, and pure silver likewise acquires the luster of gold. (Rcūm 10.117)

{The extraction of essence from *rasaka* (1):} Having ground a crucible with turmeric, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *rāla*, rock salt, *dhūma*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and *aruṣkara*, each in a one-fourth portion, together with acidic substances; Rcūm_10.118.
Having smeared a bottle-gourd into the crucible and dried it, and having sealed the crucible,
one should place a shallow dish over the mouth of the crucible and then blow upon it.
If, when the crucible has been removed, the flame becomes blue or white,
then one should hold the crucible with tongs and turn it face downwards.
One should strike it gently against the ground so that the stalk does not break; having taken up the substance that has fallen, which has the luster of tin, one should employ it. (Rcūm 10.121)

In this way, after three or four cycles, all the essence (*sattva*) shall emerge. {This is the extraction of the essence from *rasaka*.} Alternatively, one should bury a vessel filled with water inside the belly of a crucible. (Rcūm 10.122)
One should place a perforated crucible over its mouth and an inverted crucible over its mouth;
then, having cast fire upon the crucible, one should heat it firmly. (Rcūm 10.123)
One should take the essence fallen into the water of the crucible and combine it; having placed that essence together with *tālaka* into an iron pan (*kharpara*), [one should proceed]. (Rcūm 10.124)
One should roast it with an iron rod until it certainly turns to ash; [this is the preparation of] *rasaka* (calamine) as a medicinal substance for use after it has been killed.
That ash, when mixed with an equal amount of the juice of the *mṛtakānta* plant, [is used]. // Rcūm_10.125 //
Eight *guñjā*s of this powder, combined with a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
should be placed in a vessel of magnetic iron (*kāntaloha*) at night and infused with sesame oil.

When regularly consumed, it certainly and swiftly destroys even diabetes mellitus (madhumeha), as well as bile disorders (paitta), consumption (kṣaya), jaundice (pāṇḍu), edema (śvayathu), and abdominal tumors (gulma). (Rcūm 10.127)
It cures the blood-born *gulma* of women, menorrhagia, and *somaroga*, as well as all diseases of the female reproductive tract (*yoni*), irregular fevers,
menstrual pain, cough, asthma, and hiccups. (Rcūm 10.128)
Mākṣika is of two kinds: hemamākṣika (golden mākṣika) and tāramākṣika (silver mākṣika).
[The origin of svarṇamākṣika:]
Among these, the first is *mākṣika*, originating from Kānyakubja, which resembles gold in appearance.
That which originates on the banks of the Tapatī river, resembling gold of five colors, is called *tāpya*; it is said to abound in stones and possesses few qualities. (Rcūm 10.130)

Mākṣīka mineral destroys all diseases, is the very life-force of mercury, and is an excellent aphrodisiac; it is the unifier of the two metals that are difficult to fuse, possesses superior qualities, and is the foremost among all elixirs (rasāyana). (Rcūm 10.131)
{Purification of honey}:
Honey is purified when processed with castor oil and citron juice.
{Purification of honey}
And it is accomplished in two ghaṭikās in the juice of plantain roots.
{Purification of honey-gold (mākṣika):} Honey-gold attains purity when heated and cast into a decoction of *varā*.
{Killing of honey-gold (mākṣika):}
Ground with the juices of *mātuluṅga* and *ambuda*, it should be placed inside the crucible.
Indeed, honey is killed when burnt five times with packets of *eraṇḍa* oil, cow’s ghee, and the juice of *mātuluṅga*. (Rcūm 10.134) [Honey:: Killing]
When firmly heated in a crucible, it becomes well-baked and resembles metal;
thus, once killed, it may be employed in alchemy as well as in the procedure for elixirs (*rasāyana*). (Rcūm 10.135)
Combined with one-thirtieth part of lead (nāga) and processed with alkalies and acids, roasted in an open crucible, the *mākṣika* ore releases its essence (*sattva*). Rcūm_10.136 //

Having melted the essence of honey-metal (*mākṣikasattva*) seven times and cast it into the juice of *nirguṇḍikā*, lead mixed with the essence of honey-metal will certainly be destroyed. (Rcūm 10.137)
The essence of *tāpya* (calamine), when purified, has a luster like a *guñjā* seed and melts like liquid lead; it is supreme for producing both the body [of mercury] and iron.
{Honey-based elixir (1)} Having made a paste of mercury with the essence of honey, and having placed an offering into it while it is melted;
having mixed and rubbed it together in the middle of a mortar, one should add the essence of quicksilver and the essence of mica. (Rcūm 10.139)
Having formed a pill in a vessel called *lavaṇayantra*, one should cook it for half a day over a gentle fire.
Once it has cooled naturally, one should grind it well and take a dose of one *valla* combined with sugar and *viḍaṅga*. (Rcūm 10.140)
Consumed with honey, it destroys old age along with its diseases and even untimely death;
it overcomes even incurable maladies after being taken seven times. Even the nectar of immortality is not equal to this. (Rcūm 10.141)
{Honey-based elixir (2)}:
half a part of purified cinnabar stone, half of that amount of purified mica, half of that amount of magnetite, and half of that amount of copper ash. (Rcūm 10.142)
Having combined everything together in one place, one should join it with equal amounts of fragrance;
having rubbed it with the juice of *nimbū*, one should subject it to heating in a closed crucible (*prapuṭa*) ten times.
One should prepare that [medicine] by grinding it with a hundred forest lotuses and twenty-one applications of water from Vyoṣa and Bāhlīka. (Rcūm 10.144)
Indeed, processed green vitriol (*mākṣika*) destroys all diseases, as well as consumption, jaundice, skin diseases, malabsorption syndrome, and ailments of the rectum. (Rcūm 10.145)

It cures weak digestion, jaundice, wasting, hoarseness of voice, loss of appetite, various forms of severe fevers, disorders of undigested matter (āmadoṣa), and choleraic vomiting (visūcikā). (Rcūm 10.146)

All those various diseases arising from wind, bile, and phlegm are [cured] without exception by the administration of after-drinks (anupāna) according to their respective suitability; among all the great medicinal juices (mahārasa), *tāpya* alone is considered the best. (Rcūm 10.147)
Rcūm, 11:
{The secondary minerals (uparasas)} are those named gandhāśman, tāla, tuvarī, kunaṭī, sauvīraka, kaṅkuṣṭha, khecara, and gairika.
The wise have spoken of secondary elixirs (uparasa) as being elixirs; however, with those [substances], even the best mercury, when bound, would not constitute an elixir.
Sulfur is indeed to be known as fourfold according to its colors, beginning with white.
[White sulfur]
In this context, "white" refers to chalk for the purpose of plastering and for the alchemical killing of metals.
Likewise, that which is of yellow color is *āmalasāra*; it is indeed *śukapiccha*, and it is the best for the elixir of mercury (*rasarasāyana*). (Rcūm 11.3)
Red sulfur,
known as *śukatuṇḍa*, is excellent for the practice of alchemy; [so too is] black sulfur.
That black-colored [substance] is difficult to obtain, and it is the destroyer of old age and death.

Sulphur (gandhāśman) is an excellent rejuvenator (*atirasāyana*), sweet in taste, pungent and hot in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and it subdues itching, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), and ringworm (*dadrū*). It kindles the digestive fire, acts as a digestive (*pācana*), releases undigested matter (*āma*), and is drying. It is an antidote to poison, bestows the potency of mercury (*sūtendra*), and, when derived from *gaurīpuṣpa*, it destroys worms; it is of the nature of essence (*sattva*) and overcomes mercury. (Rcūm 11.5)
Sulfur was formerly consumed by Bali for the sake of obtaining great strength;
as he was dragging Vāsuki, it was melted by the flame from his mouth.
The fat, rich with the scent of sulphur, issued forth from every part of the body;
it attained the state of being sulphur, and from that, the poison became fragrant.
Therefore, sulphur, which is exceedingly captivating, is called *balivasā*.
When sulphur has been steamed in milk for the duration of one *ghaṭī* and then washed with water, it is indeed purified. (Rcūm 11.8)
When washed with cow's clarified butter and strained through cloth, it attains purity;
thus thoroughly purified, it casts off the stones within it into the sky. (Rcūm 11.9)
Just as poison in clarified butter takes on the form of chaff and becomes a solid lump by itself, so too the pure sulphur (gandhāśman) abandons its transformation into lead. 11.10.
If handled otherwise due to negligence, it would kill like the Hālāhala poison when drunk;
however, sulphur (gandhaka), once melted, becomes purified when cast into the juice of *bhṛṅga*. (Rcūm 11.11) [Sulphur:: Purification]
Sulfur, having been steamed seven times with its juices, becomes completely purified.
{The purification of sulfur (3)} Having poured milk into a vessel and tied a cloth over its mouth, Rcūm_11.12.
Having placed powdered sulfur there in the form of sand,
one should cover that sulfur with a wide and long earthen pan.
One should heat it above a crucible with forest chaff and stones;
when the scent falls into the milk and dissolves, it becomes completely purified.

Thus, when purified and mixed with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), clarified butter, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and honey, and consumed in a dose of one *śāṇa*, it makes the pair of eyes equal to those of a vulture and bestows a long life free from disease. (Rcūm 11.15)
Take sulfur combined with a one-sixteenth part of the three pungents (vyoṣa), finely powdered;
having scattered it over a cloth measuring one cubit (aratni) in length, wrap it up. (Rcūm 11.16)
Then, having wrapped it with thread, one should immerse it for a watch (yāma) in oil;
holding the wick with tongs, one should then set it entirely ablaze. (Rcūm 11.17)
The liquefied fragrance should fall drop by drop into a glass vessel;
one should place three drops of that liquid upon a leaf of the betel vine (*nāgavallī*).
One should thoroughly rub the pure mercury measured by a *valla* with [the plant];
then, with the finger, one should consume that liquefied extract along with its leaf and the mercury. (Rcūm 11.19)
It produces intense digestion, destroys consumption, anemia, cough, dyspnea, pain, and even the most difficult-to-cure malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī). (Rcūm 11.20)
Pure sulfur, when melted in an iron vessel smeared with ghee, quickly destroys undigested matter (āma) and produces lightness. (Rcūm 11.21)
One should consume two niṣkas of it, cast from a ladle smeared with ghee;
it destroys diseases such as consumption and, in particular, leprosy. (Rcūm 11.22)
For the benefit of one's health during the consumption of pure sulfur, one should indeed avoid alkaline substances, acids, oils, fermented gruel, pungent foods, and pulses. (Rcūm 11.23)
Sulfur mixed with an equal amount of black pepper, combined with six times its weight of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
and rubbed with the root of *śampāka*, when drunk, destroys all forms of skin disease (*kuṣṭha*). (Rcūm 11.24)
One should grind its root in water and apply it to the body every day; this is a proven remedy, possessing irresistible power in all cases. (Rcūm 11.25)
The illustrious Somadeva has correctly proclaimed here:
having drunk two niṣkas of sulphur combined with oil. (Rcūm 11.26)
Then, having anointed his entire body with Apāmārga water mixed with oil and black pepper, he should thereafter remain in the heat of the sun.
In the third watch of the day, one should indeed eat rice with buttermilk;
likewise, having risen early in the morning, one should attend to the sacred fire at night.
Having smeared himself with buffalo dung, he should bathe with cold water;
then, having anointed his body with ghee, he should bathe with pleasantly warm water. (Rcūm 11.29)
By this sequential method, it is certain that even long-standing, difficult-to-conquer scabies and itching will be destroyed with extreme rapidity. (Rcūm 11.30)
A thousand applications of the fragrant substances have not been proclaimed here by King Somadeva, for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Haritāla is said to be of two kinds: that called *patra* (leaf-like) and that known as *piṇḍa* (mass-like). [The leaf-like variety:
*pattratālaka*.
Its physical properties are:
it is gold-colored, heavy, glossy, capable of being made into thin leaves, and radiant.
That is called leaf-tālaka; possessing many leaves, it is an elixir (rasāyana).
{Piṇḍatālaka: physical properties}
Leafless, resembling a lump, possessing very little vitality, and likewise heavy—that which steals the menses of women is the piṇḍatālaka, deficient in its qualities. (Rcūm 11.33)

Haritāla (orpiment) is said to destroy phlegm, wind, poison, blood disorders, and malevolent spirits; it specifically removes the menstrual flow of women. It is unctuous, hot, pungent, digestive, and a destroyer of skin diseases. (Rcūm 11.34)

{Purification of Haritāla}: It is purified by means of the *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) when steamed in the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd, or in water mixed with sesame alkali, or in water combined with powders. (Rcūm 11.35)
Having placed haritāla mixed with kulattha decoction, saubhāgya, buffalo ghee,
and curd into a vessel, one should cover it with a lid provided with a hole. (Rcūm 11.36)
Having properly restrained the fire, one should kindle it, increasing it gradually;
indeed, for the duration of one watch (three hours), one should cover the opening with cow-dung.
At the end of the watch, having opened the aperture and seeing pale smoke,
one should remove the cool vessel, extract the essence, and take it.
There are indeed millions of varieties of all types of stone-beings;
however, fearing excessive prolixity in the text, I have certainly not written of them here.
That which is easy to perform everywhere, easily obtained, and bestows fruit— precisely that is described here among the mercury, secondary minerals, and metals.
One should grind *pattrālaka* with the milky sap of the sun-plant (*arka*) for one day to effect the falling of the essence (*sattvapātana*).
Having cast the sixteen-year-old [girl] into oil and mixed her therein, one should then cook it.
And in an unobstructed place, one should certainly collect a white being that has been lying beneath for seven watches until its body has become cold. (Rcūm 11.42)
Then, having diligently ground haritāla (orpiment) together with the excrement of a young goat for two days, one should cause its *sattva* to fall. (Rcūm 11.43)
One should place it, combined with the group of fluxing agents, inside a glass flask;
having smeared it three times with clay and dried it thoroughly in the hot sun, [one should proceed].
Then, having inserted that half-cup and the small jar into the opening of the crucible,
one should kindle the fire for a period of twelve hours.
One should collect the white essence situated at the neck of the crucible when it has cooled.
Having bound half a *pala* of *haritāla* (orpiment) in a firm, white cloth, [one should proceed with the extraction]. (Rcūm 11.46) [Extraction of the Essence of Haritāla]
Having smeared it with *balī* with effort, one should dry it three times;
when three *pala* of copper have been liquefied, one should throw the *tālaka* (mica) packet into it. (Rcūm 11.47)
One should quickly cover it with ash, encased in copper, and white; from this, one should extract the soft essence, as prescribed for the elixir of mercury.
That fine earth produced from the mines of Saurāṣṭra which is considered *tuvarī*—
that which adheres to garments and binds the dye of madder— is [the substance known as] *tuvarī*. (Rcūm 11.49)
Tubarī is proclaimed to be of two types: phaṭikā and phullikā.
[Regarding phaṭikā: its physical characteristics are as follows:
Slightly yellow, heavy, and unctuous, the *pītikā* variety destroys poison.
*Phullikā* removes wounds and leprosy, and specifically destroys all types of *kuṣṭha*.
That which is weightless, white in color, glossy, and slightly sour is considered superior;
it is called *phullatuvarī*, and by its application as a paste, iron quickly moves [becomes malleable]. (Rcūm 11.51)
Tutthaka (tutthi) is astringent, pungent, and sour; it is beneficial for the throat, promotes hair growth, destroys wounds, and neutralizes poison.
It removes vitiligo, is good for the eyes, pacifies the three *doṣas*, and acts as an antidote to mercury. (Rcūm 11.52)
{Purification of Tuvarī}:
Tuvarī attains purification after being placed in *kāñjika* for three days. {Extraction of the Essence from Tuvarī}
When rubbed with alkaline and acidic substances and then blown upon [in a furnace], it certainly releases its essence.
Realgar (manaḥśilā) is said to be of three types: Śyāmāṅgī, Kaṇavīrikā, and that called Khaṇḍā; its characteristics are described here after having been analyzed. (Rcūm 11.54)
Śyāmāṅgī has dark limbs; Śyāmā is red, while Sagaurā is pale; Śyāmikā is considered to be heavy.
Kaṇavīrikā...
Physically,
it is radiant, not pale, and has a coppery luster like that of the *kaṇavīra* flower.

The *khaṇḍapūrvikā* has limbs that are powdered and exceedingly red; it possesses its constituent ingredients and is proclaimed to be superior to the preceding types, containing an abundance of *sattva*.
Realgar (*manaḥśilā*) is the foremost of all elixirs (*rasāyana*); it is bitter, pungent, and hot, and it destroys phlegm and wind.
Being of the nature of consciousness (*sattva*), it removes possession by spirits, poisons, sluggish digestion, itching, and skin eruptions (*koṭha*). (Rcūm 11.57)
Realgar is purified by being infused seven times with water from the leaves of the Agastya plant,
or else with the juices of ginger. (Rcūm 11.58)

Manahshila (realgar) releases its essence when it is sealed within a crucible with an eighth part of its own dross, along with jaggery, guggulu, and clarified butter, and then strongly heated. Rcūm_11.59

Having prepared a crucible with *kāravellī* leaves and water, one should place therein realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *bhūnāga*, purified *saubhāgya*, and *madana*, all thoroughly ground together. (Rcūm 11.60)
Immediately thereafter, one should blow [the breath] upon a stone ground with alkaline acid;
indeed, when blown for just two ghaṭikās, it releases its essence (sattva).
Sauvīra collyrium is declared [the first], followed by rasāñjana;
then there is sroto’ñjana, and another is indeed puṣpāñjana.
For their true nature here is described as being like blue collyrium.
Sauvīrāñjana is smoky-colored, cold, and removes *rakta-pitta* (bleeding disorders);
it destroys vomiting, hiccups, and eye diseases, and it cleanses and heals wounds. (Rcūm 11.63)
And *rasāñjana*, which has a yellowish luster, removes poison, blood disorders, and diseases.
It cures dyspnea and hiccup, improves the complexion, and destroys wind, bile, and blood disorders.
Srotoñjana is cooling, unctuous, astringent, sweet, and scraping.
Indeed, *netrī* cures hiccups, poisoning, vomiting, and the provocation of phlegm, bile, and blood.
Pushpāñjana is white, unctuous, and cold; it cures all eye diseases.
It is extremely difficult to restrain, yet it destroys hiccups and removes poisons, fevers, and diseases.
Blue antimony (nīlāñjana) is heavy, unctuous, beneficial for the eyes, and removes the three humors (doṣas).
It is a rejuvenative (rasāyana), it destroys gold [impurities], and it softens iron. (Rcūm 11.67)
Minerals are purified by the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* leaves;
[this is] the precipitation of the essence of the minerals.
One should collect the essence of the collyriums, which possesses a being like that of Manohvā.
Kaṅkuṣṭha is produced on the peaks at the foot of the Himavat mountains. [Regarding the subtypes of kaṅkuṣṭha:]
Among those, one is indeed called the *nalikā*, while the other is considered to be the *reṇuka*.
The first type of *kaṅkuṣṭha*, known as *nālikā*, is yellow in luster, heavy, and unctuous; it is the best.
As for *reṇuka*: [it is]... [its physical properties].
Indeed, *reṇuka* that is dark, yellow, light, and devoid of essence is not desired.
Regarding *kaṅkuṣṭha* [as originating from feces], some say that it is the excrement of a newborn elephant;
it has a dark yellowish appearance and is described as a purgative. (Rcūm 11.71)
Some say that the substance known as *kaṅkuṣṭha*, which has the appearance of white and yellow, is a very potent purgative. (Rcūm 11.72)
Kaṅkuṣṭha is the best for elixirs (rasāyana) when it is devoid of essence and free from many defects; it is bitter and pungent, hot in potency, and a powerful purgative. (Rcūm 11.73)
Kaṅkuṣṭha removes wounds, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), colic, pain, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, and anal pain;
it becomes purified by being soaked three times in the best water. (Rcūm 11.74) [Kaṅkuṣṭha: Purification]
The extraction of its essence has not been described because it is composed of essence itself.
[This concerns the medicinal use of kaṅkuṣṭha.]
One should consume this for the purpose of purgation with a dose the size of a barley grain, along with substances that cause constipation.
It destroys undigested matter and, having purged it in a mere moment, when eaten with betel leaves, it quickly causes purging and eliminates [the disorder]. (Rcūm 11.76)
A person should drink repeatedly an equal mixture of the decoction of *barbūrī* root, cumin, and *saubhāgya*, along with *kaṅkuṣṭha*, for the destruction of poison. (Rcūm 11.77)
Kāsīsa is of two types: one beginning with *vālukā* and another beginning with *puṣpa*.
[The first is] *vālukākāsīsa*.
Kṣārāmla is heavy, smoke-colored, hot in potency, and an antidote to poison. Vālukāpūrvaka kāsīsa destroys vitiligo and dyes the hair. (Rcūm 11.78)
Flower-copperas (puṣpākāsīsa), which is very well known, is heating, astringent-sour, and exceedingly beneficial for the eyes.
It destroys diseases caused by poison, wind, and phlegm, as well as wounds; it cures leucoderma and consumption, and it dyes the hair black.
Kāsīsa becomes stainless when moistened once with the water of *bhṛṅga*. [This is the purification of kāsīsa.
Regarding the precipitation of the essence (*sattva*) of kāsīsa:
One should extract the essence from this as well, just as one extracts the essence from *tuvarī*.
Regarding the use of *kāsīsa*:
iron *kāsīsa* killed by mercury and *kānta* iron killed by *kāsīsa*—both in equal parts combined with *triphalā* and *vella*. (Rcūm 11.81)
Taken in the morning at the dose of one śāṇa, soaked in equal parts of ghee and honey, it swiftly destroys leucoderma, anemia, and consumption. (Rcūm 11.82)

When consumed for the duration of a year according to the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana), it completely cures abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, colic, and urinary diseases without exception. (Rcūm 11.83)
The consumption of *āmā* is excellent for kindling a weak digestive fire;
it certainly destroys gray hair along with wrinkles. (Rcūm 11.84)
There are two types of red ochre (*gairika*): the first is stone ochre (*pāṣāṇagairika*) and the second is golden ochre (*svarṇagairika*).
[Regarding stone ochre:]
The mineral red ochre (pāṣāṇagairika) is said to be hard and copper-colored.
Stone-ochre (pāṣāṇagairika) is sweet, unctuous, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, astringent, and a subduer of blood-bile (raktapitta).
Gold ochre (svarṇagairika) destroys hiccups, vomiting, and poison; it also cures hemorrhaging.
And another variety, stone-geru, is inferior in its qualities compared to the former.
Regarding the purification of red ochre (*gairika*):
indeed, red ochre attains purity when processed with cow's milk.
Regarding the extraction of the essence (*sattva-pātana*) from red ochre: [it is as follows].
For red ochre is indeed proclaimed by Nandin to be the form of *sattva*.
Some have said that a sattva falls from gairika heated with alkaline acid;
it attends upon the lord of mercury (sūtendra) and becomes a single substance of superior quality. (Rcūm 11.89)
{Common substances}: Kampilla, and furthermore gaurīpāṣāṇa, navasāraka, kaparda, vahnijāra, girisindūra, and hiṅgula. (Rcūm 11.90)
Boddāraśṛṅga and the others—these eight are considered common minerals;
they are declared by the masters headed by Nāgārjuna to be effective for the perfection of alchemical elixirs. (Rcūm 11.91)
*Kampilla* resembles brick powder, is rich in luster, and is highly purgative. It is found in [the region of] Kampilla.
For that *kampillaka* is considered to have originated from the country of Saurāṣṭra.

Kampillaka destroys bile-born ulcers, flatulence, and constipation; it is the enemy of phlegm, abdominal pain, worms, and tumors. It removes colic in the bowels, fever, and swelling, and as a purgative, it dispels diseases. (Rcūm 11.93)
Gaurīpāṣāṇaka is yellow, irregular, and reduced to powder.
Gaurīpāṣāṇa binds mercury, is unctuous, destroys the [three] humors, and enhances the potency of rasa.
When the wood of the *karīra* and *pīlu* trees is being burnt, an alkaline substance arises; this is *navasāra*, known by the name *cūlikā-lavaṇa*.
The light, white salt produced by burning bricks is called *navasāra*; it is also known as *cūlikālavaṇa*. (Rcūm 11.96)
Navasāra (caustic alkali) facilitates the digestion of mercury, liquefies metals, and stimulates the digestive fire;
it destroys abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, and dryness of the mouth, and promotes the digestion of consumed meat and other foods.
And that which is called *viḍa* salt is considered a *cūlikā-lavaṇa* (peak salt) that destroys the three *doṣas*.
The cowrie shell (*varāṭikā*) is yellowish in luster, knobby on its back, and possesses a long stalk-like opening.
It is designated by physicians of mercury as "the one named Carācara" (moving and unmoving).
The best [cowrie shell] is valued at one and a half *niṣkas*; the middling is said to weigh one *niṣka*;
and the lowest is proclaimed to weigh three-quarters of a *niṣka*.
[The medicinal properties of the cowrie shell:
It cures colic resulting from indigestion and other such disorders, and destroys chronic diarrhea and consumption.
Pungent and hot, it stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and removes wind and phlegm.
It is prescribed for the digestion of mercury and is recommended among the substances used in *biḍa* salts.
But other varieties of cowrie shells are heavy and increase phlegm and bile.
Indeed, cowries do not undergo purification by being repeatedly washed and then subjected to further transformations;
they attain purity only after being soaked in sour gruel for a watch (three hours). (Rcūm 11.102)
The placenta of the fire-crocodile was cast out by the ocean;
dried up by the heat of the sun, it is known as *agnijāra* (fire-born). (Rcūm 11.103)
{Purification of agnijāra}:
It is thoroughly purified by sea salt; therefore, no further purification is required for it.
{Medicinal properties of agnijāra}
Agnijāra destroys the three *doṣas*, cures *dhanurvāta* and other wind disorders, increases the potency of *rasa*, and likewise acts as a digestive stimulant and a digestive ferment.
Among the great mountains, there is a small amount of liquid situated within the stone; when dried, it is red and designated by the name *rasasindūra*. (Rcūm 11.105)
Girisindūra pacifies the three doṣas, acts as a purgative, and is the foremost among those that bind mercury.
Girisindūra is said to be beneficial for the body, for iron, and for the eyes.
Cinnabar is of two types: that called *śukatuṇḍa* and another known as *haṃsapāka*.
[Regarding the properties of *śukatuṇḍa*:]
Among them, the first, possessing few virtues, is called the *carmāra*.
Haṃsapāka is said to have white streaks and the luster of coral. Darada [is described as follows].
Cinnabar destroys all defects, stimulates digestion, and is an excellent elixir.
It removes all diseases, is aphrodisiac, and is highly praised for the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*).
The mercury extracted from this *hiṅgulākṛṣṭa* is equal in its qualities to mercury that has been processed with sulfur (*jīrṇagandha*). (Rcūm 11.109)
Cinnabar is purified by being dried and then soaked seven times with the juice of fresh ginger or with the water of *lakucha* fruit;
thus it becomes truly free from defects.
The *bodāraśṛṅga* gem,
possessing eight facets and yellow in color, is found in the region of Gurjara.
On the side of Mount Arbuda is situated Boddāraśṛṅgaka.
Lead ore (sīsasattva) pacifies wind and phlegm and removes male diseases.
It is the most excellent binding of mercury and the supreme means for dyeing hair black.
All common metallic essences (sādhāraṇa-rasa), having been processed three times with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and water, and then dried, become free from defects. (Rcūm 11.113)
The common flavor:
the purification of the *sattva*—
whatever beings there may be, they are all purified without exception.
Blown by the group of purifiers, they meet with one another.
Rcūm, 12:
[The twelve jewels] are ruby, pearl, coral, emerald, topaz, diamond, and sapphire; [and the remaining four are: cat's-eye, moonstone, lapis lazuli, and amber.
Gomedaka and then Vidūraka are the gems of the nine planets in their respective order.

For the attainment of desired success, one should wear as amulets, in their respective order, the planets' friendly gems: kuruvinda, coral, pearl, emerald, diamond, sapphire, hessonite, and cat's-eye.
For the purpose of attaining success in alchemy, elixirs, giving, wearing [amulets], and the worship of deities, gems of excellent characteristics and noble origins are prescribed. (Rcūm 12.3)
The first subtype is called *māṇikya* or *padmarāga*, and the second is *nīlagandhi*.
{Examination:}
It is cool, possessing the luster of a lotus, clear, unctuous, heavy, and transparent.
A ruby that is round, well-proportioned, and symmetrical in all its parts is said to be the best.
Regarding the examination of the blue variety:
that which originates from the waters of the Gaṅgā is blue, with an interior hue of blue and an outer luster of reddish-brown.
That ruby, excellent like a former ruby, has a blue luster.
{Examination:
Poor Quality} It is endowed with porosity, hardness, impurity, dryness, and clarity.
A ruby that is flattened, light, and crooked is defective in eight ways.
Ruby possesses medicinal properties: it is digestive, aphrodisiac, and removes the afflictions caused by phlegm, wind, and consumption;
it destroys evil spirits, vampires, and sins, and eradicates diseases born of past actions.
A pearl of excellent quality is pleasing, white, light, glossy, radiant, pure, and large.
The pearl known as *toyaprabha* is round and auspicious; thus, the pearl is of nine types.
A pearl that is rough-textured, waterless, dark, copper-colored, or resembles salt is of inferior quality.
One should discard pearls that are half-white, misshapen, or knotted.

Pearl is considered to destroy phlegm, bile, and consumption; it cures cough, asthma, and weak digestion; it is nourishing, aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and a quencher of burning sensations. (Rcūm 12.10)
Having the luster of a ripe bimba fruit, circular and elongated, and free from curvature.
Lustrous, free from blemishes, and thick—coral is considered to be of seven such types.
Pale, greyish, rough, scarred, and possessed of cavities— these are the characteristics of inferior coral.
Coral that is free from weight and of a bright white color is considered to be of eight kinds.
Coral (vidruma) destroys consumption, bile, and hemorrhaging, cures cough, stimulates digestion, is easily digestible,
pacifies poisons and malevolent spirits, and removes eye diseases. (Rcūm 12.13)
An emerald of excellent quality is green in color, heavy, lustrous, radiant with a multitude of shimmering rays, and auspicious.
The body of Tārkṣya is considered smooth, radiant, and endowed with seven qualities.
Brownish, rough, bluish, pale, black, and light— these are the qualities of an inferior emerald.
A tortoise that is flat, deformed, black, or rough is not commended as a Tārkṣya.

Emerald (tārkṣya) removes fever, vomiting, poison, asthma, and the derangement of the humors (sannipāta), as well as weak digestion; it cures hemorrhoids, anemia, and swelling, and increases vitality (ojas). (Rcūm 12.16)
A top-quality *puṣparāga* (topaz) is heavy, glossy, transparent, large, even, and soft.
It has the luster of a *karṇikāra* flower, is smooth, auspicious, and eightfold.
Lacking luster, rough, dry, yellowish, dark, and unevenly raised and depressed— these are the characteristics of an inferior puṣparāga gem.
One should avoid that which is brownish-red, tawny, pale, or the color of a topaz.

Topaz (puṣparāga) removes poison, vomiting, phlegm, wind, and sluggish digestion; it pacifies burning sensations and skin diseases, stimulates the digestive fire, is light, and acts as a digestive aid. (Rcūm 12.19)
The *vajra* is said to be of three types: male, female, and neuter.
Each preceding one is more excellent than the next in terms of its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect.
The male vajra is said to be eight-sided, having eight facets, six-cornered, and exceedingly brilliant; it resembles a water droplet, a rainbow, or a man. (Rcūm 12.21)
That very [vajra] with a flattened shape is the female vajra (*strīvajra*), which is circular and elongated;
[this is] the neuter (*napuṃsaka*).
That which is circular, with a blunt corner-tip and somewhat heavy, is neuter.

The female, male, or neuter *vajra* should be joined with the female, male, or neuter [consort] respectively; through inversion it yields no fruit, and nowhere is there success without the male *vajra*. (Rcūm 12.23)
Each of these is fourfold according to the distinction of colors, such as white and so forth;
they are Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, bestowing the fruits corresponding to their respective castes.
"For indeed, even the highest and most excellent caste yields its fruit when [placed] upon a low caste;
this principle was declared by Bhairava regarding all things whatsoever. (Rcūm 12.25)

Vajra bestows longevity, swiftly grants excellent qualities, is aphrodisiac, pacifies the three humors, and destroys all diseases; it effects the binding and killing of mercury, acts as a digestive stimulant, and like nectar, conquers death. (Rcūm 12.26)
Swallowing, trembling, a dot, a line, and containing water— these five defects are considered common to all jewels. (Rcūm 12.27)
"Defects arising from the field or the water do not adhere to jewels," Bhairava replied, "but a defect remains a defect in every respect."
Vajra, having been steamed for the duration of one watch (three hours) in a decoction of *kulattha* beans or in a decoction of *kodrava* grain, is certainly purified. (Rcūm 12.29)
The *vajra* [mantra] should be visualized four times with the blood of a bedbug;
then, having wrapped it with pills made from the flesh of fragrant mice, one should proceed. (Rcūm 12.30)
Thereafter, one should seal it with thirty applications of the so-called "boar" (varāha) puṭas;
then, having repeatedly heated it a hundred times, one should immerse it in a decoction of horse gram (kulattha).
Others have stated that this ritual procedure should be performed one hundred times with a paste made by grinding *lakucha* juice mixed with a decoction of horse gram (*kulattha*). (Rcūm 12.32)
Having placed the vajra in a crucible smeared with clay and sealed it,
one should properly roast it eight times with dried wild blue lotuses.
Then, having blown [the furnace] one hundred times, when pure mercury has been cast [into it],
the diamond is certainly killed and becomes ash that is easily soluble in water.
Satyavāk, the commander of Soma’s army, who was curious about alchemy and possessed of verified experience, spoke this lethal application of the vajra.
Smeared seven times with the blood of a bedbug and dried,
it is then placed in an iron vessel filled with the juice of *kāsamarda*.
When blown upon seven times, it indeed becomes vajra-ash;
this sequence was proclaimed by the lord of sages, Brahmajyoti.
When the blue *jyotirlatā* root is rubbed upon a diamond and dried in the heat,
the diamond is reduced to ashes, just as karma is by the fire of gnosis.
Having smeared [the substance] with a paste made from the juice extracted from the fruit of *madana* and earthworms, one should roast it twenty times in a closed crucible (*puṭa*). (Rcūm 12.39)
Then, having powdered that vajra and combined it with a small amount of borax, // Rcūm_12.40 //
One should certainly cause twenty *kharabhūnāga* units to revolve;
when smelted with an equal amount of gold, it should be added to mercury and other substances. (Rcūm 12.41)
Having thoroughly ground it with a threefold amount of juice and formed it into pills, holding one in the mouth quickly cures the looseness of the teeth. (Rcūm 12.42)
Vajra-ash, measured at thirty parts; gold, one-sixteenth part; silver, eightfold; the excellent nectar of Śivā (mica), one-eleventh part;

calamine, one-fourth part; vaikrānta, eightfold; and rasaka, sixfold—this is declared to be the "extracted juice from the aforementioned juices" for the sake of achieving the sixfold qualities. (Rcūm 12.43)
The *jalanīla* sapphire and the *indranīla*, and among those two, the *śakranīla* is the best.
[Examination of the *jalanīla*:]
That which has a blue luster with whiteness within it is light, the *jalaniilaka*;
that which has a blue luster with blackness within it and possesses weight is the *śakranīla*. (Indranīla Examination) *Ratnacuḍasūtra* 12.44.
A sapphire of excellent quality is uniform in luster, heavy, glossy, transparent, and compact in form.
The excellent blue [mantra] consists of seven syllables, with its light shining softly and moderately. (Rcūm 12.45)
The *jalanīla* gem is of seven kinds: it may be soft, or of excellent color, or weightless, or fragrant with a scent of blood, or flat in appearance, or rough. (Rcūm 12.46)

Sapphire is said to cure cough and asthma, to be aphrodisiac, to destroy the three *doṣas*, and to be a great stimulant of digestion; it destroys intermittent fevers, hemorrhoids, and sin. (Rcūm 12.47)
{Gomeda: Etymology} Gomeda is called the *gomeda* gem because of its resemblance to the color of a cow.
{Gomeda: Examination}
Gomedaka of excellent quality is praised as being of eight kinds: resembling the luster of very clear cow's urine, transparent, glossy, even, heavy, free of flaws, smooth, and radiant. (Rcūm 12.48)
Lacking luster, light in weight, rough in texture, flattened, and covered with a film— such is a low-quality *gomeda*.
A *gomeda* that is lusterless and has the appearance of yellow glass does not bring good fortune.

Gomeda destroys phlegm and bile; it cures consumption and anemia, stimulates digestion, promotes the digestion of food, improves the appetite, is beneficial for the skin, and awakens the intellect. (Rcūm 12.50)
{Examination of Vaiḍūrya:
Good Quality} Vaiḍūrya that is dark-blue and bright in luster, even, clear, heavy, and translucent [is of good quality].
It is declared that [the posture] is auspicious when the beautiful upper garment is tucked in and arranged in a circular fashion.
A low-quality *vaiḍūrya* is dark, has a luster like water, is flattened, light, and rough.
A red inner garment and lapis lazuli are not at all recommended.
Vaiḍūrya (lapis lazuli) destroys *rakta-pitta* (bleeding disorders), increases wisdom, longevity, and strength,
cures diseases dominated by *pitta*, stimulates digestion, and facilitates the elimination of waste. (Rcūm 12.53)
A ruby is purified by acid, likewise a pearl by *jayantī*;
coral by the group of alkaline substances, and emerald by cow’s milk.
One should purify a *puṣparāga* with fermented rice-gruel mixed with the decoction of *kulattha* beans;
a *vajra* with the water of *taṇḍulīya*; a *nīla* with the juice of indigo; a *gomeda* with yellow orpiment; and a *vaiḍūrya* with the water of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (Rcūm 12.55)
With *śilā*, *gandhaka*, and *tālaka* ground together with the juice of the *lakuca* fruit,
other gems— excluding diamond— are indeed killed by means of eight crucibles.
As for the liquefying agents (*druti*): asafoetida, the five salts, the three alkalies,
meat-liquefier, *amlavetasa*, and likewise *cūlikālavaṇa*.
The ripe fruit of the *sthalakumbhī*, as well as the auspicious *jvālāmukhī*, *dravantī*, *rudantī*, *payasyā*, and *citramūlaka*. 12.58.
Then, having diligently crushed all the milk of the *snuhī* and the *arka* plants together, one should form a ball and subsequently place [the mercury] into its center. (Rcūm 12.59)
Having fashioned that ball from birch bark— made of virtuous, noble, and auspicious gems— and having carefully wrapped it with thread, [one should place it within].

Then, having wrapped it again with cloth and placed it in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) inside the belly of a jar completely filled with a fermenting mixture (*saṃdhāna*) containing all types of acids; 12.61.
One should subject it to sweating with a fierce fire for three days and nights;
then, having extracted it and washed it thoroughly, one should take the liquid essence produced from the jewels.
It possesses a luster equal to a gem, is light, beneficial for the body and for iron, and is auspicious;
yet, because it is difficult to fuse with the king of mercury (rasarāja), it does not attain oneness with it.
It undoubtedly mingles with the group of substances beginning with asafoetida;
when Mahādeva is well-pleased, for whom does liquefaction not succeed? (Rcūm 12.64)
Devotion to Viṣṇu is indeed difficult to attain; the binding of aesthetic relish (rasa) is difficult to attain;
and the melting [of the heart] in this world is difficult for men of meager fortune to attain. (Rcūm 12.65)

The wearing of gems is declared to always remove the afflictions caused by the sun and other planets, bestow long life, health, the rise of good fortune, luck, subjugation, wealth, and energy, grant fortitude, and take away the misfortune arising from contact with bad omens and shifting dust; it destroys all calamities such as those caused by malevolent spirits.
The foremost among the virtuous, the jewel-like Soma, spoke to the collection of all the qualities of jewels, saying "No," for he himself was possessed of those very qualities.
A gem endowed with the proper color, marks, and birth bestows its fruit;
this varies according to whether it is used for alchemy, elixirs, giving as a gift, or wearing as an ornament.
Rcūm, 13:
One *karṣa* of auspicious *māṇikya-rasāyana*, which is *māṇikya* ash possessing the qualities of a noble species;
The ash of gold, mica, copper, and kāntaloha [iron] should be taken separately.

One should rub that which has increased through the three qualities with equal parts of fragrant substances, and then carefully subject it to five rounds of firing in a forest-fire ash and mountain-soil crucible.
In this manner, one should prepare an auspicious collyrium (kajjalī) from realgar, orpiment, blue antimony,
and equal parts of fragrant stone and mercury.
Then, having carefully taken that kajjalī, immediately thereafter,
one should melt it in an iron vessel over a mild fire of *bādara* wood.
Having cast the ashes of ruby and other gems into it, one should mix them therein;
then, having ground that collyrium with the juices of *ārdraka*, [one should apply it]. (Rcūm 13.5)
Having thoroughly dried and powdered it, one should then place it in a beautiful casket;
this elixir, beginning with māṇikya, is equal in measure to the three pungents (vyoṣa) and clarified butter. (Rcūm 13.6)
If one who eats wholesome food licks this together with *vyoṣa* and clarified butter for six months, it destroys all diseases, including those of old age and gray hair. (Rcūm 13.7)
Taking food only three times a day, he shall live for a hundred years,
free from all diseases such as consumption and other ailments, by means of the appropriate medicinal drinks.
{The Elixir of Pearl}:
Pearl, ground with the juice of *jayantī* and killed with *śukapiccha*, [is taken] in a quantity of one part; gold ash, however, is two parts. (Rcūm 13.9)
Having added three parts of ash produced from *kāntaloha* and four parts of the essence of the sky (*vyomasattva*), one should then add *gandhasaubhāgya* processed with ginger.
Having roasted it twenty times and melted it through a cloth filter,
one should prepare a collyrium with an equal amount of mercury and *bali* juice.
Having caused [the obstacles] to flee as before, one should scatter ashes, pearls, and other such items;
having mixed them together, one should pour into that place milk produced from a goat.
Having dried it thoroughly and then powdered it, one should place it in a glass flask;
when consumed in a dose of one *valla* along with long pepper and honey, [it yields great results]. (Rcūm 13.13)
Indeed, by means of the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana), within a year he makes [himself] free from wrinkles and graying hair, and devoid of old age.

Endowed with good ears, teeth, and other [faculties], possessing a lifespan of a hundred years and keen sight, he is endowed with the strength of an elephant in rut and achieves victory in debate. (Rcūm 13.15)
Licked with honey, ghee, and oil, along with *kaṇa* and *aśvagandhā*, this certainly destroys the disease of consumption (*kṣayaroga*) within half a month; this is certain. (Rcūm 13.16)
Taken with appropriate adjuncts for various diseases, it destroys all ailments;
indeed, it bestows sons upon barren women and is a destroyer of postpartum disorders. (Rcūm 13.17)
It is supremely wholesome for children, an excellent aphrodisiac, and bestows longevity;
when taken while seated upon a python's belly, it also overcomes the excessive flow of women.
Combined with *haiyaṅgavīna* ghee and mixed with sugar, it is proclaimed to be highly recommended for all diseases of pregnant women. (Rcūm 13.19)
*Pravālarasāyana*:
Four *palas* of coral ash and an equal amount of dead silver (*mṛtatāraka*); copper twice that [of the coral ash], and half as much *ākṣika* as the coral. (Rcūm 13.20)
The vajra consists of thirty parts, and the blue [pigment] sixteen parts;
the *vyomasattva* is equal to all [the other ingredients], and the *tālaka* is equal to everything else.
Having rubbed it with the juice of *luṅga* for four days,
[one should then treat] the mercury that is half-purified by all [the aforementioned means], followed by twice as much sulphur (*gandhaka*).
Having properly melted the prepared kajjalī as before, one should cast in the ashes of coral and other substances and thoroughly mix them. (Rcūm 13.23)

Having properly extinguished [the fire] with cow's ghee that is twelve years old, and having enclosed it within a pair of earthen saucers, one should slowly steam it while smeared with ghee. (Rcūm 13.24)

Having powdered it, one should saturate it with *bhṛṅga* juice seven times; combined with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*) and clarified butter, it destroys the disease of colic within three days. (Rcūm 13.25)
And by means of half the maṇḍala, one cures consumption, malabsorption syndrome, anemia, jaundice, the disease of chronic jaundice, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), and ascites. (Rcūm 13.26)

It completely cures urinary disorders (prameha), the increase of fat (medas), diseases of the wind (vātavyādhi), ailments of phlegm (kaphāmaya), diseases of the anus, weak digestion, and disorders of urine and flatus. (Rcūm 13.27)
It completely cures diseases of the temples, seminal disorders, sterility, and skin ailments by means of trikaṭu, ghee, and citrata water taken as an after-drink. (Rcūm 13.28)
For a person in whom the pain of cholera arises again and again,
this elixir should indeed be administered for three cycles;
furthermore, it should be given by physicians for as long as a year in cases of chronic digestive disorders.
One *śāṇa* of *tārkṣya* (guggulu) ash, half that amount of *vajra* (diamond) ash, and two *niṣkas* each of purified gold, *arka* (copper), and *kānta* (iron) [are to be taken]. (Rcūm 13.30)
One should grind iron ash and dead mercury together in one place,
and then roast them twenty times using the so-called *kukkuṭa* (cock) type of *puṭa* vessels.

One should roast it ten times with seven applications of liquid consisting of *amṛta*, water, realgar (*śilā*), sulphur (*gandhaka*), and yellow orpiment (*tālaka*), along with ten applications of the powder.

Thus is established this elixir named Tārkṣya, rich in potency; when drunk mixed with a small amount of black mustard and combined with the juices of *citraka* and fresh ginger, it is perfected. (Rcūm 13.33)

It causes excessive hunger for all diseases born of the three humors (tridoṣa), as well as those arising from phlegm and wind (kapha-vāta), even those incurable by all physicians despite millions of medicines; it digests what has been eaten in an instant. (Rcūm 13.34)
{The Elixir of Topaz}: One and a half *pala* of auspicious ash derived from topaz, half of that amount of yellow glass, and half of that amount of copper ash. Rcūm 13.35.
Half copper and half silver, with gold equal to half of that;
half of that again is diamond ash, and the same amount as all of these combined is dead mica.
One should indeed roast that [substance] together with an equal amount of sun-crystal (sūryakānta) and mercury (balin),
and then repeatedly coat it ten times with an equal amount of mercury.
The individual capsules of blue collyrium and lotus stalks as well; thus is declared this perfected elixir of topaz.

It destroys all diseases such as consumption, is the supreme remover of leprosy, alleviates the pain of hemorrhoids and abdominal tumors, and is excellent for procuring sons, aphrodisiac, and highly rejuvenating. (Rcūm 13.39)
Likewise, this is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that quickly removes abdominal tumors (gulma) in women;
it is declared to be a supreme digestive stimulant (dīpana) and a destroyer of jaundice and anemia.
What more need be said here? It is the destroyer of all diseases. (Rcūm 13.40)
One *karṣa* of *vajrarasāyana* consists of one part of dead *vajra*, an equal amount of *bhūnāgasattva*,
twice that amount of gold, and an amount of *khasattva* equal to the gold. (Rcūm 13.41)
All that amount of iron is made entirely water-like;
and one-eighth part of mercury is proclaimed to be superior to all [the other metals].
One should grind together equal parts of *śukapiccha* and sour chickpeas;
having formed this into a beautiful ball (*golaka*), one should dry it in the shade. (Rcūm 13.43)
Then, one should indeed cast the substance *bhūnāga* together with sulfur;
having been enclosed [in a crucible], it should be heated a hundred times and subjected to a hundred cycles of heating.
Then, having milked the *sūryaparṇa* leaves twenty times,
it should be covered with the powder of *bhūnāga*, along with *guñjā*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and beeswax.
Having rolled that ball, one should smear it with this paste;
then, having dried it in the hot sun until it is half a finger-thick, [one should proceed].
One should place it in a sand-oven and cook it for five days;
thereafter, with the milky sap of *gaṇḍīra* growing on a triangular ground, combined with sulfur, [it should be processed].
Having kneaded that ball, one should roast it twenty times;
then, having made a powder from the cloth, one should place it inside a casket.
One should consume this delightful vajra-rasāyana in the measure of a guñjā seed for all various diseases, whether known or unknown.
Indeed, it should be administered by the physician along with appropriate adjuncts for each specific disease;
for there is no disease in this world that is not pacified by it. (Rcūm 13.50)
When consumed according to the method of elixirs (*rasāyana*), it certainly brings about the perfection of the body—causing wonder to the entire world—for three cycles;
with the single exception of the *bilva* fruit, everything else is proclaimed here to be wholesome. (Rcūm 13.51)
One *pala* each of the ash made from blue gems (*nīlarasāyana*), diamond,
gold, silver, magnetite, pyrite, and *nṛpavartaka*. (Rcūm 13.52)
All of this should be in equal proportions, and the mercury (śulvaka) should be equal to all of it.
All of this, once reduced to a powder (mṛta), should be taken together with an equal amount of sulfur (gandhaka).
One should grind it with *kaṅguṇī* oil for eight days;
having applied sulfur above and below, one should roast it twenty times in a closed crucible (*puṭa*). (Rcūm 13.54)
Thereafter, one should saturate it seven times with the juice of white muṇḍī;
thus is perfected the beautiful blue elixir (nīlarasāyana), rich in power. (Rcūm 13.55)
When consumed in a dose of one guñjā, it destroys all diseases:
fever, anemia, consumption, cough, colic, hemorrhoids, and abdominal tumors. (Rcū 13.56)
Abdominal enlargement, leprosy, and likewise the five types of asthma—each of these is eradicated by the application of its respective medicinal treatment. (Rcūm 13.57)
Having subjected gomedaka stone to a process of heating (puṭa) ten times with a mixture of fragrant substances and the juice of *lakucha*, one *pala* of ash is produced. (Rcūm 13.58)
Gold, silver, and lovely [substances], all of which have been processed with medicinal herbs,
are transmuted by a quarter-step [of mercury] when treated with the water from the crest [of the mountain].
When the substance to be heated is processed ten times with gandharva oil and subjected to the puṭapāka method,
it becomes ash that is "niruttha" (without residue), which is in every respect superior in its qualities.
Having melted the kajjalī prepared from half that amount of mercury and sulphur,
one should throw the three previous ashes into it, mix them thoroughly, and collect the resulting compound.
Having pulverized it, one should saturate it seven times with the juices of *muṇḍikā*;
then, having made it into a fine powder, one should place it inside a casket. (Rcūm 13.62)
For this is the supreme and most excellent *gomedaka* elixir;
it should be employed for all diseases, accompanied by appropriate adjuncts according to each specific ailment.
It produces an intense illumination, is worthy of all, and is pleasing;
it bestows supreme nourishment and strength comparable to that of Bhīma;
it is the highest aphrodisiac, promotes longevity, is beneficial for the eyes, and removes diseases of the mouth. (Rcūm 13.64)
Vaidūrya-rasāyana:
Vaidūrya, together with its fragrance, is killed by means of an ointment of *kānta* iron;
with one-eighth of a *śāṇa* of that ash, and half as much dead gold (*mṛtahema*). (Rcūm 13.65)
Equal parts of sharp iron filings and dead silver,
and equal parts of dead and pure [mercury], all being thoroughly rubbed together.
Having mixed it with the essence of *mocaka* and formed it into pills, one should dry them;
then, one should rub them with *śilājatu* in a paste the thickness of half a finger-breadth. (Rcūm 13.67)
One should cook it slowly for half a fortnight inside a sand-bath apparatus;
once it has cooled naturally, one should collect it together with the essence of the root of the *kumārī* plant.
Having crushed it and then dried it with the water of *pīlu* roots, and likewise with the water of *citra* roots and the essence of *kanthārī* roots; (Rcūm 13.69)
Having dried it with the juices of *cirabilva* and having reduced it to powder,
this is indeed the "Reviver of the Dead," the elixir (*rasāyana*) of *vaidūrya*.

A dose the size of a *guñjā* seed, combined with the juice of fresh ginger or with variegated waters, should be administered as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) in cases of unconsciousness due to *sannipāta*.
Once the binding of the teeth has been accomplished, one should diligently rub this juice, measuring a *valla*, upon the two feet; thereafter, one shall attain the desired effect.
When he has begun to move, one should pour cool water, sweet and measured at a hundred *kumbhas*, upon his head; from that, intense hunger arises. (Rcūm 13.73)
Whatever anyone asks for, that desired thing should be given to him;
as long as his lifespan remains, that man lives happily.

In diseases arising from the three humors (tridoṣa), [this medicine] should be administered in the measure of one *taṇḍula* (rice-grain) combined with half a *pala* of sugar; otherwise, it kills the patient. (Rcūm 13.75)
When a disease arises from a single humor, or likewise when it is produced by a combination [of humors],
the physician must certainly not administer the Vaidūrya elixir.
When these jewels are worn, honored, of noble origin, and well-praised, they remove every misfortune and constantly fulfill one's desires exactly as wished. (Rcūm 13.77)
These elixirs (rasāyana), which bestow longevity, are beneficial and produce all kinds of jewels; they constantly remove misfortune and all diseases here produced by evil deeds. (Rcūm 13.78)
Rcūm, 14:
Pure metal consists of gold and silver; base metals consist of copper, iron, and the essence of stone (cast iron); and two types of impure metal are declared, namely lead and tin.
The three alloys are declared to be mixed metals; brass, bell-metal, and copper are considered metals. The word *loha* is understood to mean metal, and it also signifies "to be scraped. (Rcūm 14.1)

Gold is traditionally said to be of five types: the natural, the innate, that produced by fire, that produced from a mine, and that born from the transmutation by the lord of mercury (rasendra). Rcūm_14.2 //
That by which the material cosmic egg is indeed enveloped, having arisen from the quality of rajas,
is called "Prākṛta"; it is difficult to attain even for the gods.
The innate Brahmā was born enveloped by a golden placenta;
that gold, having assumed the form of Mount Meru, is indeed that which is innate.
The Śaiva splendor, born of fire and emitted by Agni, was drunk [by the gods]; though extremely difficult to endure, it became gold.
That which was thus designated is "suvarṇa," the gold born of fire.
This divine triad of gold, endowed with sixteen qualities,
shall by its mere wearing make the body free from old age and death.
Whatever is produced from the mines in various mountains is called *khanija*; enriched with fourteen colors, when consumed, it removes all diseases. (Rcūm 14.7)
That which is produced by the transmutation (*vedha*) of the lord of mercury (*rasendra*) is declared to be "born of transmutation" (*vedhaja*).
Indeed, that which is born of transmutation is the most excellent elixir (*rasāyana*), a destroyer of sins. (Rcūm 14.8)

Silver is said to be that which arises from mercury, tin, and mica, or from tin, mercury, and gold-ore (mākṣika); indeed, by virtue of its color, it is gold when it possesses four times the quality of the color of a single digit (kalā). (Rcūm 14.9)
When rubbed, it is red in color like saffron; when heated and cut, it is slightly white, not brownish, free of fissures, and possesses great weight.
Gold that is smooth, devoid of streaks, rich with a thick red luster, and possesses an incomparable, radiant, and beautiful color is declared to be the best.
Gold that is rough, discolored, dull, hard, and black when heated, yet pale on the touchstone, is of inferior quality.
One with thick limbs, one who is excessively corpulent, one who is tawny, and one whose gold-like complexion is blotchy—these ten types are not auspicious.
Through the combination of gold, silver, and other [metals], mixed metal (*miśraloha*) is produced.
[Its] purification is achieved by means of [the following].
Goldwork would not be possible by means of that [impurity]; therefore, purification is prescribed.
It is not only gold that must be purified; one should purify other metals as well. (Rcūm 14.12)

A gold leaf weighing one *karṣa*, covered with a protective sheath (*śarāva*) and treated with potent minerals, should be placed upon charcoal for half a *prahara*; when blown [with a bellows], it will indeed attain its full color. (Rcūm 14.13)
The killing of all metals is best accomplished by means of mercury-ash;
they say it is middling when done with root-herbs, and inferior when done with sulfur and other such substances. (Rcūm 14.14)
The killing of iron with copper imparts inferior qualities;
having performed [the killing], one should smear gold leaves that have been pierced by thorns. (Rcūm 14.15)
By means of ten *puṭa* applications of mercury processed with *luṅga* juice and ashes, [the metal] is killed;
one should then cast the killed mercury, in a quantity equal to the weight of the metal, into molten gold.
Having powdered it and combined it with realgar and the juice of *luṅga*,
gold with the luster of saffron is produced after twelve *puṭa* applications.
For the purpose of killing and ensuring non-rebirth,
[one should use] the stalks of *śleṣmāntaka*, along with the tubers of *kāñcanāra* and those known as *kukkuṭa*.
Through thirty measures, there shall be no further rebirth; this should also be applied to all the yogas without exception.
Having made a paste with mercury extracted from gold, one should seal the gold in a shallow dish;
combined with a small amount of blue collyrium, it is then burnt with a few forest lotuses.

The ash, which has the luster of saffron, should be employed in the alchemical processing of mercury; [it is prepared] with the milk of *snuhī*, asafoetida, cinnabar, realgar, vermilion, and sour gruel.
Folded ten times, it becomes lifeless gold;
it is highly praised for use in alchemy, elixirs, and the coloring of metals.
Gold is unctuous, promotes intellect, removes poison and toxins, is nourishing, a preeminent aphrodisiac, supreme for pacifying consumption and insanity, and destroys diseases of the body.
Gold produces intelligence, intellect, memory, and happiness; it destroys all defects and diseases, is appetizing, digestive, pacifies old age, and has a sweet post-digestive effect.
