This ash produced from gold, taken in a dose of two *guñjā* with *kaṭu* and ghee, destroys consumption, loss of digestive fire, and debility in men, along with asthma, cough, and anorexia. It increases the *ojas* and bodily constituents, bestows strength, cures anemia, acts as an aphrodisiac, removes all poisons, wards off evil spirits, and eliminates disorders of the *grahaṇī*. (Rcūm 14.23)
It utterly destroys all diseases without exception, removes the fear of *bhūtas* and *pretas*, binds future ailments, and dispels the fear of the three poisons. (Rcūm 14.24)
In this practice, everything else is commended except for the bilva fruit.
For one who has practiced for ten years, no disease whatsoever shall afflict him—provided he eats and moves about according to his own will—for as long as he lives; of this there is no doubt.
Silver is considered to be of three types: innate, produced from a mine, and artificial; indeed, each preceding one is superior to the next in its own qualities. (Rcūm 14.26)
Silver originating from mountains such as Kailāsa is "innate" (sahaja);
indeed, when touched, it becomes the destroyer of great diseases for embodied beings. (Rcūm 14.27)
That silver which is produced on the peaks of the Himācala mountains is indeed called *khanija* (mineral-born) by those who know it; for it is the supreme elixir.
That mercury which, when applied to the sandals of Śrī Rāma, has attained the state of silver, is called *pādarūpya* (sandalsilver); it is artificial and destroys all diseases. (Rcūm 14.29)
Silver of good quality is dense, glossy, soft, and translucent; it is white when heated or cut, and heavy.
Silver that has the luster of a conch shell, is smooth, free from pockmarks, and auspicious; Rcūm 14.30.
Silver of inferior quality is red, yellow, or black when heated; it is rough, porous, and light.
Silver that is coarse-grained and rough-textured should be rejected; thus, [silver] is to be avoided in eight ways.
For the purification of silver:
one should prepare a crucible using ash and powder all around; having placed the silver there together with an equal amount of tin, [one should proceed]. (Rcūm 14.32)
One should repeatedly smelt it until the lead and tin are exhausted;
then the purified silver, being clear, may be added to the mercury and other substances.
One should prepare a paste of silver using the juice of *lakuca* and urine; having placed sulfur above and below it, one should seal it within the interior of a crucible. (Rcūm 14.34)
One should heat it in a sand-vessel (*vālukāyantra*) for one day with a steady fire;
once it has cooled of its own accord, that paste should be ground together with sour *tāla* (mica).
If one performs twelve *puṭa* roastings, silver is reduced to ashes;
likewise, iron filings (*mākṣika*) ground with the juice of *luṅga* and subjected to slow roasting [is similarly destroyed]. (Rcūm 14.36)
When that mercury is subjected to thirty cycles [of heating], it becomes ash;
there is no doubt that all metals will become red upon an excess of *puṭa* (roasting).
And they dye those that are red, serving the purpose of both the body and metals.
Silver has a sweet post-digestive effect (vipāka), a slightly astringent and sour essence, is cold, laxative, highly scraping, and appetizing.
It is unctuous, subdues wind and phlegm, kindles the digestive fire, provides strength, stabilizes youth, and is aphrodisiac.

Pure silver that has been reduced to ash, along with equal parts of space (ether) and the sun (gold), combined with all [the aforementioned ingredients] and mixed with *trikaṭu*, honey, and clarified butter— when licked in the morning, it utterly destroys consumption (*yakṣma*), anemia, abdominal diseases, hemorrhoids, cough, asthma, eye diseases, old age, and all disorders of bile without exception. (Rcūm 14.39)
Copper is of two types: *mleccha* and *nepālaka*; of these two, *nepālaka* is the best.
That which arises from a mine other than Nepal is designated as *mleccha*.
Mlecchatāmra has a white, black, or reddish luster; it is brittle and hard.
And yet, when washed, this copper of the barbarians turns black once again.
Nepalese copper is very glossy, soft, red, capable of withstanding heavy hammering, and heavy.
Copper that is free from defects and excellent in its qualities is called Nepāla.
Copper that is pale, blackish-red, light in weight, and characterized by cracking is of inferior quality.
A copper with rough surface, impurities, or a verdigris-like patina is not desired for alchemical work.
Excessive moisture, delusion, dizziness, burning, and piercing pain are indeed the difficult-to-subdue defects of copper.
Through purification, it becomes free from its own defects and, in its taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation, becomes like nectar. (Rcūm 14.44)
Copper, combined with alkalis and acids, melted and mixed with red ochre, should be immersed seven times in the buttermilk of a buffalo and in dried cow-dung cakes. (Rcūm 14.45)
It becomes free from the five defects and fit for the application of ash.
{The purification of copper:} Copper leaves, beaten thin and smeared with sea salt... [Rcūm 14.46]
By blowing [the fire] and throwing [the copper] into *sauvīraka* eight times, it is purified.
Having been smeared with *nimba* water and *paṭu*, they are heated eight times. (Rcūm 14.47)
Copper leaves are purified by immersion in the juice of *nirguṇḍī*;
one should then prepare copper leaves that have the appearance of palm leaves. (Rcūm 14.48)
Having boiled it in sour gruel for one watch (yāma) and purified it with ashes,
and having boiled it in milk for one watch, one should leave it in that very [liquid] for a day.
For one day, having wrapped it in a paste of tamarind fruit mixed with salt and ground with the juice of jambīra, and then with pungent [salt], [one should proceed].
Having blown [the bellows] into it, one should immerse half of the copper once in the midst of goat's urine, along with rock salt and boiled lemon juice. (Rcūm 14.51)
Having smeared it and blown upon it, one should cast that copper into buttermilk mixed with buffalo dung;
then, [the copper] combined with an equal portion of gold and *mākṣika* [pyrite]. (Rcūm 14.52)
Thereafter, one should heat it once with very firm charcoal;
then, without using crucibles, one should form the *cakrikā* three times.
Then, one should let it sit for three days in a decoction of the three pungents (trikaṭuka);
thereafter, having boiled it again, wiped it with ash, and washed it with honeyed water.
Having smeared it three times with white *sāragha* honey, one should enclose it in *vanotpala* leaves; the copper will then become equal to gold in its qualities.
When a copper leaf is placed between two leaves of the *kumārī* plant and enclosed within them,
it becomes free from defects and turns white.
Copper thus purified, being free from all defects, becomes fit for alchemy (*rasāyana*) and is supreme for bringing about the transformation of the body and metals. (Rcūm 14.57)
Only Śiva or Nandikeśvara understands this purity;
likewise, only the illustrious Somadeva, the refuge of all the worlds, and no other.
Copper struck by mercury and processed seven times will be completely freed from all defects and become like nectar.
Having smeared copper leaves with a paste made from the juice of *lakucha* fruit ground with fragrant minerals, and having placed them inside a vessel, one should seal it shut. (Rcūm 14.60)
One should cook it properly for exactly one watch (yāma); once the copper is reduced to a powder, one should grind that ash and wrap a dose of one *valla* in a betel leaf. (Rcūm 14.61)
Then, having induced vomiting and purging for two watches of the night after consuming it,
one destroys fever in men, even when accompanied by colic and flatulence.
Poison and *gara* certainly cause vomiting with great force;
in this case, wholesome *gotakraka* mixed with rice should be administered. (Rcūm 14.63)
In cases of excess, excessive vomiting, or extreme distress, one should apply cooling remedies according to the specific requirements of each situation.

In the case of excessive vomiting, one should consume cooled, fried pieces of sugarcane, or alternatively, one should have the patient drink a decoction made from bilva fruit mixed with sugar. (Rcūm 14.65)
The juice of *barbūra* bark should be drunk with buttermilk for purgation,
together with mercury equal in weight to copper and an equal amount of *balī*.
Having prepared a smooth kajjalī, resembling split collyrium, with a thickness of half that part and a width of half that again, using both a mallet and a stone; (Rcūm 14.67)

Within the interior of a crucible as specified in the chapter on mechanical devices (*yantrādhyāya*), one should alternately place lampblack and copper leaves; one should cook them for the duration of a *yāma*, and once they have cooled naturally, one should grind them into a powder. (Rcūm 14.68)

Copper is bitter and astringent, sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), hot in potency (vīrya), and slightly sour; it subdues pitta and kapha, and brings an end to abdominal pain, skin diseases, indigestion, and colic.

It purifies both upward and downward, removes grossness caused by sensory objects, stimulates hunger, cures hemorrhoids, consumption, and anemia, is beneficial for the eyes, and is an excellent scraping agent.

Copper, measured at two *vallīs* and taken with appropriate adjuncts that alleviate specific diseases, when licked, certainly cures chronic abdominal pain (*pariṇāma-śūla*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), fever, tumors (*gulma*), splenic disorders, liver ailments, consumption, loss of digestive fire, urinary disorders (*meha*), diseases of the bladder (*mūlāmaya*), and malignant dysentery (*duṣṭa-grahaṇī*); this is known by the name Somanātha. (Rcūm 14.70)
Nothing else is as sweet and free from defects as this copper;
nothing else destroys all defects completely, is aphrodisiac, and is suitable for healthy men. (Rcūm 14.71)
With one *pala* of copper for the killing [rite], and with that same substance measured by a *rajju*,
together with the best of poisons— *viṣatindu*, *agniśamyāka*, *vatsanābha*, and *paṭu*— {copper:: māraṇa}.
Having made a powder of *kalihārī* stone, *vyoṣa*, *tāla*, betel nut (*pūga*), and *karañjaka*, it should indeed be thoroughly liquefied with the juice of *jambīra*. (Rcū 14.73)

Having placed all of that indeed into a single vessel, thereafter one should hide within that paste copper leaves weighing one *pala* each, which have been pierced with needles and upon which a portion of mercury has been smeared. (Rcūm 14.74)

This [medicine], proclaimed by Śrī Somadeva, produced from the richness of all its qualities, when consumed in a dose of two *guñjā* seeds along with parched grain and clarified butter, indeed destroys abdominal enlargement caused by spleen, liver, and constipation; it cures colic, sluggish digestion, and diseases arising from wind, phlegm, and wasting, as well as the multitude of *pāṇḍu* disorders and chronic fever when eaten. (Rcūm 14.75)
One should give wholesome food appropriate for the disease and avoid sour tastes;
by him for whom this has become habitual, death is conquered. (Rcūm 14.76)
Iron is known to be of three types: *muṇḍa*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *kānta*. As for *muṇḍa*, its subtypes are as follows:
The shaven head (muṇḍa) is said to be of three kinds: soft, blunt, and tawny.
{Softness::
physical properties} It flows easily when melted, does not crackle, is smooth, supple, and auspicious.
{Dullness:: physical properties}
That which, when struck, emits a sound like a bursting water-pot is known as the *muṇḍa* of the middle quality;
that *muṇṇḍa* which breaks with a black sound upon fracture is the *kaḍāraka*.
Muṇḍa is exceedingly soft; it cures disorders of phlegm and wind, colic, abdominal distension, urinary disorders, jaundice, and anemia.
It indeed cures abdominal tumors, disorders of undigested food (āmavāta), and stomach ailments; it stimulates digestion, removes swelling, promotes blood formation, and purifies the internal organs.
Hard, strong, *honnāla*, *tārāpaṭṭa*, *bhājara*, and that which is called black iron (*kālaloha*): these six types are said to be *tīkṣṇa* (sharp/iron). (Rcūm 14.80)
That which is rough, free from dross, possesses the brilliant luster of mercury when broken, and bends yet remains resilient, is declared to be *kharaloha*. (Rcūm 14.81)
That iron which has a blade fragile due to its velocity is called *sāra-loya*; that which is pale, appears as if joined with gold, and originates from the earth is called *sāra*. (Rcūm 14.82)
That which has a body that is blackish-white, possesses thighs resembling the beak and seed of a *cañcu* bird,
and is extremely harsh when cut, is called *honṇāla*. (Rcūm 14.83)
That which is covered with dense, fine lines resembling diamonds due to its mineral impurities, and whose body is dark-colored, is proclaimed as *bhājara*. (Rcūm 14.84)
Kālāyasa (black iron) is considered to have a dark-blue or black luster, to be dense, smooth, heavy, and radiant; its edge remains unbroken even when struck by other metals. (Rcūm 14.85)
Everything beyond iron is superior to each preceding one by a factor of one hundred.

Kharaloha is dry, very sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cold in potency (vīrya). It is bitter and hot; it destroys phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal ailments, spleen disorders, and anemia (pāṇḍu). It immediately removes colic, liver diseases, wasting (kṣaya), old age, urinary disorders (meha), and rheumatism (āmavāta). It is highly stimulating, an excellent rejuvenator (rasāyana), strength-promoting, and it eliminates hemorrhoids and obesity. (Rasendracūḍāmaṇi 14.87)
Magnetite (kāntaloha) is said to be of four types: romaka, bhrāmaka, cumbaka, and drāvaka; among these, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
From whatever beautiful stone (*kāntapāṣāṇa*) being excavated radiant hairs indeed emerge, that beautiful [stone] is considered *romaka*. (Rcūm 14.89)
The magnetizing stone (*bhrāmaka*) is easily found here and there on the finest of mountains; by casting iron into its mouth, it certainly revolves like a wheel. (Rcūm 14.90)
On the Vindhya mountain, magnetic stones attract an iron pin;
they draw it forth with great speed, just as a woman captivates the heart of young men.
That substance which, upon contact, completely liquefies metals such as gold and the like,
is obtained with great difficulty on the mountain Tuṣāradhara.

When a drop of oil spreads upon its surface without clinging, when asafoetida does not release its own odor, and when a paste of neem does not impart its bitterness; when milk being boiled forms a peak-like crest and does not spill onto the ground—that is the *kāntaloha* (magnetite) described by the defining characteristics, and nothing else. (Rcūm 14.93)

Kāntaloha (magnetite) is the most excellent among the supreme elixirs; it bestows long life upon the healthy, is unctuous, cures urinary disorders, pacifies the three *doṣas*, and removes colic and indigestion.

It alleviates diseases of the abdominal tumors (*gulma*), spleen, liver, and wasting, destroys jaundice and abdominal dropsy, is bitter and hot in taste yet cold in potency—what more need be said? Through its application, it removes all ailments. (Rcūm 14.94)
All iron possesses qualities increasing ten-fold at each successive stage;
magnetic iron possesses ten-million-fold qualities, and even that is further superior in its qualities.
Iron, including all varieties such as muṇḍa and the rest, when smeared with rabbit blood and heated three times, is freed from all defects. (Rcūm 14.96)
Iron purified by being heated with sea salt and then quenched in a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) will surely abandon its mountain-born defects. (Rcūm 14.97)
{Iron Purification (3)} A decoction of the fruits and leaves of the tamarind tree and so forth removes impurities.
{Iron Purification (4)}
Alternatively, one may boil it for a moment in cow's urine together with the three fruits.
Having cast iron filings mixed with mercury and sprinkled with clarified butter into an iron pan,
one should cook it while stirring with an iron rod until even a blade of grass thrown into it is consumed by the fire. (Rcūm 14.99)
Having ground it repeatedly in this manner five times, one should cook it with the juice of *dhātrī* leaves or with water boiled with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (Rcūm 14.100)
Iron that has been processed four times in a crucible will indeed become as light as water; [this is] the killing of steel.
The leaves of steel, stripped of their impurities, [should be placed] in a firm fire. (Rcūm 14.101)
Having blown [the fire] and immediately cast it into water within the hollow of a stone mortar, one should grind with violent blows using a thick iron pestle. (Rcūm 14.102)
Having taken coarse fragments from among them and placed them between two pestles, one should heat them, douse them thoroughly with water, and then grind them as before. (Rcūm 14.103)
One should roast that powder twenty times with jaggery and sulphur;
after each roasting, it must be ground again most thoroughly. (Rcūm 14.104)
Thus, iron reduced to ash should be applied for its respective diseases.
Now, regarding the previously mentioned sharp iron (*tīkṣṇaloha*), it should be processed with *vasubhallaka* and *vāsa*. (Rcūm 14.105)
If one carefully folds it thirty times with leaf-water,
the ash produced will take on the appearance of vermilion.
Alternatively, having ground iron ash— or the powder produced from sharp-edged leaves— with the juice of the three myrobalans (triphalā),
one should add a small amount of cooked rice and form it into a disc.
Having dried it with great effort, one should cook it with five *puṭas*;
for that ash is red in color and should be employed according to the specific requirements.

Having smeared all the iron with *matsyākṣī*, *gandha*, and *vāhlīka* ground together with the juice of *lakuca*, and having concealed it within a paste of *matsyākṣī*, [one performs] the *niruttha* killing of iron. (Rcūm 14.109)

Having blown [the crucible] very firmly with two bellows until the trident emerges, one should then take it out and cast it into a decoction consisting of the three myrobalans and cow's urine. (Rcūm 14.110)
Therefore, having taken it out and struck it, and having taken the dead iron,
one should blow it again as before and kill all the metal.
Having then roasted it together with fragrant jaggery and triphalā, one should seal it in a *puṭa* twenty times; it will certainly become *niruttha*.
Iron ash, equal in quantity to sulphur, along with iron powder, should be rubbed with Kumārī juice;
after being formed into a mass and kept in the shade for some time, the iron indeed dies [is reduced to ash]. (Rcūm 14.113)

This ash of iron, which prevents rebirth, is indeed a divine nectar and a perfectly accomplished elixir (*rasāyana*). When combined with *trikaṭu*, *vella*, clarified butter, and honey, a dose of one *niṣka* destroys old age, death, and diseases; it bestows virtuous sons. This was formerly prescribed by the illustrious Giriśa for the sake of Kālayavana’s father when he had fallen ill.
For those who cultivate this practice, accumulations of disease do not arise;
moreover, a glorious son is born, endowed with intelligence, fortitude, and strength.
One should prepare this ash using black iron (kālaloha) and magnetite (kāntaloha), which are of superior quality.
Ash produced from other metals does not possess such qualities as these.
Iron that has been ground with *matsyākṣī*,
milk, and *gandhāśman* is heated twenty times in a closed crucible (*puṭita*); it then becomes an irreducible ash.
Then, one should cook eight *pala* of that ash with eight times its quantity of cow’s urine in an iron vessel, stirring it with an iron ladle. (Rcūm 14.118)
Thus, this perfected iron, when measured at two vallas, destroys all diseases arising from their respective humors. (Rcūm 14.119)

It cures consumption, jaundice, abdominal tumors, colic, and diseases of the roots (genital-urinary tract), as well as urinary disorders, obesity, weak digestion, enlargement of the liver and spleen, and jaundice.
It cures dyspnea, cough, leprosy, and fever accompanied by pain. (Rcūm 14.121)

Kāntaloha (magnetite) equal in weight to the essence of mica, four *caraṇas* of gold, an equal amount of *arka*, *vaikrānta*, *tāpya*, silver, and equal parts of *krimiripu* and *kaṭuka*—when licked with the oils of *devadru*, this bestows upon men abundant perfection of the body; and when taken as a wholesome diet as previously described, it swiftly removes the entire multitude of diseases. (Rcūm 14.122)
This delightful elixir of love destroys all diseases; it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, conducive to the birth of noble sons, auspicious, and a supreme stimulant of the digestive fire. (Rcūm 14.123)
Half a *palā* of iron, impregnated with semen, should be ground repeatedly with the juice of young *bilva* fruit and cooked; it will indeed quickly be reduced to ashes. (Rcūm 14.124)
Likewise, by means of the juice of *liṅgī* fruit and water, and with the juice of *dhātrī* fruit, one should kill the metal as before; it becomes even more excellent in quality. (Rcūm 14.125)

The ash of all types of iron, taken in a dose of one *śāṇa*, along with the alkalis of *punarbhū*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *apāmārga*, *vajriṇī*, and the bark of *tintiḍī*, [is used for medicinal purposes]. (Rcūm 14.126)
A person should drink a decoction combined with triphalā every month for the purpose of purifying *maṇḍūra*, the dross of iron; otherwise, urinary calculi (*aśmarī*) arise. (Rcūm 14.127)
For impure metals, vomiting [of impurities] is considered necessary, as if it were poison;
however, for the sake of purification, Nandin has declared that purified metal is equal to nectar. (Rcūm 14.128)
If one consumes daily for six months, at dawn, a handful of sweet water from *varāmitrā* kept overnight in an iron bowl (*kānta-śarāvaka*),
it will indeed destroy various diseases of bile and phlegm, as well as leprosy, urinary disorders, anemia, consumption, jaundice, intestinal worms, and wind-born ailments. (Rcūm 14.129)
Impure iron that has undergone re-melting, having demonstrated its medicinal qualities, may produce only a small effect.
It causes indigestion, weak digestion, loss of appetite, abdominal tumors, swelling, diarrhea, lethargy, and constriction of the chest. (Rcūm 14.130)
Tin is said to be of two types: pure (khuraka) and mixed (miśraka). Among these, the pure is superior in its qualities, while the mixed is considered not beneficial.
White, soft, glossy, melting quickly, and heavy— these are the physical properties of *khuraka*.
As for the mixed types (*miśraka*), their physical properties are as follows:
Niḥśabda has hoof-marks that are indistinct, while Miśraka is dark and white.
Tin (vaṅga) is bitter and hot, dry, and slightly aggravates vāta;
it destroys diseases of fat and phlegm, kills worms, and cures urinary disorders.
Having melted [the substance] and cast it into the juice of *nirguṇḍī* mixed with *niśā*, the horn and tin are purified in three cycles; of this there is no doubt. (Rcūm 14.134)
Tin, when ground with sour buttermilk, *varṣābhū*, poison, and rock salt,
and placed inside a bitter bottle-gourd, undergoes a second purification. (Rcūm 14.135)
{The killing of tin}:
Having smeared the leaves of tin with the milk of *arka* mixed with *tāla*, one should then apply the ashes of the bark of *bodhi* and *ciñcā* and give them small *puṭa* treatments. (Rcūm 14.136)

Having crushed it, one should apply the ash; that is recommended for mercury and other substances. {The killing of tin (2):} Having melted tin in an iron pan, one should add mercury equal to one-sixteenth part [of the tin]. Rcūm 14.137.

Having given very small amounts of *alaka* from the wood of the descendant of Bharadvāja and having ground them, one should employ that ash in elixirs (*rasāyana*) and other such preparations; so it is proclaimed. (Rcūm 14.138)
One should grind tin ash, iron oxide (kānta) ash equal to that, and sky-ash (vyomabhasma) equal to that,
with water from the kanyā plant and also with the juice of nimba leaves. (Rcūm 14.139)
Then, having added the ashes of *bhūpālāvarta* in equal parts, one should thoroughly rub it together with cow's urine and water containing mineral pigments (*śilādhātu*). (Rcūm 14.140)
Then, having rubbed it with guggulu resin for eight days,
dried it, and ground it into a powder, one should combine it in equal parts.
Then, one should add roasted *barbūra* resin and the powdered seeds of *vākucī* into the vessel, having first filtered it through a cloth.
One should drink this delightful mercury-elixir (vaṅgarasāyana), equal in measure to four *vallakas*, together with the essence of turmeric ground in buttermilk. (Rcūm 14.143)
By this, the twenty types of urinary disorders (meha) are certainly destroyed.
Śāli rice, mung bean soup, fresh butter, sesame oil, paṭola,
bitter tuṇḍīra, and buttermilk are praised as wholesome and beneficial.
Pure lead melts easily, has great weight, is black when cut, and shines brightly;
it has a foul odor and is black on the outside; otherwise, it is impure.
Lead is extremely hot, unctuous, and bitter; it subdues wind, destroys the defects of urine and water, stimulates digestion, and cures *āmavāta*. (Rcūm 14.146)
For the purification of the head:
one should add powdered turmeric to a decoction of *sinduvāra* roots;
then, one should repeatedly immerse molten lead three times in the juice of *nirguṇḍī*. (Rcūm 14.147)
In this way, the *nāga* [tube] shall indeed be pure; one should not employ methods such as fainting or cracking.
One should place a pot with its opening facing downward into a horizontal-shaped furnace (*tiryagākāra-cullī*), which is a type of *bhrāṣṭrayantra*.
And one should carefully cover everything except that opening with clay;
this is called the "frying-pan" (bhrāṣṭrayantra) method, the supreme means for killing a nāga.
Regarding the "lead-killing": one should place twenty *pala*s of lead (*nāga*) into that machine called the *bhrāṣṭrayantra*, and cast a fierce fire beneath it. (Rcūm 14.149)
When the mercury has become fluid, one should cast in one *karṣa* of pure, auspicious lead;
having stirred it, one should then add each alkaline substance, one *pala* at a time.
Having separately cast alkali upon an *arjuna* tree, a mountain, a great king, a pomegranate, and a peacock, [one should proceed]. (Rcūm 14.151)
In this manner, one should cook it for twenty nights over a fierce fire,

Three parts [of each] in equal proportions, combined with an equal amount of trikaṭu (vyoṣa) and viḍaṅga (jantughna),

By melting together copper in eight parts and tin in two parts,

Spotless, glowing red when heated, and [possessing other qualities]; bell-metal (kāṃsya) is praised as being of six kinds.
That copper which is yellow when heated, hard, rough, and unable to withstand hammering is of inferior quality.
One should discard bell-metal that has lost its luster and produces a dull sound when struck.
Bell-metal (kāṃsya) is light, bitter, and hot; it is scraping, clarifies the vision, destroys worms and parasites, subdues wind and bile, and is beneficial when used as a vessel. (Rcūm 14.176)
Except for ghee alone, everything else served by humans in bronze vessels (*kāṃsya*) bestows health and happiness; it is beneficial and promotes physical well-being. (Rcūm 14.177)

It is killed by means of fragrance and *tāla* through five *puṭa* applications of *niruttha*.
Bell-metal (kāṃsya), copper (ārka), brass (rīti), iron (loha), and that which is produced from [the element] fire— these constitute vartaloha.
This very same substance is designated as "fivefold metal" (pañcaloha) by those who are experts in metals.

Vartaloha is cold, sour, and pungent; it is dry, destroys phlegm and bile, stimulates the appetite, is beneficial for the skin, kills worms, is good for the eyes, and purifies the impurities. (Rcūm 14.180)
Everything prepared in vessels made of vartaloha— whether it be grain, condiments, or soup—

{Purification of Vartaloha} Vartaloha, when cast into the urine of a horse while molten, becomes purified.

Round iron is killed by being encased with both sulphur and talc.

Gems, metals, and substances produced from cowries, oyster shells, and stones—such as hooves, horns, and thorns—which have their hard bodies reduced to ash by means of the great essences (*mahārasa*) and other agents, are indeed fit for the mercury (*sūta*). (Rcūm 14.184)
For the purpose of liquefying diamonds, I shall describe the *sattva* (essence) derived from *bhūnāga*.
The supreme splendor indeed resides in both the king of elixirs (sūtarāja) and the diamond (vajra).

One should grind purified *bhūnāga* (antimony) produced from *sattva* with the juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*, with the juice of *nimbū*, and with the fresh sap of *nirguṇḍī*, separately for three days each. (Rcūm 14.186)
Having ground that [substance] together with a fluxing agent and formed it into pills,
one should seal it firmly in a crucible and heat it strongly for two daṇḍas.

Having personally gathered cool [water] and placed it upon a cloth, one should apply *ravaka* seeds equal in size to mustard seeds, as well as grains and even dust particles, until the vessel is full.
Having smelted the *ravaka* [residue] combined with one-twelfth part of *arka*, one should proceed;
by means of that, one may perform the liquefaction of diamonds and other substances as desired. (Rcūm 14.189)
This is declared to be the essence of khara, an unsurpassed elixir;
it is certain that the essence is produced within two, three, or even a single crucible.
Having taken four *prastha* measures each of the "earth-snakes" (*bhujaṅgama*) produced from gold, silver, copper, iron, and magnetite, which arise from the earth; 14.191.
Having washed [the wound] with water from the night-lily and also with cool water,
one should apply [medicine] to a peacock, a hero, or a cock that has fasted.
Then, having caused it to circulate gradually, one should collect its excrement;
having ground it together with alkaline substances and acids, one should dry it in the hot sun. (Rcūm 14.193)
Then, having placed it in a crucible and roasted it, one should prepare ink;
this ink, combined with the fluxing agents and thoroughly ground, [is used]. (Rcūm 14.194)
Having sealed it within the crucible, one should heat it for two ghaṭikās; once the crucible has cooled, one should extract the *khoṭa* and grind it. (Rcūm 14.195)
Having quickly washed the fragments and carefully collected them,
one should blow upon them like a goldsmith’s measure, and having produced the sound, one should apply it.

The *sattva* arising from *bhūnāga*, declared by the illustrious Somadeva as the most excellent, should be given in a measure of one *pāda* along with two *śāṇas* of gold; with that, one should have a ring made.

Anointing with the water washed from it destroys all poisons arising from mobile and immobile beings, eye disease, colic, diseases of the root [of the body], ear ailments, and the afflictions caused by childbirth and planetary influences. (Rcūm 14.197)
The extraction of *aṅkola* oil is now described; it was employed by the illustrious Devasūnu, the great minister of Puṇyaśloka, in the preparation of mercury-ash and other compounds. (Rcūm 14.198)
Having ground the seeds of old *Aṅkola* until they form a thick paste, one should place an *āḍhaka* measure of it into a jar, seal it, and [set it aside]. (Rcūm 14.199)
And one should insert an iron rod through the hole at the bottom of the jar into a well-formed pit that is one and a half cubits in depth and width.
There, having placed a lead vessel into a small pit and having secured the cloth, one should perform the sealing of the joints.
Thereafter, one should fill the cavity up to the neck with the laddis;
after six months, one should collect that oil contained within a lead vessel.
Those stones from the earth that have been thoroughly saturated with that *aṅkola* oil,
when washed and thrown into a well, will burn for a long time at night. (Rcūm 14.203)
Anointed with that and spoken over in the same manner, the seed-syllable certainly arises;
the mercury is bound and killed by this oil, without a doubt. (Rcūm 14.204)
Indeed, if oil-cake produced from chickpeas has been kept in hot oil for exactly one month,
and a fourth part of it is consumed, it will cause purging sixty times.
Thereafter, buttermilk and boiled rice should be given as wholesome diet for the pacification of the purgation;
at the end of a fortnight, one should indeed induce purging again with half a *dālikā* dose, just as before.
Then, with one-third of the dālī and half of the powder, after that,
by means of purgation once every fortnight, all skin diseases (kuṣṭha) are destroyed.
All diseases curable by emetics are destroyed without a doubt; all diseases curable by emetics, and white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*) in particular. (Rcūm 14.208)
Mercury, purified by a mere drop of *aṅkola* oil and measured at the size of a *guñjā* seed, should be rubbed with the leaf of the *ahilatā* creeper and consumed along with that leaf. (Rcūm 14.209)
At that very moment, it indeed produces a blazing and fierce fire,
and it makes even the man who serves it like a voracious wolf.
This aṅkola oil indeed promotes the growth of the body and the skin;
by anointing with this oil, white leprosy (śvetakuṣṭha) is destroyed.
This oil from the *aṅkolaka* tree is declared to be of great potency;
like clarified butter, it becomes solidified, and all of that is so described.

{The Procedure for Distilling Aṅkola Oil (2)} Having removed the husks from aṅkola seeds and slightly crushed them, one should place them in a *vidyādhara* apparatus and cook them slowly for half a *daṇḍa*. Rcūm_14.213 //
One should place the oil collected from the upper part of the vessel onto a betel leaf;
having rubbed mercury the size of a *guñjā* seed into it, one should swallow it along with the leaf. (Rcūm 14.214) [Aṅkola oil: medicinal use]

One should administer this potent digestive stimulant, which pulverizes even the heaviest substances; it destroys the eight types of *gulma*, loss of appetite, splenic disorders, and one's own diseases.
It quickly cures all forms of leprosy beginning with *śvitra*, anemia, fever, colic, diseases of the root-organ (genitals), edema, dyspnea, and cough in men. (Rcūm 14.215)

{The Procedure for Extracting Aṅkola Oil (3)} Having crushed the aṅkola seeds and made them fine with warm water, one should place them in a goatskin bag and immediately remove their husks. Rcūm 14.216.
Then, when the alkali has been placed in the vessel, one should indeed add water;
into that, one should throw a crushed root of *tilaparṇī* in the proper measure. (Rcūm 14.217)
After it has stayed there for two nights, others should pour it into a vessel;

The husks of the chickpeas remain there for three months;
from that, one should indeed give a quarter-measure to a leper at the first [stage].
Immediately after that, he should be made to vomit thirty times;

In the *Rasārṇava*, [the subject] was not fully revealed by fifteen [chapters], which are like oceans of mercury;
now, with eighteen [chapters], I shall describe the action of the king of mercury. (Rcūm 15.1)
The essence of all medicines, beginning with nectar, is established within mercury;
O mortals, practice it together with each other in order to become immortal.

Mercury bestows longevity and adamantine strength upon men; gold grants beauty of limb and complexion; mica provides the power that intoxicates the intellect; copper imparts fierce hunger; silver brings peace to the eyes; and this lovely iron cures all diseases. Thus the glorious mercury is perfected as a healer of the body and of metals. (Rcūm 15.3)

At the beginning of the kalpa, when the sexual union of Śiva and Śivā had commenced out of mutual affection and a desire to conquer one another— an act that caused the agitation of the three worlds— Rcūm_15.4.
Sent by the gods, Agni was dispatched to prevent their dalliance,
desiring the birth of their son in order to slay the demon Tāraka.
He beheld Agni, who had assumed the form of a pigeon in a cave of the Himalayas;
agitated by his loss of wings, he gazed upon him with a smile born of passion.
Seeing that, Śambhu was ashamed; ceasing from the act of love, he then caught with one hand his own emitted seed.
It was cast into the mouth of the fire and fell into the Gaṅgā;
and it was cast out by the Gaṅgā herself, who was being intensely scorched.
Therefore, the minerals, possessing superior qualities and equal to nectar, were produced;
indeed, that which fell from the hand of Śiva became mercury.
By that [process], they became immortal, ageless, and the best of the thirty-three gods;
and from its impurity were produced the eight constituent elements (dhātus).
That which fell from the mouth of the Purifier indeed became the elixir;
for it was consumed by the lords of the nāgas with the desire to conquer old age and death.
But that which had fallen with reverence was drunk by the one with the serpent’s face;
indeed, it fell into a well a hundred yojanas deep.
Slightly yellowish within and rough, that *sūta* (mercury) produces strength and iron.
[The method for obtaining mercury with naked women:

And where that path has many pits dug in it, the King of Alchemists stands repeatedly; indeed, he is thus brought there by the people living in that place. (Rcūm 15.13)
As mercury was being carried by the wind along the Ganges due to its weight,
it fell indeed in a distant land; that region is known as Pārada.
O Sūta, when that [mercury] is rubbed with that [substance] according to the procedure for precipitation (pātanā), it is brought forth; it should be known as *gada-pārada* (the mercury of disease).
Thus, having understood that the fourfold manifestation—the auspicious and Śiva-like great light arising from Sūta—is of this nature, a person is not afflicted by diseases. (Rcūm 15.16)
Rasendra and Rasa—both of these are perfected elixirs (siddharasa);
the other two are to be accomplished (sādhya), arising after a long time through the application of specific locations such as the earth and so forth.
Mercury is called *rasa* because it tastes (*rasanāt*) old age, death, misfortune, and disease;
this is indeed according to the meaning of the verbal root *ras*, "to taste. (Rcūm 15.18)
Because it produces the perfection of a body made of gold, it is therefore considered *sūta* (mercury); because it enables one to cross the ocean of disease, it is called *pārada*. (Rcūm 15.19)
When that which is being purified by precipitations has one quarter remaining while three quarters have gone to destruction, it is known as *pādarasa*. (Rcūm 15.20)
Thus was mercury born, the destroyer of mortal death and disease.
Having seen humans by their power, equal in strength and lifespan to the gods.
Requested by Indra, Rudra endowed that nectar with twelve defects; even without prior purification, it was nevertheless a bestower of success.
The defects of mercury are impurity, dross, poison, fire, intoxication, and pride; their results are fainting, death, constant burning, boils, and dizziness of the head. (Rcūm 15.23)
The seven sheaths (kañcukas) of mercury are those arising from earth, stone, water, copper, iron, lead,
and tin; by means of these, mercury becomes like poison.
The coverings (kañcukas) gradually produce leprosy, numbness, affliction by wind, burning sensation, constriction of the throat, insanity, and great colic. (Rcūm 15.25)
If a physician should administer these five and seven defects inherent in the juices without having first eliminated them, he becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
Having removed these twelve great defects, one should give the juice;
he shall obtain immense merit and immeasurable, great fame.

Eighteen refinements (*saṃskāra*) are declared: sweating (*svedana*), rubbing (*mardana*), fainting (*mūrchā*), reviving (*utthāpana*), falling (*pāta*), restraining (*rodha*), and regulating (*niyama*); inflaming (*proddīpana*), that which arises from the morsel (*grāsaja*), measuring (*māna*), moving (*cāraṇa*), internal and external liquefaction (*garbhabāhyajanitadruti*), its digestion (*tajjāraṇā*), coloring (*rāga*), stretching (*sāraṇaka*), the procedure of circulation (*parikramavidhi*), piercing (*vedha*), and thereafter, service (*sevana*). (Rcūm 15.28)
Then, according to the procedure prescribed by Nandin, the thorough purification of the defects and the coverings is revealed exactly as it is.
If the impurity (sūta) is less than five palas, it has been purified but yields little fruit;
above ten palas, it attains complete purification.
Through sweating, rubbing, and fainting, and by means of seven upward sublimations,
the king of mercury (rasarāja) becomes completely freed from all defects. (Rcūm 15.31)
Sweating, massaging, and likewise submerging it seven times—Bhāskara has declared that this brings about accomplishment and produces excellent qualities. (Rcūm 15.32)
"Dineśvara says that [the practitioner] is purified by means of massage, sweating, and renunciation;
however, according to the opinion of Bhāluki, purification occurs through the upward and downward movements of the breath."

Sweating, rubbing, fainting, rising, falling, suppression, and restraint— these seven are considered the pure [processes] of the king of elixirs (sūtarāja), as determined by the venerable Lord Govinda. (Rcūm 15.34)
Now, the purification of the king of essences (*rasarāja*), which destroys all defects without exception, is proclaimed according to the method taught by Śrīnandin. (Rcūm 15.35)

{1. The process of steaming (svedana-saṃskāra):} The mercury, having been steamed for three days in a *dolāyantra* with *kāñjika* [sour gruel] along with radish, fire (*agni*), pungent mustard, ginger, and the three acrids (*vyoṣaka*) in sixteen parts of its own weight, becomes free from impurities. (Rcūm 15.36)

{2. Mardana-saṃskāra} The mercury should be rubbed for three days with burnt wool, house-soot, lotus, and mustard seeds, along with jaggery and brick powder, each in a sixteenth part [of the mercury], in order to pacify its fiery nature. (Rcūm 15.37)
As each portion is repeatedly consumed, the mercury must indeed be rubbed with these very same medicinal herbs, for it is thereby rendered pure and takes on color. (Rcūm 15.38)

{3. Mūrchana} By rubbing the mercury with a decoction of lakucha combined with vyoṣa and saubhāgya for three days, the mercury becomes "mūrchita" (coagulated) and releases its difficult-to-restrain intoxication. Rcūm 15.39.
When mercury is kept for three days with *saubhāgya*, *triphalā*, *śyāmā*, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* along with *kāñjika*, it completely abandons its own poison. (Rcūm 15.40)
Boiled with the juices of *sarpākṣikā*, *kākamācī*, and *uṣaṇa*, and then brought back to the surface, it quickly removes *darpa*; thus is the purification of the *doṣas*. (Rcūm 15.41)
Remaining in a place sheltered from the wind, one should consume the liquid with alkaline or sour substances and warm water;
this destroys its potency by neutralizing its coldness. (Rcūm 15.42)
Mercury,
rubbed for a day with yellow orpiment, green vitriol, and *luṅga* juice,
and then washed and ground with fermented rice-water (*kāñjika*), abandons its earthly sheath (*bhūkañcuka*). (Rcūm 15.43)
The mercury, processed with the natural juices of *adrikāñcuka*, *girikarṇī*,
and *jayantī* three times, truly casts off its own covering consisting of the *girijā* [mica]. (Rcūm 15.44)
Boiled for three days with a decoction of *guḍa*, *guggulu*, and *nimba*,
mercury (*sūta*) sheds its watery sheath (*jalakañcuka*), which is the source of many defects. (Rcūm 15.45)

Having rubbed [the copper] with a tin coating, white salt, fresh *kataka* fruit, and lime, and having then raised it up and washed it with warm cow urine, one should discard the tin coating from the copper.
The mercury, when rubbed with the juices of *kāravelly*, *karkoṭī*,
and iron armor (*ayaḥkañcuka*), shall cast off its iron coating just as a fickle person abandons friendship.
Mercury, processed as a copper paste with lead and tin, when dropped into a *pātanāyantra* (falling apparatus),
will quickly shed its coating derived from lead and tin. (Rcūm 15.48)

Having smeared the interior of a vessel—which contains water—on its upper rim with a paste of tin, mercury, realgar, sal-ammoniac, drumstick (*śigru*), black mustard, and collyrium, one should release [the mercury] all around by means of a mild fire; for then the tin-encasement (*kañculikā*) indeed leaves behind its tin-like covering. (Rcūm 15.49)
Thus the charioteer, possessing the luster of a flickering streak of lightning, was struck down; and from that, he was released from the coils of the serpent. And then this occurred: (Rcūm 15.50).
Whenever the mercury (sūta) should become afflicted by the indigestion of its "food" (grāsa),
it must then and there be precipitated (pātana) by this very method.

Mercury (sūta), having been subjected to refinement through processes beginning with sweating and ending with precipitation, becomes weak in potency; therefore, one should perform the nourishing rite (*āpyāyana*). (Rcūm 15.52)
A charioteer stationed for three days upon a salt-laden horse provided with water, having regained his strength once more, would not remain impotent but would become powerful. (Rcūm 15.53)
After [the preliminary] rules, Bhāluki taught the methods of fomentation (sveda) and its cessation;
he was determined to make his mouth capable of consuming all metals. (Rcūm 15.54)
Having placed the liquid in a vessel set over glowing coals, one should heat it;
when it becomes variegated by means of a sixteenth part [of the additive], that is considered here to be *svedana*. (Rcūm 15.55)
Endowed with power and superior in qualities, he shall indeed remove all diseases; there is no doubt that the bestowing of fruits occurs with speed. (Rcūm 15.56)
Likewise, through renunciation, [the state] arises together with alkaline, sour, and salty tastes;
indeed, this occurs in the manner specified in the fourth chapter regarding taste. (Rcūm 15.57)
It possesses hunger, pervasiveness, intensity, the quality of impelling speed, the capacity to remove all diseases, and the state of having abandoned defects. (Rcūm 15.58)

The digestive activation (*dīpana-saṃskāra*) of mercury is achieved by means of black pepper, lotus, *asurī*, drumstick tree, earth, sulphur, and borax, combined with binding agents, through sweating for three days. (Rcūm 15.59)
And by means of the *dīpanīya* group of drugs specified in the ninth chapter, one should effect the stimulation of the digestive fire (*rasa*); that brings about the highest benefit. (Rcūm 15.60)

When mercury, combined with gold in an eighteenfold proportion, has been heated, it indeed acquires a mouth [orifice] by means of alkaline and acidic substances free from defects, thereby becoming capable of consuming [other metals]. (Rcūm 15.61)
The *rākṣasavaktra* [preparation] is prepared by combining gold that is twice the amount of the copper used,
along with citric acid (*cukra*) and *cūlikā-lavaṇa*. (Rcūm 15.62)
One should indeed rub it with the alkaline water of chickpeas and the juice of *rājanimbu* within a heated mortar, using great strength.
For twenty-one days, eating at every watch day after day,
one will undoubtedly become a man with the face of a rākṣasa and a devourer of all things.
Indeed, the eighteen activities of men do not succeed through alchemy alone,
without good fortune, austerity, and the grace of the Lord.

When the elixir, which destroys leucoderma, is released by the alchemist—endowed with all various methods and delightful refinements—it brings about a purification of manifold virtues that is easy to accomplish, as described by Nandin; this the lord of the foremost city, Somadeva, proclaims when combined with *pathyā*. (Rcūm 15.66)

Having bound mercury for three days with the three alkalis (trikṣāra) combined with the five salts (paṭupañcaka) and sour substances (amla), along with khaṃ, lavaṇa, and sulphur, inside a crucible made from bāhlīka, asura, viśva, and piṇḍa, one should then place it in a sand-bath (sandhāna).

For three days, one should cook it over a mild fire in the apparatus known as the *dolāyantra* (swinging furnace); thus freed from impurities, the mercury becomes equal to the essence of nectar (*sudhārasa*) and grants success even without the need for medicinal diets.

However, in this matter, the measurement of the mustard seed, the Viśva, and the asafoetida is to be understood through the teacher’s oral instruction; otherwise, it does not yield the intended result. (Rcūm 15.68)
Lead and tin are two great defects that are difficult to conquer even by millions of purifications;
since they are removed by precipitation (*pātana*), it is considered the "greatly purified mercury. (Rcūm 15.69)
By ten applications of the process of falling (*pātanā*), the odor arising from lead and mercury is destroyed; the mercury will then no longer possess defective qualities.
Pātanās performed according to the prescribed method on mercury—neither less than ten times nor more than a hundred times—are said to produce great qualities. (Rcūm 15.71)

Through the processes of precipitation (*pātana*), mercury (*rasendra*) attains great excellence, friendship with fire (*śikhin*), equal potency even against minor diseases, the quality of an elixir (*rasāyana*), and great majestic power. (Rcūm 15.72)
Rcūm, 16.

Now, therefore, the meritorious process of digestion (*jāraṇā*), which brings about the perfection of mercury and is easy to perform with readily available materials, having been previously practiced, is now described. Rcūm_16.1.
In this [practice], he who offers a leafless morsel to the mercury is satisfied by Gaurī’s Lord as much as by the gift of the three worlds. (Rcūm 16.2)
He who seeks to bind the mercury without first cutting its wings is a person of wicked intellect; through attachment to sense-objects, he desires liberation by means of mere seeds. (Rcūm 16.3)
Without the essence of the cloud (ghanasattva), there is nothing else that can sever the wings of mercury.
With its wings clipped and its path obstructed, the *rasa* becomes impassioned and is bound.
Even *niścandra* leaf-ash, once processed with mercury, should indeed be made to circulate;
when it has been divided sevenfold and processed, one should then cause it to be vomited up. (Rcūm 16.5)

Even when its constituent parts have decayed, if the mercury is joined with various appropriate adjuncts (yogas), it quickly bestows the specific result for each respective disease; for this reason, mercury is exceedingly powerful.
That in which the essence is abundant and the seed is swift in the process of digesting mercury (rasajāraṇa) is declared to be excellent, possessing eightfold qualities.
The final element of Śiva and Śivā is abhraka (mica) and likewise pārada (mercury);
through the union of these two, where is death for men, and where is poverty?
Mercury indeed does not consume pure *abhraka-sattva*; even if it were consumed, it would do so with extreme difficulty and would not pervade all its limbs. (Rcūm 16.9)

Therefore, it is proper that [the mercury] be combined with other metals and with *dhātu* and *sattva* substances; when prepared with the alkali of mica (*abhraka*), it alone bestows perfection of the body. (Rcūm 16.10)
The unification [of all things] by means of the cloud is described as the melting of metals.
With equal parts of lac, molasses, resin of the *sarja* tree, *dhātakī*, *guggulu*, and borax,
ground with breast milk, even metals that are difficult to fuse are brought into union. (Rcūm 16.12)
When combined with the powder of *tāpya* (calamine), a pair of metals will certainly merge;
by blowing [the furnace] two or three times, they will surely become like milk and water. (Rcūm 16.13)

The essence of mica (abhrasattva), when combined with an equal portion of the essence of copper pyrite (tāpyasattva) and subjected to smelting until only the mica remains, becomes easy to digest through the process of *jāraṇā*. (Rcūm 16.14)

Alternatively, when twice the amount of *tāpya* (sulphate of iron) has been processed within the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), that which is thus internally digested quickly brings about the perfection of mercury. (Rcūm 16.15)
In this way, mercury should process the essence of mica with tin and lead;
that essence is noble for the alchemy of metals, yet it is censured for the attainment of the perfection of the body.
These two, nāga and vaṅga, are extremely impure and possess great defects;
indeed, when consumed in excess, they quickly cause diseases. (Rcūm 16.17)

Having melted that essence by means of *garbhadruti* through a cloth, it is combined with the *ravaka*; then, it is thoroughly rubbed with the *raseśvara* contained in a copper vessel using a tenth part [of the former]. (Rcūm 16.18)
Pure mercury, combined with one sixty-fourth part of that [substance] and mixed with alkali,
acid, and salt, should be heated in a mortar for three days.
Having washed it with hot infusions and placed it in a glass jar,
one should apply *viḍa* salt above and below it, amounting to one-eighth part of the mercury.
Having placed birch bark upon its face, one should wrap it with a single thread;
then, having wrapped the casket with cloth, one should perform the rite according to the procedure for a swinging mechanism.
One should steam it for three days with all sour substances, cow’s urine, and fermented rice-gruel;
then, having placed it in a vessel made of iron, stone, or shell, [one should proceed].
Having washed it with hot infusions and removed that liquid with a cloth, one should dry it and, after rubbing the adhered substance with the hand for a moment, [extract] the mercury. (Rcūm 16.23)
If all the juice were to come out by squeezing a cloth folded fourfold very tightly,
then the morsel would likewise dissolve instantly within the womb.
Failure of the dissolution within the womb;
repetition.
When there is still a remainder of the morsel, one should again cause it to sweat with *viḍa* salt;
thus, having diligently administered three more morsels, [one should proceed]. (Rcūm 16.25)
When sixty mouthfuls remain after the miscarriage of the fetus,
one should employ the machine known as the "tortoise" (kacchapa), as described in the fifth chapter.
One should cook the mercury combined with *viḍa* salt using a *puṭa* method over a mild fire and with stones;
then, having extracted it from the apparatus, one should wash it again with warm *kāñjika*. (Rcūm 16.27)
One should rub it for the duration of one watch (yāma) according to the procedure described by Mardana;
thus, being rendered stainless, it takes up the dyes in order to achieve purity. (Rcūm 16.28)
Therefore, mercury should be diligently triturated with each morsel and in each crucible;
thus thoroughly ground, it becomes capable of destroying diseases. (Rcūm 16.29)
For the process of *cāraṇa* (roaming/mobilization) of mercury,
the substances to be processed are combined with *bhūsarjikā*, salts, and *kāñcī*,
and then treated with *kāñjika* (sour gruel).
All substances such as *sattva* and *upala*, when combined with excellent copper leaves and treated with acid, are declared suitable for the process of *cāraṇā*.

When processed for seven days in *kāñjika* with one part each of *rambhā*, *paṭu*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *lāṅgalikā*, half a part of *niśā*, and one part each of *śobhāñjana*, *aṅghri*, and *kharasañjarikā*, this mercury (*sūta*) indeed devours a mass of moistened iron. (Rcūm 16.31)

This *viḍa* salt, having been infused ten times with the four alkalies, the six salts, and liquid acids, is prescribed for the purpose of extracting the internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) of gold and other metals, as well as the essence of mica (*abhraka*). (Rcūm 16.32)

The *daṇḍadhārī*, whose impurities have been removed, having consumed five *śāṇas* of the essence born from space (*sattva*) in the fire of sixty-fold alkaline salt, truly proceeds with speed through the stages of *sāra* and *dhūmāyana*; he is declared by the sages to be equal to that [state] and is known by the name *daṇḍadhārī*. (Rcūm 16.33)
When the mercury is born conjoined with Garbhadrutī, a blade of grass thrown [into it] remains fixed;
this mercury, which holds the staff upright, is considered a Daṇḍadhārī.

If a mortal indeed consumes mercury in which mica has been fully digested (abhrajīrṇa), measuring one *guñjā* daily for a full month, according to the lunar regimen (*śaśadharaparipāṭyā*) through the method of gradual ingestion, he shall become happy, healthy, and live for a hundred years, freed from the defects of old age. (Rcūm 16.35)
He too shall be free from wrinkles and grey hair, and likewise free from disease.
Indeed, the great elixir (mahārasa) should be applied by means of this or that specific yoga.
The Khasattva produces intense hunger and removes the multitude of diseases. (Rcūm 16.37)
The second morsel is mercury; having digested double the amount of mica, the second morsel should be administered according to the eighth-part method.
In this manner, the movement and the melting are likewise conceived as before.
The process of *jāraṇa* (digestion) should also be performed using the apparatus named *kūrma*;
the *kūrma* apparatus is specified within the fifth chapter.

When the essence (*sattva*) produced from the ore, measuring one *pala*, has been subjected to twenty *puṭas* in mercury and has undergone forty cycles of sublimation (*cāra*), it becomes digested (*jarita*).
When the excellent nectar was twice as thick with milk-sediment and the clouds were intensely rumbling, it was scattered forth in the form of a liquid essence accompanied by thundering sounds.

The king of mercury (sūtarāja), having been digested with double its weight of mica (gagana) and consumed here daily in a dose of one guñjā for the duration of a year, [yields its medicinal benefits].
They bestow an excellent kalpa equal to that of the ocean and Kandarpa, as well as a long life of one thousand years.
This mercury, the size of a *guñjā* seed, when treated with the water of the sun (*arkavāri*), cures all diseases such as consumption (*kṣaya*), even those that are difficult to cure. (Rcūm 16.42)

By this sequential method, the third dose of mercury that has been processed with the three qualities of sulfur (triguṇābhra) should be administered within the intermediate machine described in the fifth chapter.
Having suppressed [the breath], the practitioner of alchemy should perform the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) upon the substance.
{3. Grasping =) leech-binding =) upward-throwing =) wing-clipping}

If that mercury, which has the form of a leech, is endowed with full density and swallows [the substance] in thirty equal turns, then that mercury, having its entire body deposited [within], emerges again; yet that *sūta* (mercury) is like one whose wings have been clipped within its own vessel.

The mercury that has been produced, its form nourished by the consumption of three times its weight of sublimated mica, reduced to ashes, and mixed with one barley-corn measure of diamond-ash and other ingredients— if a mortal constantly partakes of this, he indeed becomes possessed of a divine body and may live for a full three hundred celestial kalpas. (Rcūm 16.45)
Having been empowered with the ashes of burnt [substances] according to the measure of two *siddhārtha* seeds, it destroys all diseases of the patient within seven recitations. (Rcūm 16.46)
The fourth morsel:
bound or reduced to ashes by men measured by *siddhārtha* seeds, combined with *vyoṣa*, *vella*, and honey, and consumed for four months. (Rcūm 16.47)
It certainly makes a man free from wrinkles and grey hair, full of the pride of a rutting elephant, like Kandarpa incarnate. (Rcūm 16.48)
A man whose form conquers the pride of Kandarpa and who is free from the torment of sin shall live for thirty-eight hundred years in this world; moreover,
through his service, he shall delight in the company of hundreds of women.
This mercury, merely by touch, effortlessly reduces even the most excellent and thick iron to a state of bondage;
it certainly brings about delight.
A mortal may raise the dead by merely casting a glance with his eyes;
having smelled [the mantra], he swiftly destroys all diseases—of this there is no doubt. (Rcūm 16.51)
{The fifth morsel} And thus the fifth morsel should be offered as an eighth part;
staying in the vessel and heated by fire, it does not depart by any means whatsoever. (Rcūm 16.52)
"He is said to have his wings clipped; he is liberated from all evil qualities.
This very Sūtra, when practiced for three months in a quantity equal to a mustard seed," Rcūm 16.53.

When the lord of mercury (sūtendra), which destroys all diseases, comes into contact with the orifices along with the gods through the mere act of smelling [the powder] made of viḍaṅga, triphalā, and honey, [it grants liberation]. (Rcūm 16.54)
These qualities of rasa have been specified by those who discourse on rasa;
all these qualities are truly proclaimed by Bhairava.
The sixth morsel, weighing four *palas*, should be administered as before;
having digested the sixfold *abhraka* (mica), it arises with qualities equal to nectar. (Rcūm 16.56)
A dose the size of a mustard seed, combined with sugar and candied sugar, taken for one month,
produces a body that lives for a hundred years.
Bound and placed within the mouth, this indeed produces the state of Khecarī;
it wards off even thousands of divine weapons.

Possessing the strength of ten elephants, glorious, and honored in all worlds; properly colored, refined, and endowed with the process of penetration (*krāmaṇa*), it certainly becomes a "piercer of ten million" (*koṭivedhī*), unbound, and a piercer even through a spear (*kuntavedhaka*). (Rcūm 16.59)
On this earth, no one is capable of describing the qualities of this aesthetic flavor (rasa);
only Śrī Somadeva or Śaṅkara truly knows its power.
{The seventh morsel} The seventh morsel should be given through the application of two sessions;
one should perform its liquefaction and digestion as previously prescribed. (Rcūm 16.61)
This elixir, reduced to ashes and consumed in a dose the size of a nit,
along with Triphalā and a piece of pomegranate, transforms a human being in half a month.
Richly endowed with a form of ten million Cupids, possessing prowess equal to Śakra,
worshipped by all the gods, and having a lifespan of a kalpa according to the Vedas.
He possesses consciousness and is endowed with knowledge of the three times;
he is capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, and he can delight hundreds of divine women—
of this there is no doubt, for such is the word of Nandin.

When this [mercury] is colored, activated, and endowed with the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), it will certainly become a penetrator by means of smoke; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (Rcūm 16.65)
{The Eighth Bite}:
Thereafter, the eighth bite should be administered with equal portions.
When the mercury (rasendra) has been processed through eight qualities and [purified] like a cloud by hundreds of bellows, it becomes the "eightfold essence" (*aṣṭaguṇasattva*). 16.66.
Even when blown upon, it does not move at all, nor is anything whatsoever diminished;
this is the one known by the name Agnisaha, from whom an immeasurable multitude of virtues arises.
Rich with light beyond counting, possessing wondrous heroism and great strength—this mercury (rasendra), the size of a nit, when consumed with sugar, [bestows these qualities]. (Rcūm 16.68)
In a single application, it makes a man beautiful in all his limbs, possessing great sovereignty equal to Rudra and valor equal to Viṣṇu. (Rcūm 16.69)
He possessed a beautiful luster equal to the moon, a majesty like that of the sun,
a lifespan equal to the four-faced Brahmā, and eyes like those of Tārkṣya.
When properly colored, infused, and endowed with the process of transference, he becomes a piercer by sound; like Śiva, he faces in all directions.
Even by Manthānabhairava and others, with their hundreds of millions of extensive [treatises],

and even by tens of millions [of verses] regarding the great qualities of this Rasa in its entirety, it is impossible to praise it fully— just as the waves in the ocean cannot exhaustively describe the ocean itself. (Rcūm 16.72)
Due to the practitioner's lack of faith, the lack of grace from Śaṅkara, ignorance regarding the medicinal herbs as they truly are, and the improper gathering of the remedies; Rcūm 16.73.

In the Kali age, the alchemist does not achieve success because of his lack of thorough knowledge regarding the fragrant substances (gandhavatī), because he employs improper means, and because he acts with doubt.

Having the characteristic of severed wings, unable to fall upwards or downwards, with its path obstructed and devoid of impurities, the mercury becomes like a withered cloud; it is called "severed-winged" (chinnapakṣa). (Rcūm 16.75)
{Mercury:: "age" according to abhra} When digested with an equal amount of mica it is a child; with double the mica it is a youth;
when it has consumed four times the mica it is a young man; and one who has digested six times the mica is [an elder]. (Rcūm 16.76)

The "grown" (vṛddha) and the "exceedingly grown" (ativṛddha) abhraka possess eight qualities; however, the "young" (bāla), when prepared through processing, brings about the perfection of the body and the metals. (Rcūm 16.77)

When the mercury (sūta) reaches the state of being ground into a paste, it becomes a maker of bodily strength; when the mercury is processed with gold, it becomes youthful and bestows spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
When it has reached the state of ash, mercury becomes old;
when it is excessively old, mercury, once placed in the mouth, bestows all accomplishments. (Rcūm 16.79)
In this regard, neither the infant nor the youth is intended for the practice of *rasāyana*;
rather, it is for the young man, for the purpose of destroying disease and likewise for the protection of the body. (Rcūm 16.80)
Both the *vṛddha* and the *ativṛddha* [types of] iron ore serve as the body and the metal; when processed with *jīrṇābhra*, it becomes slightly capable of withstanding fire suddenly. (Rcūm 16.81)
When processed with double the amount of mica, the lord of mercury does not undergo the state of fuming;
when combined with triple the amount of mica, it attains a firmness like that of curd.
The mercury that effects the perfection of the body, when processed four times in the void (vyoma), bestows longevity;
however, the mercury in which sixfold mica has been digested bestows the lifespan of Brahmā.
When seven-fold processed mica is consumed, it bestows longevity along with vigor;
when eight-fold processed mica is digested, it grants the lifespan of Śaṅkara.
[Measures for the indigestion of morsels.]
Having caused the undigested essence of the morsel to fall down, one should ignite it again and cause it to be digested.
Then, having prepared the seeds of copper, iron, magnetite, silver, and gold, one should cause them to undergo complete digestion.
The liquefaction and digestion [of mercury] with copper should be performed according to the method described for mica.
The *rañjanī* is said to be for mercury; it effects the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of sharp, beautiful, and solar [substances]. (Rcūm 16.86)

One should diligently treat it with various alkaline, acidic, and sudorific applications; indeed, copper that has been processed through mercury three times over becomes reduced to a hundredth part when spread upon cinnabar.
Through *jāraṇā*, the mercury becomes like a molten ruby;
by means of copper, the powerful mercury attains a prowess equal to the sun.
This elixir, though entirely consumed by the three humors, is fully capable of restoring life.
If this elixir is consumed daily for a month in a dose equal to a *guñjā* seed,
it will make a mortal as powerful as Bhīma, even in the strength of his arms when he has finished eating.
With *tīkṣṇaloha*, mercury undergoes *krāmaṇa*, *jāraṇa*, *vedha*, *rañjana*, and the production of velocity.
From a dose of *tīkṣṇa* iron that has been processed one hundred times with *hiṅgula*, [the desired state] arises in the mercury.

Mercury (tīkṣṇasūta) processed with equal proportions [of other metals] and consumed in a dose of one-quarter part for two months makes a mortal free from the fear of death, endowed with great strength, destroyed of disease, and possessed of excellent progeny. (Rcūm 16.91)

When mercury is processed with a sharp [metal] in ratios of two, three, four, or five times [the quantity], by whom here can its progressively increasing qualities be described? {Mercury:: digestion::}
Likewise, mercury that has been digested by *kāntaloha* becomes ten million times more effective in its qualities.
Twice as radiant when processed, mercury destroys and removes the affliction of disease in an instant; it turns away the gaping mouth of illness.
This sovereign mercury (*rasendra*) produces wrinkles, gray hair, and deformities, brings about suffering, poverty, and death, yet also bestows excellent sons and virtuous conduct.
{Mercury:: jāraṇa:: with gold} [This is done] by one-quarter part, by half a part, by three-quarters, by an equal part, by two parts, by three parts, and likewise by five parts. (Rcūm 16.94)

A great mercury that has been processed a hundred times with *ākṣika* and has digested gold becomes worthy of worship by the three worlds, its arising equal to that of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).

Vid salt, prepared by soaking and washing sulphur with cow’s urine mixed with the alkaline ash of the five parts of the *mūlaka* radish, causes the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of gold and other metals. (Rcūm 16.96)
Gold that has been thoroughly processed by mercury is highly venerable for all its potencies; when consumed in a dose of one *māṣa* for a single day of the Sun (one day), it bestows all powers.
It destroys severe old age, liberates one from many kinds of diseases, and produces a fierce fire that is as firm and powerful as a wolf's belly.
It undoubtedly destroys the infertility of a woman and all incurable diseases of a man; it makes a man a possessor of a hundredfold wealth. (Rcūm 16.98)
